articles.title: Alexandra of CABS: our fight is against illegal hunting
articles.body: Interview: Shireen Bou Rafoul Alexandra watches birds during fieldwork in Lebanon. From watching migration routes to documenting offences, CABS volunteer Alexandra discusses her field experience in Lebanon and Europe, and the patience, risks and cooperation involved in protecting birds. In this interview, she explains why she distinguishes responsible hunters from people who break the law. Alexandra, please introduce yourself and tell us how your work protecting birds and volunteering with CABS began. I’m Alexandra, I’m 33, and I have been volunteering with CABS for more than three years. I studied conservation biology in Vienna, where I explored species protection in depth and developed a particular love of birds. In my main job, I work with BirdLife Austria on combating the illegal persecution of birds of prey in Austria, so I am involved professionally as well as through volunteering. You are German, live in Austria and take part in field operations in different countries. What keeps you going? My strongest motivation is to do my part to stop people destroying nature. I believe we should stand up for the things that matter to us. Of course, this work can sometimes be very frustrating and exhausting, but I draw strength from the people fighting alongside me. Celebrating small and large victories together, and giving each other courage and support, is something beautiful. What is your role within CABS, and what are your main responsibilities during field campaigns? As a volunteer field activist, my main task is to monitor hunting areas, identify and document illegal hunting, and gather strong evidence, such as photographs and videos, that can be handed to the competent authorities. The material we collect is also used in our international awareness campaigns and media activities. Alexandra documents observations with a camera during fieldwork in Lebanon. What does monitoring and documenting hunting offences actually involve on the ground? It means staying alert all the time. It takes patience, calm and perhaps a little stubbornness. Giving up quickly is not an option. You also need a high tolerance for frustration. You spend a lot of time sitting, watching and waiting; then events can suddenly move very fast, and you have to be ready to act. You have taken part in field operations in Lebanon. What impressed or surprised you most about hunting and bird migration there? Bird migration here is truly astonishing. Because of Lebanon’s unique position between the sea and the mountains, it is a very important bottleneck for migrating birds. For example, almost all the world’s lesser spotted eagles pass through Lebanon. You can also see an impressive number of species in concentrations rarely encountered elsewhere. It is a remarkable natural spectacle. At the same time, I have never seen so many birds of prey being shot at or targeted. That contrast is very difficult to comprehend. From your experience in different countries, what are the main differences between Lebanon and Europe when it comes to illegal hunting? Compared with Austria or Germany, the motives for killing birds are very different. In Austria, some people shoot or poison birds of prey because they see them as pests or competitors for hares and pheasants. Here, migrating birds are shot as a hobby or for food. The second difference is the enormous number of birds killed illegally: it is on an entirely different scale. Have you ever faced difficult or dangerous situations during fieldwork? How did you handle them? Not in Lebanon, but in northern Italy someone once pointed a hunting gun at me. It was my first field operation, and of course I was frightened. Fortunately, nothing happened, and my colleague was very supportive and helped me get through it. For a moment, I thought: “What the hell am I doing here?” Just twenty minutes later, we found illegal trapping nets, and I realised again that it was all worthwhile. How important is cooperation between international organisations, local teams and security forces to achieving real results against illegal hunting? Cooperation with the police is essential. Without it, we do not have a real chance of tackling poaching. The same applies to cooperation within the team between Lebanese and international members. CABS brings decades of experience and expertise in combating poaching, which is essential to working effectively. But the Lebanese part of the team is equally important: its members understand local conditions and work on the ground all year round. Only by working together can we achieve real results. If you could specialise more deeply in one area of combating poaching, what would it be, and why? Combating poaching is not just about birds; it covers other groups of animals too. I already work in a very specialised field: the illegal killing of birds, particularly birds of prey. I do not think further specialisation would be useful, because having varied skills also gives us many advantages in this work. Alexandra during an activity in Austria.Photo: BirdLife Away from work, what are your hobbies and interests? Which activities best reflect your personality? I have played volleyball since I was nine. I love spending time in nature, whether hiking, gathering mushrooms or watching birds. I also really enjoy growing my own vegetables. Some people think combating illegal hunting means opposing hunters. How do you explain the distinction between a responsible hunter and illegal hunting? First, the key issue is the law: that is the main distinction. A responsible hunter hunts within the law and respects hunting seasons, protected species and permitted quotas. Illegal hunting means ignoring all of that: shooting protected species, hunting during closed seasons and using prohibited methods. Our fight is not against hunters themselves, but against people who break the law and threaten wildlife. After your experience in Lebanon, what message would you like to give hunters, young people and everyone interested in protecting birds and nature? Bird migration is one of nature’s greatest wonders, and Lebanon lies at the heart of that route. I would ask hunters to see these birds not as targets, but as precious living beings crossing their skies. To young people, I say: go outside, look up at the sky and help protect nature. The more people know and love these birds, the better their chances of surviving and completing their journey. Related reporting

articles.title: Alpine Swift
articles.body: Alpine Swift Tachymarptis melba Identity and identification Alpine Swift Tachymarptis melba belongs to Apodidae. Larger than Common and Pallid Swifts, it shows white belly and throat separated by a dark breast band. Wings are long and powerful. The older name Apus melba refers to the same species, not an additional encyclopedia bird. It is placed in the order Apodiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It catches airborne insects above mountains, coasts and towns. Feeding birds may range far from nesting cliffs, so a feeding location does not locate a nest. Groups give strong calls; the white belly helps identify high-flying individuals. Breeding and parental care Rock and building crevices hold nests made with light material bound by saliva. Three eggs are usual; both parents incubate and feed young. Species references describe roughly six to ten weeks of nest care, varying with conditions. Nest departure requires adequate flight development. Range and Arab occurrence Its range includes southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, extending farther south and east. In Lebanon it is a local cliff-nesting migrant breeder and passage migrant. Birds above a coast are not necessarily nesting in every building they cross. Seasonality and observation Lebanon’s checklist gives breeding from February to July, spring passage in February–April and autumn passage from July to mid-October. November follows most usual local passage. Document belly and breast band to avoid confusion with other distant large birds. Ecological role and conservation Loss of nesting crevices, disturbance and changing insect supplies are pressures. Respecting cliff colonies during climbing and construction matters. Distant viewpoints permit belly views without approaching nests. References Ramadan-Jaradi et al. — Updated checklist of the birds of Lebanon, Sandgrouse 42 (2020), 186–238. articles.title: Bar-tailed Godwit
articles.body: Bar-tailed Godwit Limosa lapponica — a coastal wader and long-distance migrant Name and classification The Bar-tailed Godwit, Limosa lapponica, is a member of Scolopacidae in the order Charadriiformes. The Lebanese guide gives an expanded Arabic name, while Kuwaiti references use the shorter equivalent of Bar-tailed Godwit. AviList 2026 recognises the same species, whose geographical populations follow different migration routes. Its northern tundra breeding grounds extend from Scandinavia through Russia to Alaska, while wintering areas span extensive coastlines in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Oceania. Field identification The long bill curves slightly upwards and usually has a pink base and dark tip. Winter birds are grey-brown above and pale below, with conspicuously patterned upperparts. Breeding males develop rich rusty colour on the face, neck and underparts; females are generally paler, larger and longer-billed. Juveniles resemble winter birds but have buff-toned feather margins. In flight, the barred tail and absence of a broad white wing stripe distinguish it from Black-tailed Godwit, which has a strong black tail-end and broad white wing bar. Winter plumage colour alone is insufficient for identification. Habitat, food and behaviour Outside the breeding season it depends on coastal mudflats, estuaries, sheltered bays and shallow shores, sometimes beside mangroves. It probes sediment for marine worms, molluscs and crustaceans. Feeding follows the exposure of suitable ground by the tide; at high water birds gather at roosts above the waterline. A safe resting place therefore complements the feeding flat, and repeated disturbance at either can reduce time available for recovering energy. On the breeding grounds it exploits tundra resources, including insects and their larvae. Breeding and life cycle The nest is a ground hollow among tundra vegetation, sometimes lined with moss and other plant material. A usual clutch contains four eggs, and both parents take part in incubation and care. The British reference gives an incubation period of twenty to twenty-one days. Chicks leave the nest early and find their own food, while the adults guard and brood them. The New Zealand reference, describing Alaska-breeding birds that migrate to New Zealand, gives fledging at about twenty-eight to thirty days. That figure concerns a specified population; laying and migration schedules differ across the species’ range. Arab distribution and November Records place it on Arab coasts in North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, within a winter range linking Africa and the Middle East. Oman’s database calls it an abundant passage migrant and winter visitor; Kuwait’s list describes a common passage migrant but uncommon winter and summer visitor. Lebanon is markedly different: the 2026 guide treats it as a vagrant, listing five records rather than a regular winter population. November coverage is consequently especially relevant to Gulf and Omani tidal flats, while Lebanese observations require careful identification and documentation. Record-breaking Pacific flights do not automatically describe the journeys of birds using Arab shores: populations follow different routes. Conservation and responsible observation Its global category is Near Threatened, NT, more precise than treating an old description as evidence of security. Populations face the loss of tidal flats, coastal reclamation, pollution and disturbance, with pressures differing between flyways. Protecting both feeding grounds and roosts supports a bird that must accumulate sufficient energy between migration stages. Observe and photograph from a fixed position away from the flock, avoiding any approach that forces flight, particularly at high tide when alternative resting ground is limited. Global conservation status remains separate from each country’s hunting legislation. References AviList Core Team — AviList v2026, 20 October 2026. articles.title: The Barn Owl
articles.body: Barn Owl (Tyto alba). The Barn Owl (Tyto alba) — also called the barn or loft owl — is a common resident breeder across Lebanon’s coast, mountains, and Beqaa Plain: a silent nocturnal hunter of rodents, and a species still threatened by habitat loss, pesticides, and illegal killing. The Barn Owl — also known as the loft or barn owl, and in English as the barn owl (Tyto alba) — is a common resident and breeder in Lebanon, found on the coast, in the mountains, and across the Beqaa Plain. It can adapt to a wide range of habitats, from farmland and pastures to forests and residential areas. Let us get to know it better… The Barn Owl is a pale, medium-sized owl with a distinctive heart-shaped face and dark eyes, lacking the barring and streaks found in many other owls. The upperparts are creamy grey; the underparts are white, sometimes yellowish. In flight it shows slender wings and body, with white underwings. Its heart-shaped facial discs help funnel sound to its ears. This unique facial feature lets it locate prey in total darkness by relying on acute hearing. Uneven ear openings allow it to pinpoint the direction of sound with remarkable precision — including prey under vegetation or snow. The Barn Owl is an exceptional nocturnal hunter that primarily takes small mammals such as mice and voles in complete silence. Specialised wing feathers reduce turbulence, allowing it to approach prey without the usual whistling sound associated with flying birds. It earned its name because it often roosts and nests in barns, abandoned buildings, and tree cavities. It does not build nests; instead it lays eggs on a bed of regurgitated pellets and prey remains. Barn Owls regurgitate indigestible parts of their prey — bones and fur — as pellets. Scientists often use these pellets to study the owl’s diet and the local ecosystem. For centuries the Barn Owl has been part of human folklore and symbolism. In some cultures it is seen as a symbol of wisdom and protection; in others it is linked to omens, superstition, and bad luck. Despite its adaptability and wide distribution, Barn Owl populations face threats including habitat loss, pesticides, and illegal hunting. Barn Owls are truly remarkable creatures that capture the imagination with their unique adaptations and mysterious behaviour — of lasting interest to bird enthusiasts and researchers alike. articles.title: Birds perfume themselves with ants
articles.body: Japanese thrush Experiments on Japanese Thrushes show how ant secretions left on feathers can help keep some insects away. The sight can seem surprising: a bird picks up ants and works them through its feathers, or allows them to crawl over its body. Known as anting, this behaviour has been reported in more than 200 bird species. What looks like a perfume bath may help protect birds against insects. In a peer-reviewed study published in early November in Scientific Reports, Japanese researchers tested this idea on the Japanese Thrush using two ant species. Chemical analysis showed that ant treatment altered the compounds on the birds’ body surfaces, notably adding an ant-derived volatile substance called dendrolasin. In an experiment involving 165 birds, the researchers compared two ant-treatment groups with a control group. They collected more louse flies and other insects that had left the birds in the treatment groups, supporting the treatment’s ability to remove some external parasites. Separate laboratory experiments tested the effects of ant secretions on mosquitoes using treated pieces of feather. Fewer mosquitoes remained on the treated feathers, while tests of some compounds also found repellent effects. Responses varied among insects and parasites. The findings offer a possible explanation for a behaviour that has long intrigued researchers: birds may borrow ants’ chemical defences to care for their bodies. Whether this reduces disease transmission, including avian malaria, still needs to be tested in the wild. “Perfuming with ants” may therefore be a useful interaction between the worlds of feathers and insects, rather than a quest for a pleasant scent. articles.title: Black-bellied Sandgrouse
articles.body: Black-bellied Sandgrouse Pterocles orientalis Identity and identification Black-bellied Sandgrouse Pterocles orientalis belongs to Pteroclidae. Its plump body, small head and pointed wings accompany a conspicuous black belly in both sexes. Males have simpler head and breast colours; females are more mottled. The tail is shorter and less elongated than in Pin-tailed Sandgrouse. It is placed in the order Pterocliformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Steppe, semiarid country and sparsely vegetated open fields provide seed food collected on the ground. Birds visit water, sometimes flying considerable distances. Tolerance of dry conditions does not eliminate water requirements, especially while raising chicks. Breeding and parental care The nest is a ground scrape, usually with three eggs. Both parents alternate incubation; a west-central Moroccan study documented about 26 days. Chicks leave early and pick up food, while the male carries water in specialised belly feathers. Parental protection remains necessary after nest departure. Range and Arab occurrence Its range includes parts of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Moroccan studies document steppe breeding, while Lebanon’s checklist describes winter visits following increased records. Lebanese winter presence does not establish local breeding; Arab sandgrouse are not all this species. Seasonality and observation Populations include residents and birds moving with water and seasonal conditions. November observation can focus on steppe and water without obstructing feeding-to-drinking journeys. Record plumage, calls and numbers to distinguish other sandgrouse. Ecological role and conservation Steppe loss, agricultural change, hunting and disturbance around water are pressures. Ground nests are vulnerable to vehicles and trampling. Open-land mosaics and safe water support feeding and breeding; drinking sites should not become traps for capture. articles.title: Black-tailed Godwit
articles.body: Black-tailed Godwit Limosa limosa — a long-billed wader between migration and wintering grounds Identity and classification The Black-tailed Godwit, also called “Baqwiqa Sultaniya” in some Arabic references, is a wader in the family Scolopacidae and the order Charadriiformes. Its scientific name is Limosa limosa, and Linnaeus described it in 1758. It is not an exclusively coastal bird: freshwater wetlands and damp meadows matter throughout its life, alongside estuaries and coastal lagoons. How to recognise it About 36–44 centimetres long, it has long legs, an extended neck and a long, almost straight bill, pink or orange at the base and dark at the tip. Breeding plumage includes rusty colouring on the head, neck and breast, with dark barring below. Males are usually more colourful; females are larger on average and have longer bills. Winter plumage is mainly grey-brown, while juveniles show a warm buff-orange wash and pale edges to their back feathers. In flight, a broad white bar crosses each wing; the rump is white and the tail has a conspicuously black end. These markings are more useful than colour alone for distinguishing it from the Bar-tailed Godwit Limosa lapponica, which lacks the prominent white wing bar, has a barred tail and a bill that tends to curve slightly upwards. A global range, several migration systems Its discontinuous breeding range extends from Iceland through Europe to northern Asia and eastern Russia. Different populations spend the non-breeding season in Europe, Africa, the Middle East and southern Asia, reaching Australasia. They do not all follow one shared journey: Icelandic and continental European birds differ in their routes and wintering areas, and some individuals change their stopovers between years. Occurrence in Arab countries Winter occurrence is documented in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania, with winter records also from Libya, Egypt, Iraq and Yemen. This does not imply equal abundance or regularity in each country. Mauritanian wetlands, including the Senegal River delta, form part of the western wintering network. In Lebanon it is a scarce passage migrant in March–April and August–November; in Jordan it is a passage migrant and a less numerous winter visitor. In Saudi Arabia it is an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor, with migration particularly evident in March–April and October–November. Oman classifies it as a common passage migrant and winter visitor. In the United Arab Emirates its distribution is very local, notably at Ras Al Khor, and a few birds remain through summer. In Kuwait it is an uncommon passage migrant, a rare winter visitor and a scarce summer visitor. Late October is therefore a fitting time to introduce it, especially in Saudi Arabia and the eastern part of the region, but is not a uniform arrival date throughout the Arab world. Summer presence does not establish year-round residence or breeding. Habitats, diet and behaviour It uses mudflats, shallow pools, marshes, flooded grasslands and rice fields, with habitat preferences varying among populations. It probes mud or picks food from the surface, taking worms, insects and their larvae, molluscs and crustaceans; seeds and rice grains may supplement its diet outside the breeding season. Birds often feed and rest in flocks, so they need undisturbed feeding and roosting sites, not simply an isolated patch of water. Breeding and life cycle It breeds mainly in open, wet meadows and marshes within its northern range; its usual occurrence in Arab countries is non-breeding. The nest is a shallow ground scrape lined with vegetation, and a clutch usually contains four eggs. Both parents incubate for about 22–24 days. Down-covered chicks can move around soon after hatching and typically become capable of flight after about 25–30 days. These are typical durations, not fixed deadlines for every nest. After breeding, birds gather and progressively move to their non-breeding areas. Conservation and responsible observation Its global category is Near Threatened (NT), which should not be confused with more severe assessments applying to particular countries. Major pressures include wetland drainage, intensive agriculture and early meadow mowing, which reduce breeding success, as well as deterioration of stopover and wintering sites. Conservation requires protecting these places across the entire migration route. Watch from a distance that does not make birds stop feeding or take flight; never chase them to reveal their wing bars. articles.title: Brown Booby
articles.body: Brown Booby Sula leucogaster A seabird hunter with a defined identity The Brown Booby, Sula leucogaster, belongs to the booby and gannet family, Sulidae. A strong-flying seabird, it is associated in the Arab world with the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and the islands and warm waters of the Indian Ocean. It is not entirely brown: the adult’s brown head, neck, upper breast and back contrast with a clear white area on the belly. Its bill is stout and pointed, the wings long, and the graduated tail tapered. This structure suits a bird that searches for fish from the air before plunging into the water. The scope of its name has changed in modern taxonomy. AviList 2026 separates Cocos Booby, Sula brewsteri, from Brown Booby; eastern Pacific populations formerly included under the latter name now belong to a distinct species. Red Sea and Indian Ocean birds remain Brown Boobies within the subspecies plotus. An old photograph labelled “Brown Booby” therefore cannot automatically illustrate the species as currently recognised without checking its origin and identity. A name in an older book may cover a broader group than the same name does today. Adults, juveniles and similar species In adults, the boundary between the brown breast and white belly appears relatively sharp. Juveniles are browner below and may show mottling, so the same contrast is not apparent. Bill, wing and tail shape remain important identification features. Females are larger on average than males, but judging sex from size alone in a single distant bird is unreliable. Bare-part colours also vary with sex, condition and age; the colour of one foot or a small facial patch cannot replace assessment of the whole bird. Masked Booby deserves comparison in the Arabian Sea. Its adult plumage is extensively white, with dark parts on the wings and face, unlike the dark-headed and dark-chested adult Brown Booby. Comparison becomes more difficult with brown juveniles. A clear view of the underside, head and pattern of contrast between neck and belly then helps. A brief encounter from a moving boat should not become a confident species record if the necessary features were not visible. It is reasonable to retain it as an unidentified booby until better evidence becomes available. Finding and catching food Brown Booby feeds on fish and squid, searching coastal waters and areas around islands, and sometimes ranging into more open water. It watches the surface and plunges head first at an angle towards prey, adjusting its flight or hovering before a dive. Alternating flapping and gliding allows it to cover broad areas rather than remain tied to one patch of water. A bird returning without a visible fish in its bill has not necessarily failed to catch food: a meal for its chick may be carried internally and delivered by regurgitation. It may feed alone or near other birds when prey gathers, and rests on islands, rocks or suitable offshore structures. Its need for fish connects conditions at sea with nesting success. A quiet colony alone is insufficient if food becomes distant or unavailable. Nor does a bird beside a boat necessarily behave tamely or need feeding. Maintaining a steady distance makes it possible to observe searching, diving and return to a resting place without changing the bird’s behaviour. Nests, incubation and chick care The bird selects a ground site on a rocky or sandy island, sometimes nesting on a rock ledge or in a depression with little construction. The amount of vegetation and natural debris gathered varies between places; a nest does not need to be large to be active. Both members of the pair share incubation and care. References usually mention one or two eggs, with three occasionally reported, and incubation of roughly six weeks. The Saudi Arabic reference gives approximately 43 days. Often only one chick reaches flying age even when two eggs hatch. Egg numbers therefore do not equal the number of young that will leave the colony. A chick grows at the site, developing white down before full feathering, and requires a continuous food supply. The Saudi reference places first flight at about 85–105 days, while wider references give a broader range influenced by conditions. Feeding continues after flight for weeks or months. Leaving the ground does not mean that a juvenile can immediately meet all its own needs. Its presence in Arab countries The 2003 PERSGA report documents breeding in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Sudan, Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia. Yemen’s Socotra archipelago is also within the breeding range described by the modern global taxonomy. The regional connection is thus not based on a single wandering bird. It does not, however, imply an even distribution across every shore or island. Nor can the old report’s figures serve as a current census: survey coverage, timing and the method of counting nests all influence the results. Saudi studies offer a more detailed picture. Research published in 2014 documented nesting on islands in the northern Red Sea. Another paper, published in 2025, dealt with surveys conducted in 2011–2013 and established additional colonies in the Al Wajh and Al Qunfudhah sectors. Its publication date does not turn those nests into field discoveries made in 2025. In Oman, the Oman birds database describes the species as an uncommon offshore visitor. It should not be promoted to a local breeder merely because it nests in nearby Yemen, or because another booby species breeds on Omani islands. A long season without one universal calendar Nesting dates vary within the Red Sea itself. The Saudi survey paper published in 2025 describes chicks in the north during May, compared with nests containing eggs in the central sector during July in the survey years. It also cites Umm al Qamari studies recording nesting throughout the year and peaks in different months. A simple description as a summer visitor that inevitably leaves in autumn therefore does not fit the species. Some populations are resident, with individual movements changing according to breeding and food. Adults and juveniles may continue to be seen in its Arab marine range in November, and care of late young may still be taking place at some sites. That general possibility does not establish that a nest on a particular island is active. The necessary evidence is behaviour watched from a distance: carrying food, feeding a chick or sustained attendance at a nest site, together with a recorded date. Repeated observation is more useful than turning one visit into a judgement about the season along an entire coast. Threats and the value of undisturbed islands Brown Booby faces pressures on both land and sea: nest disturbance, introduced animals, fishing debris, pollution and changing food resources. The Saudi study published in 2025 described adults leaving nests when people approached, exposing eggs to predation. This is a direct connection between a visit and an ecological consequence. Even someone who never touches an egg or chick can damage a nest’s prospects by forcing a parent to leave at a critical moment. An older global conservation assessment that included Cocos Booby should not automatically be transferred to the species after the taxonomic split. The practical priority is to protect known colonies and measure breeding success and threats at each site. Observation should remain outside the colony, without chasing birds with boats or drones or feeding them for photographs. An individual entangled in fishing equipment should be reported to a qualified rescue organisation rather than pulled from a distance or handled in ways that endanger bird and people. Safe islands and healthy seas are both necessary for this distinctive marine diver to persist. Photo: Don Wellmann / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Cairo Shooting World Cup: gold for Privratsky and Teh Xiu Yi
articles.body: Men’s air-rifle competition at the Cairo Shooting World Cup, 12 October 2026. Source: ISSF 12 October results: the Czech wins men’s air rifle and the Singaporean takes women’s 25m pistol gold, with competition continuing until 15 October. Czechia’s Jiri Privratsky and Singapore’s Teh Xiu Yi won Monday’s two titles on 12 October 2026 at the ISSF Rifle and Pistol World Cup at Egypt International Olympic City in Cairo. The event runs from 8 to 16 October. Men’s air rifle gold for Czechia In the men’s 10m air rifle final, Privratsky scored 251.3 points to finish 1.1 ahead of Sweden’s Marcus Madsen, who took silver with 250.2. France’s Dimitri Dutendas earned bronze with 229.9, according to the International Shooting Sport Federation. Singapore wins the women’s pistol title In the women’s 25m pistol final, Teh Xiu Yi secured gold with 38 hits, ahead of France’s Heloise Fourre on 37. Bulgaria’s Miroslava Mincheva claimed bronze with 32 hits. Arab participation ahead of Doha The competition brings together 385 athletes from 51 countries, according to the ISSF. The final entry list includes athletes from Egypt, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Libya and Yemen. The programme covers air rifle and air pistol, three-position rifle, sport pistol, rapid-fire pistol and mixed-team events. Competition began on 10 October and continues until 15 October. Tuesday’s programme, on 13 October, includes the women’s 50m rifle three positions final, with the remaining finals taking place over the following two days. Cairo remains a preparation stop before the World Championships in Doha, from 1 to 14 November, where the first shooting quota places for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics will be awarded. No Olympic quota places are awarded at the Cairo World Cup. The city will also host the 300m Rifle World Championship from 15 to 20 October. articles.title: Cetti’s Warbler
articles.body: Cetti’s Warbler Cettia cetti Identity and identification Cetti’s Warbler belongs to Cettiidae. Reddish-brown upperparts, pale underparts, a fine eyebrow and a broad tail help identify this small bird. Its powerful song often reveals it before it emerges from dense cover. Habitat and food It inhabits reeds, brambles and dense vegetation near water, feeding mainly on small insects. Continuous wetland vegetation provides food and shelter throughout the year. Breeding and development BTO gives a typical clutch of 4–5 eggs, incubated by the female for about 16–17 days. The young need care and feeding in the nest and normally fledge after 14–16 days. These are general developmental intervals, rather than a fixed calendar across its range. Arab occurrence and seasonality The 2026 Birds of Lebanon guide describes it as a common resident breeder in dense vegetation near water. Its presence in November therefore continues a resident life cycle, rather than marking the arrival of a winter visitor. Observation and conservation The species is globally listed as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List; local habitat protection remains important. The Lebanon guide also identifies illegal hunting and agricultural expansion as pressures. Wait and listen from a path edge without entering reedbeds or using playback to draw birds out. Protecting river margins from drainage and fire conserves its habitat. articles.title: Common Goldeneye
articles.body: Common Goldeneye Bucephala clangula Identity, sex and age Common Goldeneye, Bucephala clangula, is a compact diving duck with a large-looking head, a short bill and a conspicuous yellow eye in adults. The breeding male has a dark, green-glossed head with a rounded white patch between the bill and eye. White breast and flanks contrast with the black back. The female has a rich brown head and a grey body; her bill often shows yellow near its tip, although the amount changes seasonally. The wings have conspicuous white areas in flight and can produce a whistling sound. Young birds and eclipse males resemble females more than fully patterned males. Immature eyes can be brownish rather than bright yellow, so the common name does not describe every age. Identification should combine the head shape, bill, eye and plumage. A female Smew is smaller and shows extensive white on the lower face, unlike the Goldeneye's brown head. Barrow's Goldeneye is the closest relative likely to enter an identification comparison. Its adult male has a crescent-like rather than rounded facial patch and a different balance of black and white. Females are harder to separate, requiring attention to bill and head proportions. Bill colour rules derived from western North American birds should not be applied uncritically to Eurasian birds; this is a case where a regional identification guide matters. Lakes, coastlines and food During breeding, Common Goldeneye uses northern lakes and rivers associated with mature woodland. The trees supply nest holes, while the water supplies food. Clear waters with abundant aquatic invertebrates can be especially valuable. The winter habitat is broader, including estuaries, coastal bays, large lakes and rivers that remain open. Thus a duck observed far from woodland in winter is not outside its normal ecological pattern. It feeds mainly underwater on aquatic animals. Insects are important in the breeding season, while crustaceans and molluscs are major foods in many winter habitats. Small fish and some plant material also occur in the diet. The mix changes with local prey availability. Groups may dive in synchrony, and a feeding flock can momentarily disappear almost completely. Short pauses between dives allow observers to count and examine the birds without moving closer. Courtship and cavity nesting Courtship is particularly conspicuous: a male stretches or throws his head backwards, points the bill upward, and combines the movement with calls and kicks on the water. Several males may display near the same female. This performance can be seen on winter waters before birds reach the breeding grounds, so display alone is not evidence of local nesting. The female uses a tree cavity and lines the nest with down; artificial nest boxes are readily accepted in appropriate breeding areas. Females may lay eggs in one another's nests. As a result, an unusually large clutch can include contributions from more than one bird, and raw egg counts do not always describe an individual female's output. Keeping cavity-bearing trees is therefore part of waterbird conservation, not simply woodland management. Eggs and the ducklings' first weeks BTO gives a typical clutch of 8–11 eggs, an incubation period of 29–30 days, and fledging at 57–66 days. Incubation is undertaken by the female. The ducklings leave the elevated cavity soon after hatching and make their way to water with her. They feed themselves rather than receiving food placed into their bills, but remain dependent on the availability of small prey and safe water. Leaving the nest and learning to fly are separated by many weeks. This is an important distinction when interpreting photographs of families: a downy youngster swimming confidently is still flightless. The female's care, the brood's food supply and the suitability of the surrounding waters all influence what happens after successful hatching. A nest box can supply a missing cavity but cannot compensate for a poor feeding lake. Northern distribution and migration The species breeds across northern Eurasia and North America. Eurasian populations occupy a broad belt extending through northern Europe and Russia; in winter they use inland waters and coasts farther south, including the Mediterranean, Black Sea and Caspian regions. The North American population occupies its own extensive breeding and wintering range. These broad patterns should not be read as evidence that transatlantic movements explain Arab records. Audubon's account notes relatively late autumn and early spring migration and a tendency for males to winter farther north than females. Water remaining free of ice influences where birds can feed. Some places hold breeders and winter arrivals, while others receive only non-breeding visitors. A national winter count describes one seasonal gathering, not necessarily the total population that breeds within that country's borders. Presence in Arab countries Iraq's checklist by Salim and colleagues describes Common Goldeneye as an uncommon winter visitor in northern Iraq. Morocco's rare-bird committee, by contrast, places it in the accidental-visitor category. These are different kinds of occurrence: the former has a stated winter association, while the latter does not establish predictable annual wintering. Syria's checklist by Murdoch and Betton, published in 2008, lists the species as a vagrant. Lebanon's Avibase checklist, hosted by Birds Canada, marks it Rare/Accidental. Tunisia's Avibase list gives the same rarity designation. These national sources support a pattern of scattered rare records around the southern margins of the main range, with a more specific winter status in northern Iraq. They do not provide evidence for Arab breeding populations, and they are not a basis for declaring the species absent from every unlisted country. Conservation and observation The global status reported by BTO is Least Concern. Locally, conserving old waterside trees, aquatic food resources and quiet winter refuges remains important. Nest boxes can help in suitable breeding regions, but their role differs from protecting a southern site used only by visiting birds. Management should match the function of the site rather than assume that every waterbody needs the same intervention. Watch through binoculars or a telescope from a stable shoreline position. For an unusual Arab observation, record facial pattern, bill shape and eye colour, with photographs from several angles where possible. Keep the distinction between adult male, female-type and definite juvenile, and record uncertainty honestly. Avoid opening occupied nest boxes or repeatedly flushing feeding flocks. A well-documented sighting contributes to understanding a scarce visitor without costing it feeding time. articles.title: Common Gull
articles.body: Common Gull Larus canus Identity and identification Common Gull Larus canus belongs to Laridae. Adults have grey upperparts, white underparts, a relatively slender greenish-yellow bill and black wingtips with white markings. The winter head becomes streaked; immature birds differ considerably from adults. Habitat and food It takes invertebrates, fish and other foods along shores, fields and water margins. Outside breeding, mixed flocks require identification of individual birds rather than assigning one name to the whole gathering. Breeding and development The vegetation nest occupies the ground or a suitable raised site. BTO gives a typical clutch of three eggs, shared incubation of 22–28 days and fledging at about 34–36 days. Growing chicks require food and protection. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist separates scarce passage in March and early November to mid-December from widespread common winter presence in December to late February. A few birds remain in summer, which alone does not prove breeding. November falls within the passage period preceding the winter peak. Observation and conservation This entry uses Larus canus under AviList 2026. Short-billed Gull Larus brachyrhynchus is separate: its photographs and records must not automatically be transferred here. Clean shores and quiet resting places support the species. articles.title: Common Hoopoe
articles.body: Common Hoopoe Upupa epops — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Common Hoopoe, Upupa epops, belongs to Upupidae and has a distinctive appearance among birds of Arab gardens. Warm sandy-rufous plumage contrasts with black-and-white wings and tail, and a long bill curves downwards. A black-tipped crest can be raised and spread or folded back. Rounded wings and successive beats make the flying bird look broader than its perched body suggests. Distinguishing similar birds The sexes look much alike. Females may be slightly smaller and paler, but these differences do not safely establish sex in every photograph. Juveniles are comparatively dull, with shorter bills and crests. A folded crest does not indicate a different species, and apparent crest length alone is insufficient for ageing. Combine the curved bill, patterned wings and crest, remembering that light and feather position can alter the impression of colour. Habitat, food and behaviour Hoopoes require ground where they can probe or collect prey, with nesting cavities nearby. Orchards, pastures, fields, gardens and open landscapes with scattered trees can provide this combination. Large insects, their larvae and other invertebrates form the principal food. The bill probes and picks; short vegetation or exposed patches make prey accessible. The repeated hollow song advertises a territory, and a bird may be heard before it is seen. Breeding and annual cycle An old tree, wall, rock cavity or suitable nestbox can accommodate the nest. The female lays and incubates inside the cavity while the male supplies food. European accounts commonly report five to eight eggs and approximately 16 days of incubation, variable figures rather than a rule for every population. Nestlings require sustained provisioning before leaving. Field research shows that food supply and a chick’s position within the brood are associated with survival prospects: abundant prey matters as much as the presence of a hole. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Arab occurrence combines breeding populations with passage migrants and winter visitors. Egypt’s population includes the subspecies Upupa epops major. Jordan records residents and migrants; the regional account describes widespread summer breeding in Iraq. The UAE supports breeding populations that expanded with suitable habitat. Oman receives substantial passage and winter numbers, with breeding more restricted, while Qatar’s reference describes passage. In October, therefore, a local bird and a migrant may occur in the same region. Finding a hoopoe in a garden does not establish year-round residence there. Ecology and conservation Hoopoes belong to food webs centred on soil and insects. Their global category is Least Concern, although declining insect resources, loss of cavity-bearing trees and changing land use can pressure local populations. Protecting holes and varied orchards, while reducing pesticide use, helps retain food and breeding resources. This conspicuous bird attracts photographers, but repeated approaches to a nest entrance can interrupt feeding. Watch from a distance that allows adults to enter and leave freely rather than trying to draw them out at the cavity. articles.title: Common Pochard
articles.body: Common Pochard Aythya ferina — a diving duck between migration, wintering and local breeding Name and identity The Common Pochard Aythya ferina belongs to the family Anatidae and order Anseriformes. It is a diving duck, not simply a red-headed version of a surface-feeding duck. KuwaitBirds documents the Arabic name “al-batt kastana’i al-ra’s”; the Lebanese Ministry of Environment guide also records “batt hamrawi” and “wans”. These names belong to documented regional contexts rather than a single vernacular shared across the Arab world. How to recognise it A male in distinctive plumage has a chestnut head and neck, black breast, pale grey body and red eye. Its sloping forehead merges into a relatively long bill, with a blue-grey central area between dark base and tip. It lacks the male Tufted Duck’s crest, and its grey body differs from that species’ black-and-white contrast. The female is grey-brown, paler on the cheek and chin, and much less contrasting. Juveniles resemble females, with less grey vermiculation on the back. A male in post-breeding eclipse plumage can also look more female-like; head colour alone therefore cannot reliably establish sex or age. In flight the pale grey wing bar is subdued. The male Red-crested Pochard Netta rufina instead has a larger orange head and red bill: these two species should not be identified as one. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses lakes, marshes, reservoirs and ponds with aquatic vegetation, requiring areas suitable for diving. Artificial lakes and treatment ponds can provide habitat when conditions are appropriate, but water alone does not guarantee habitat quality. Its food includes aquatic plants, seeds and small invertebrates, with proportions varying between sites and seasons. Often seen in groups, it may associate with other ducks. Resting flocks do not mean that a site is unimportant: research in Algeria’s Guerbes–Sanhadja wetlands found that diving ducks also used the site for daytime resting, sleeping and preening. Quiet resting places complement feeding areas; disturbance to either can reduce the value of the wider wetland. Distribution and Arab-country occurrence Its range extends across Europe and Asia, with some populations moving to warmer wintering regions, including North Africa and the Middle East. Its African wintering range includes Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt and Sudan. A range map does not, however, mean that every site within those countries regularly holds similar numbers. In Morocco, passage and wintering overlap with local breeding; a recent study documented residency and regular nesting at Merja Fouwarate. In Lebanon it is uncommon on passage in October–November, rarer in March–April, and a scarce winter visitor. Kuwait’s official list describes scarce passage and winter occurrence. The Birds of Oman database instead calls it a fairly common winter visitor, an important contrast with Kuwait. UAE reports document locally concentrated winter presence, sometimes more numerous on particular lakes. These differences do not justify treating it as resident or breeding across the Gulf. Breeding and life cycle Nesting is associated with vegetation near water that conceals the female and clutch. She usually lays eight to ten eggs and incubates them for about twenty-five days. Downy chicks are mobile soon after hatching and typically become capable of flight after roughly fifty to fifty-five days. These are typical values, not a fixed timetable for every country or nest. Ducklings accompanying a female provide stronger breeding evidence than adult ducks merely remaining through summer. Why late October matters Late October falls within the documented autumn passage in Lebanon and may coincide with growing arrivals at wintering sites. Monitoring at Morocco’s Fouwarate found autumn and winter increases on top of local presence. This does not establish a regional arrival date or make late October a universal peak. Record location, date, count and apparent sex, distinguishing direct observations from assumptions about the birds’ origins. Conservation and responsible observation Its global status is Vulnerable (VU), not Least Concern simply because large flocks occur on some lakes. Pressures include wetland loss and degradation, hunting, pollution and lead poisoning from ingested ammunition. Protecting water, vegetation and resting areas are interconnected measures. Use binoculars at a distance that does not force birds to dive away or take flight; do not chase them to check wing markings or obtain a photograph. articles.title: Common Starling
articles.body: Common Starling Sturnus vulgaris — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Common Starling, Sturnus vulgaris, belongs to Sturnidae. About 21 cm long, it has a compact body, short tail, slender bill and pointed wings in flight. Adult plumage is dark with green and purple iridescence. Fresh feathers carry pale spots that become less conspicuous as their tips wear; a dark, sparsely spotted bird is not automatically another species. The bill is yellow during breeding and darker outside that period. Juveniles are grey-brown before acquiring spotted plumage. The sexes broadly resemble one another, and subtle differences require a good close view. Similar species The short tail, wing shape and walking gait help separate starlings from longer-tailed blackbirds. In the Maghreb, compare carefully with Spotless Starling, Sturnus unicolor: absence of spots alone is insufficient, especially in worn plumage. Adult Rosy Starlings combine pink and black, but juvenile birds require closer attention to bill, feather pattern and proportions. Habitat, food and behaviour Pasture, lawns, cultivated fields, orchards, parks and urban areas all provide opportunities. Starlings walk while searching for invertebrates and probe the ground with their bills; they also eat fruits, seeds and other available foods. Their varied diet does not make them invariably beneficial or harmful to every farm. Outside breeding, flocks may roost communally in reeds, trees or suitable structures. Coordinated flock movements arise from birds responding to their neighbours rather than moving randomly. The complex song incorporates whistles, rattles and imitations. Breeding and development Nests occupy holes in trees, buildings and suitable nest boxes. A typical clutch contains 4–5 pale blue eggs, with incubation lasting about 12–15 days. Both parents feed the chicks, which leave the cavity after roughly three weeks, with variation. Growing young rely heavily on protein-rich animal food. A later or replacement brood is possible, but not universal across populations. Independent juveniles gather into flocks and develop more adult-like plumage through moult. Migration and Arab-region seasons This is a partial migrant, with resident populations and others moving south or west in autumn. Winter numbers become substantial in Mediterranean parts of the Arab world, followed by a reduction as visitors leave in spring. This does not imply that the species never breeds in Arab countries: breeding populations occur in northern Iraq. In Saudi Arabia, winter occurrence is concentrated in the northern half, with conspicuous Eastern Province flocks and much scarcer occurrence farther south; it is not treated there as a breeding species. Abundance varies among farmland, towns and roosts, and between years. A single flock cannot establish population size or a universal seasonal calendar. In Lebanon, autumn passage is conspicuous in October–November, with winter flocks concentrated in open and cultivated Beqaa habitats. At a documented Moroccan daya wetland site, October–February winter records included birds mixing with resident Spotless Starlings; these dates describe that site rather than the entire country. Ecology and conservation Starlings consume invertebrates, disperse some seeds and provide food for raptors. Globally they are Least Concern, but substantial declines in parts of Europe show that spectacular flocks do not remove the need for monitoring. Loss of suitable pasture, changing farming practices and reduced food availability are studied pressures. The species is introduced outside its native range in several regions; this label should not automatically be applied to natural visitors in Arab countries. Quiet observation should keep its distance from nests and communal roosts and distinguish demonstrated local problems from a blanket reputation. articles.title: Common Tern
articles.body: Common Tern Sterna hirundo Identity and names Common Tern, Sterne pierregarin in French, is Sterna hirundo, a species in Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. About 35 cm long, it is slender and long-winged with a forked tail. “Common” describes relative abundance over a broad range, not a guarantee of plentiful birds in every country or season. Nor is it exclusively marine: rivers, lakes and other inland waters are important, particularly across parts of its breeding range. Identification Breeding birds have silvery-grey upperparts, a black cap, pale cheeks and a pointed red or orange-red bill, often with a black tip. The outer wing is darker than the inner wing and the tail distinctly forked. Outside breeding, the forehead turns white and bill and legs become darker. Markings vary with age and population, so bill colour alone cannot confirm identity. The sexes look similar. Comparing juveniles or moulting birds with Arctic, White-cheeked and other terns requires attention to structure and wing, tail and head patterns rather than one briefly glimpsed feature. Habitat, food and behaviour It searches for food over sheltered coastal waters, estuaries, lakes and rivers, sometimes hovering before dropping bill-first towards the water. Small fish are important prey, alongside other aquatic animals according to availability. Sandy beaches, islands and open shores provide resting places, and breeding birds often form colonies. A fishing tern need not be close to its nest: birds move between feeding, resting and breeding sites. Conservation therefore needs to consider more than a single point on a map, including both water quality and quiet shores. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds across large parts of Europe, Asia and North America, with populations moving south to different wintering areas. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes common passage along coasts and islands and says it formerly bred on the Palm Islands; that wording does not establish continued breeding today. The Kuwaiti reference describes an uncommon passage migrant, with no confirmed nesting within Kuwaiti territory. Oman’s official list gives common passage and uncommon winter occurrence. Presence in the northern Gulf therefore does not automatically imply the same seasonal pattern as the Sea of Oman or eastern Mediterranean. Breeding and development The nest is usually a simple ground site; specially prepared platforms are also used in some conservation programmes. BTO gives a typical clutch of 2–3 eggs, incubation of about 21–22 days and fledging at about 22–28 days after hatching. Downy chicks can move before they can fly but still need feeding and protection. These are approximate reference intervals affected by conditions, not evidence of a particular country’s breeding calendar. Carrying a fish or wearing breeding plumage does not by itself establish a new colony; breeding requires clear evidence obtained without disturbing nests. November and responsible observation In November, Common Tern may occur as a winter visitor at some Omani sites, but it should not automatically be described as a common winter bird on every Arab coast. Record country, site and date, and obtain views of head and wing patterns without approaching. Keep away from resting birds and their route to the water rather than flushing them: repeated displacement reduces feeding and resting time. On islands, obey paths and local restrictions, avoiding landings beside groups that may contain nests or camouflaged chicks. Do not feed birds or use calls to lure them into a photographic position. Conservation It is globally Least Concern (LC), yet individual colonies can suffer despite its wide distribution. The Lebanon guide identifies disturbance, oil spills, fish poisoning, pesticides and avian influenza; the Kuwaiti reference highlights marine oil pollution. Keeping breeding and resting places quiet and protecting waters that support prey is more useful than preserving the shoreline’s appearance alone. If dead or injured birds are found, report them without touching them or gathering around them; do not infer disease or cause from one photograph. articles.title: Crested Tit
articles.body: Crested Tit Lophophanes cristatus Identity, life and distribution Crested Tit Lophophanes cristatus is a small bird with a black-and-white crest and strongly patterned face. The crest may be raised or flattened, so its height in a single photograph is not decisive. It is associated with European woodland, especially coniferous habitats. It searches branches and trunks for insects and pine seeds, stores food for winter and may join mixed tit flocks. The female excavates a nest site in suitable dead wood and lines it with soft material. BTO gives a typical clutch of five or six eggs. Suitable dead wood is therefore part of a living forest’s nesting infrastructure. The photograph was taken in Estonia and illustrates the species, not its occurrence in Morocco. Avibase, using Clements treatment, mentions rare vagrancy to Morocco. That differs from an established population. www.bto.org — Crested Tit · www.rspb.org.uk — Crested Tit · avibase.bsc-eoc.org — Crested Tit Photo: Yehor Yatsiuk

articles.title: Desert Lark
articles.body: Desert Lark Ammomanes deserti Identity and identification Desert Lark Ammomanes deserti belongs to Alaudidae. Sandy or brown plumage matches local rock, with a relatively strong bill and lightly marked breast. It lacks Crested Lark’s prominent crest. Geographic colour variation makes bill shape, tail and calls useful alongside upperpart colour. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Rocky hills, dry slopes and wadis are more characteristic than extensive bare sand. It walks for seeds and insects and uses shade in harsh conditions. Pairs or small parties may appear; movement among rocks often reveals otherwise well-camouflaged birds. Breeding and parental care A ground nest is partly sheltered by stone or vegetation and may be bordered with small pebbles. Chicks need regular food, especially invertebrates. Rainfall and food availability influence local breeding opportunities; seeing an adult pair does not demonstrate a confirmed nest. Range and Arab occurrence It is widespread in rocky dry habitats of North Africa, the Middle East and Arabia. Kuwait’s national report lists it as a breeding resident. Lebanon has a rare, local resident presence in the northeast. This contrast reflects habitat suitability rather than range size alone. Seasonality and observation Usually resident, it can be watched in suitable November habitats, with possible local movements. Clear side views of bill and tail help distinguish similar desert larks. Matching sandy colour alone is insufficient identification. Ecological role and conservation It depends on intact rocky ground and sparse vegetation. Excavation, roads and off-track vehicles can destroy nests and feeding patches. Conserving small habitat features, from shaded stones to plants, matters in a low-productivity desert. articles.title: Brotherly Love wins opening-night cup as Colour Up returns to winning ways at Meydan
articles.body: Horse racing at Meydan Racecourse in Dubai. Archive photo. Results from the Dubai Racing Carnival opener, with racing returning on 20 November. Brotherly Love won the Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashed Al Maktoum Cup, the feature on the Dubai Racing Carnival’s opening night at Meydan on Friday, 6 November 2026. Trained by Britain’s Jamie Osborne and ridden by Danny Tudhope, he beat Sirocco Winds by five and a quarter lengths in the Emirates-sponsored 1,600-metre race. In the opening 1,200-metre race, eight-year-old Colour Up recorded his first Meydan victory since 2023. Pat Dobbs rode the Doug Watson-trained horse to a half-length win over Ma Yetal. Union Security, trained by Ahmad bin Harmash and ridden by Connor Beasley, won the 1,400-metre Emirates Skywards race for three-year-olds ahead of Magic Art, scoring on opening night for the second consecutive season. Saudi trainer Abdullah Al Monif’s two runners, representing AMM Racing and owner Ayman AlRajhi, both finished sixth: Allajayn in a field of six in the Emirates Skywards, and Brave Vekoma in a field of ten in the 1,200-metre Emirates Courier Express maiden. Al Monif, 34, began his equestrian career in show jumping before moving into flat racing and gained experience in Ireland, Britain and the United States. He currently trains around 30 horses in Saudi Arabia and hopes his participation in Dubai will give him international experience and test his horses against new rivals. The carnival resumes on Friday, 20 November, with the Listed Dubai Creek Mile as the feature. The season comprises 16 race nights running until 12 March 2027. Season highlights include Festive Friday on 18 December, Fashion Friday on 22 January and Emirates Super Saturday on 27 February. Following the carnival’s conclusion, Meydan will host the Dubai World Cup on 27 March 2027, featuring nine races with total prize money of US$30.5 million. articles.title: Dunnock
articles.body: Dunnock Prunella modularis — A discreet visitor beneath the shrubs Name and identity Dunnock is Prunella modularis, called Usfur al-shawk in the Lebanese guide. It belongs to Prunellidae within Passeriformes, not to the sparrow family despite its similar size, brown plumage and the English folk name “hedge sparrow”. AviList 2026 retains the same scientific name. Its native range extends across Europe towards the Urals and adjoining areas, with some populations migrating to the Mediterranean, North Africa and Middle East. Human introduction established it in New Zealand, unlike the natural migratory arrival of birds in the Levant. Identification Adults have a grey head and breast, a streaked brown back, a fine pointed dark bill and pinkish-brown legs. The sexes have similar plumage; juveniles are more strongly streaked and show less obvious grey on the head and breast. The slender bill distinguishes it from House Sparrow’s heavy conical bill, and it lacks the male sparrow’s strong head pattern. Other accentors also require attention: Siberian Accentor, for example, has a more contrasting head and a stronger eyebrow. Watching it walk beneath vegetation reveals a slim, discreet bird rather than a typical sparrow. Habitat, food and behaviour Dense scrub, hedges, gardens with a rich lower layer and woodland edges provide suitable habitat. It searches near the ground for beetles, flies, ants, spiders and other small invertebrates, also taking small seeds. Quick movements through litter and soil keep it close to cover into which it can retreat. Calls are thin; a breeding male may climb to an exposed branch to sing. Retaining shrubs and leaf litter provides feeding and hiding places: a garden stripped of every weed and fallen leaf is not necessarily better habitat for birds. Breeding and parental care The female builds a concealed cup nest in a shrub or dense vegetation and lays blue-green eggs. BTO records a typical clutch of four or five, incubated by the female for 14–15 days; young leave approximately 12–15 days after hatching. The female feeds the chicks and male participation varies with the mating system; care continues after departure. Birds may form a monogamous pair, or a female may associate with more than one male; additional social arrangements occur. Its breeding life therefore cannot always be reduced to a fixed pair. Broods may be repeated within the season. These reference breeding facts are not evidence of nesting in Lebanon, where it is classified as a passage and winter visitor. Distribution and migration in the Arab region The 2026 Lebanese guide describes it as a common passage migrant and winter visitor using low scrubby slopes and woodland undergrowth. November is therefore an appropriate time to search quietly along vegetation edges, rather than only among sparrow flocks. Migratory populations reach North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, but broad range does not mean equal abundance among countries. Kuwait’s checklist treats it as a vagrant, with only a few accepted records, so it should not be described as a familiar winter visitor throughout the Gulf. Clear photographs of the head, bill and breast, accompanied by date and location, help document observations away from its usual areas. Ecological role and conservation AviList 2026 conservation data place it globally in Least Concern. Local pressures include removal of hedges and scrub, habitat simplification and illegal hunting; abundance and weather responses vary regionally. It contributes to food webs as an invertebrate consumer and prey, without this implying an unmeasured level of agricultural pest control. Retaining diverse low vegetation and avoiding nest disturbance are practical priorities. Winter photographers can wait at a distance that allows natural feeding rather than repeatedly flushing birds from cover. References AviList Core Team — AviList v2026, 20 October 2026. articles.title: Eastern Imperial Eagle
articles.body: Eastern Imperial Eagle Aquila heliaca Identity and identification The Eastern Imperial Eagle is a large Accipitridae raptor. Adults have a dark body and pale golden nape, usually with white shoulder patches; juveniles are paler and more streaked. AviList 2026 treats it separately from the Spanish Imperial Eagle Aquila adalberti. Habitat and food It favours landscapes combining trees with pasture and open fields, taking small mammals and birds and also using carrion. Eagles need suitable resting and nesting trees as well as extensive feeding habitat. Breeding and development The Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds LIFE project describes a tree nest built of sticks and usually two eggs. Incubation takes about 43 days, mainly by the female, with male food delivery and relief. Young continue to receive food and learn to hunt after leaving the nest; first flight is not independence. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2026 guide records rare passage in late February–mid-April and mid-September–October, without describing regular wintering. Qatar’s list gives rare passage. Oman’s official 2026 list instead describes common to abundant passage and winter visits, making Oman’s winter presence particularly relevant in November. Observation and conservation The Eastern Imperial Eagle is globally classified as Vulnerable (VU) on the IUCN Red List. Reducing power-line hazards, poisoning and disturbance supports its conservation. Maintain observation distance and do not disclose nest or roost locations. articles.title: Egypt: New Hunting Rules and Field Action as Autumn Migration Begins
articles.body: A field researcher removes a bird from illegal nets. Egypt’s Ministry of Local Development and Environment announced a new decision regulating hunting, as the Environmental Affairs Agency began monitoring with the start of the autumn migration season. At Burullus Protected Area, about 200 migratory birds were released and roughly 750 metres of illegal nets were removed. The ministry is also holding a community dialogue with NGOs and specialists to shape clearer rules specifically for hunting migratory birds. A team to tackle illegal bird hunting The Egyptian team to combat excessive and illegal bird hunting was launched at the Journalists’ Syndicate on 30 September 2026, on the initiative of Nature Conservation Egypt, in cooperation with the Association of Environmental and Development Writers. Al-Ahram reported Mahmoud Bakr’s description of it as a voluntary coordination platform involving government and parliamentary representatives, researchers, civil society and the media. According to Press Street, the team supports the national 2026–2030 roadmap through five committees: legislation, policies, enforcement and compliance; research and monitoring; economic alternatives and ecotourism; funding, institutional empowerment and capacity building; and awareness, media, ethical and cultural values. Al-Watan reported Khaled El-Noubi’s announcement of preparations for an “Invitation to a Code of Honour” initiative during the current hunting season in Matrouh, El-Dabaa and Ras El-Hekma, on the northwestern coast. It seeks voluntary agreements with hunters and local community leaders to curb excessive hunting.

articles.title: Eurasian Bittern
articles.body: Eurasian Bittern Botaurus stellaris Identity and identification The Eurasian Bittern is a large Ardeidae heron whose buff-brown plumage and dark markings camouflage it among reeds. It has a strong pointed bill and dark crown, and may stretch its neck upwards when alert. Habitat and food It hunts in shallow water and marsh vegetation, taking fish, amphibians and other aquatic prey. Slow movements and cryptic plumage may conceal it even at close range. Breeding and development BTO gives a typical clutch of 4–6 eggs, incubated by the female for about 25–26 days. Chicks need feeding and care and normally become capable of flight at 50–55 days. Moving among reeds does not mean development is complete. Arab occurrence and seasonality The 2026 Lebanon guide records scarce passage from mid-September to November and mid-March to late May, with individual birds overwintering in wetlands. Qatar’s list describes a rare winter visitor. November fits the transition into winter, with different abundance and regularity in the two countries. Observation and conservation The Eurasian Bittern is globally classified as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List. Keep a safe distance from concealed birds and resting places. Protecting reeds and water from drainage and pollution is more useful than forcing a camouflaged bird into view. articles.title: Eurasian Blue Tit
articles.body: Eurasian Blue Tit Cyanistes caeruleus Identity and names The Eurasian Blue Tit, Cyanistes caeruleus, is a small member of the tit family Paridae and the order Passeriformes. Its French name is Mésange bleue; Arabic references use “blue tit”, with “Eurasian” distinguishing it from its African relative. It is about 11–12 cm long, with a wingspan around 18–19 cm and a mass near 11 g. Older books place it in Parus, so Parus caeruleus denotes the same species rather than another bird. Identification Adults combine a blue crown, wings and tail with a greenish back, yellow underparts and white cheeks crossed by a dark eye stripe. A narrow dark mark may run down the belly, unlike the conspicuous broad stripe of the larger Great Tit. The sexes look similar, although males tend to be brighter; colour alone is an unreliable field test of sex. Juveniles have duller plumage, a greener crown and yellowish cheeks. In shade, check the whole facial pattern rather than judging a single blue feather. Habitat, food and behaviour Broadleaved woodland, wooded valleys, orchards, parks and tree-filled gardens provide feeding places and cavities. The bird searches leaves, buds and fine branches for small invertebrates, frequently hanging upside down. Caterpillars are especially important for growing chicks; seeds and other plant foods supplement the adult diet outside the breeding season. Autumn and winter birds may travel with other tits in mixed feeding parties. A short burst of movement through several trees is therefore not necessarily directed migration, and a feeder visit is only one part of its feeding activity. Range and Arab occurrence Its main range covers much of Europe and western Asia, but abundance in a European garden is no guide to its status in an Arab country. The 2026 Lebanon guide describes a rare resident breeder, increasing over the preceding decade, a scarce winter visitor and an even scarcer passage migrant. Woodland and river valleys are relevant Lebanese habitats. In Morocco, the familiar breeding blue tit is the African Blue Tit, Cyanistes teneriffae. The Moroccan checklist treats Eurasian Blue Tit as a doubtful accidental visitor, not a widespread resident; old broadly defined “blue tit” records require taxonomic care. Breeding and development A tree hole or suitable nest box holds the nest. BTO gives a typical clutch of 8–10 eggs, female incubation of 13–14 days and fledging after 18–21 days from hatching. These reference values are not measurements of every Lebanese population. Both parents bring food to the young, whose dependence continues beyond their first flight. Nesting is generally concentrated in spring and linked to food availability; the laying date varies with locality and conditions. A bird examining a cavity is not sufficient evidence that eggs or chicks are present. November and responsible observation November offers a chance to follow feeding parties through woodland without assuming that every individual has arrived from abroad. In Lebanon, resident birds and seasonal visitors must be distinguished at the population level; one brief sighting cannot establish origin. Record the date, habitat, number and diagnostic plumage, and photograph from an established path if possible. Do not tap nest boxes, open cavities or repeatedly play calls. Leave birds uninterrupted access to vegetation, especially during cold or wet weather when feeding time matters. Conservation The global IUCN category reported in AviList 2026 is Least Concern. This does not imply equal security everywhere or permission to capture the birds. The Lebanon guide identifies wildfire and climate change among pressures. Retaining old cavity-bearing trees, varied native vegetation and insect-rich foliage helps conserve both nesting and feeding opportunities. Avoid unnecessary insecticide use. Where feeders already operate, careful hygiene matters because congregation can spread disease; feeders are not a substitute for an intact, diverse habitat.
