articles.title: Eurasian Collared Dove
articles.body: Eurasian Collared Dove Streptopelia decaocto — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Eurasian Collared Dove, Streptopelia decaocto, belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae. Its overall grey-buff plumage carries a black half-collar across the back of the neck. It has a dark bill, reddish eye and a long tail with conspicuous white outer and terminal areas. The flight feathers are darker than much of the wing. Its apparently simple colouring varies with light, so the collar, tail pattern and voice together are more useful than an isolated shade of grey. Age, sex and similar species Males and females look very similar and cannot reliably be sexed from colour alone. Juveniles may lack a complete collar and show pale feather edges. The European Turtle Dove has warmer, patterned upperparts and a striped neck patch. The smaller, warmer-coloured Laughing Dove has a speckled patch on the front of the neck instead of this rear half-collar. The Collared Dove’s repeated three-part coo contrasts with the Turtle Dove’s purring voice. A young bird without a collar should therefore be assessed using body shape, tail and wings, not rejected solely on that missing feature. Habitat, diet and behaviour Villages, towns, farms and orchards provide habitat; trees, water and grain within human-used landscapes are valuable resources. Seeds and grain dominate its diet, supplemented with some fruit, plant material and invertebrates. Much food is collected on the ground. Birds may gather around feeding resources and away from nesting territories. Males coo from elevated perches and perform breeding displays. Success close to people does not make all open land suitable: food and places to rest and nest still matter. Breeding and life cycle The nest is a simple twig platform, with the male bringing material and the female assembling it. A clutch commonly contains two eggs. Both parents incubate and care for the young. Incubation lasts roughly two to under three weeks; young usually leave the nest after approximately another two to three weeks. Exact ranges differ between references and populations. Repeated broods are possible under favourable conditions, but their number and timing are not identical in every country. Arab-region distribution and seasonality In Lebanon and Jordan the species is a resident breeder, so an autumn sighting does not necessarily indicate migration. Saudi sources describe widespread occurrence in human-associated habitats, with limited presence in the western highlands. The UAE national assessment, conducted in 2019 and published in 2021, describes a widespread resident that increased alongside agriculture and irrigation. Breeding can occur throughout the year there, peaking in March–May. Breeding peaks elsewhere vary with local conditions. In Morocco, fieldwork in 2018–2019 linked records to settlements and farmland within the study area. Ecology and conservation The global conservation category is Least Concern. The UAE assessment also assigned Least Concern nationally, with an increasing trend; these are distinct assessment scales. A grain consumer and prey for predators, the dove participates in local food webs. Habitat changes, disturbance or disease can affect particular populations. Abundance does not establish that hunting is legal: local legislation determines species, seasons and conditions. Recording breeding birds, nests and habitats helps monitor expansion and identify important sites. articles.title: Eurasian Whimbrel
articles.body: Eurasian Whimbrel Numenius phaeopus Name and taxonomy Eurasian Whimbrel, Numenius phaeopus, belongs to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. Lebanon’s 2026 guide calls it karawan al-maa al-saghir; Kuwait’s reference uses karawan al-ghayt. It is not a stone-curlew, which belongs to another family: an Arabic common name alone is insufficient for identifying records or photographs. AviList 2026 recognises Eurasian Whimbrel separately from the American Hudsonian Whimbrel, Numenius hudsonicus. This account concerns the Eurasian species, breeding in parts of the northern Old World and spending the non-breeding season on its coasts, rather than movements or numbers of the American species. Identification It is streaked grey-brown with pale underparts. The long down-curved bill is shorter than Eurasian Curlew’s and bends more noticeably towards the tip. A pale central crown stripe lies between two dark crown bands, above a pale eyebrow. Shape and head pattern help identify it in mixed wader flocks. Flight reveals a pale back and rump and barred tail, with faster wingbeats than the larger curlew. Rapid repeated whistles are useful when details are hard to see. The sexes look broadly alike, and plumage colour does not establish sex. Age assignment needs clear feather detail; a distant image may identify the species without establishing age or sex. Habitat, food and behaviour Outside breeding it uses estuaries, intertidal mudflats, mangrove edges and sandy or rocky shores. It probes mud or picks prey from the surface, taking worms, crustaceans and other small animals. Feeding can occur by day or night according to access to food. Birds may disperse while feeding and gather at shared resting places, sometimes with other species. The coast functions as connected habitat: exposed mud supplies food at low tide and higher safe ground at high tide. Eating invertebrates places it within coastal food webs, while migration links northern and warmer ecosystems. Breeding and chick development It breeds in the north during the warmer season on open ground with low vegetation, including tundra. Territorial behaviour includes aerial displays; the nest is a shallow depression among plants. Cryptic eggs and chicks offer concealment in relatively exposed surroundings rather than an elevated tree nest. BTO records a typical clutch of four eggs, within three to five, with both parents incubating for usually 27–28 days. Downy chicks are mobile and can leave the nest site, while still needing parental care and protection. The reference gives about 35–40 days to flight, a different stage from leaving on foot. These are reference ranges, not an identical timetable for every nest. Migration and Arab occurrence Its Eurasian breeding range is patchy across the north, followed by non-breeding movements to Old World coasts. Arab occurrence primarily concerns passage and winter visitation rather than regular nesting on these shores. North African, Red Sea, Gulf and Arabian Sea coasts fall within its regional occurrence, with varying numbers and lengths of stay. Lebanon’s guide records scarce passage and winter visitation on coasts and islands. Kuwait describes common passage but rare winter and summer visitation; Oman’s database describes abundant passage and winter visitation. November therefore offers opportunities, particularly on Omani shores, with different expectations in Kuwait and Lebanon. Dated records with numbers and habitat clarify local patterns better than generalising from one bay. Conservation and responsible watching Older references list Least Concern, LC, for Whimbrel under the broader pre-split concept. AviList 2026 supplies no separate Red List category in the split Eurasian species’ record, so the earlier category is not presented as a new assessment. Protecting feeding and resting sites remains important where reclamation, oil pollution and disturbance reduce usable coast. Wait outside feeding routes and keep access to resting ground open. If your approach makes birds raise their heads or stop feeding, increase the distance. A photograph obtained without forcing flight preserves natural behaviour and leaves energy for migration and daily needs. articles.title: Eurasian Wigeon: a grazing duck connecting northern Eurasia with Arab wetland winters
articles.body: Eurasian Wigeon When a group of ducks leaves the water to graze on short grass, Eurasian Wigeon may be among them. A brightly plumaged male combines a pale forehead with a chestnut head and grey body, but the forehead is not its only identifying feature. This migratory duck links Eurasian breeding areas with wintering sites, including Arab wetlands whose value changes with water, food and freedom from disturbance. Identity card Arabic: الصواي الأوراسي; also الصواية English: Eurasian Wigeon French: Canard siffleur Scientific name: Mareca penelope; older sources use Anas penelope Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 42–52 cm Habitat: lakes, marshes, wet grassland, sheltered bays and coastal lagoons Arab-world status: chiefly passage migrant and winter visitor; abundance varies among countries Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Why watch for it in late October? This period combines continuing autumn movements with the first settlement of some ducks at wintering sites. In Saudi Arabia: passage in October–November, wintering in November–March, and no breeding. These are regional dates, not a calendar to apply uniformly from Morocco to Oman. In practice, record repeated presence, flock size and behaviour rather than assuming that the first sighting marks the completion of winter arrivals. [8] From the Maghreb to the eastern Arab world and the Gulf In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Egypt, BirdLife and its partner Nature Conservation Egypt identify Lake Nasser among its stopover and wintering sites. These examples do not describe its entire Arab range, but provide specific evidence rather than suggesting a uniform distribution across a broad map. [11] [12] In Palestine, the Wildlife Society describes it as locally common in winter and on passage. “Locally” matters: it does not mean common at every site. In the UAE: uncommon to fairly common on passage and in winter, with some summering individuals. Summer presence does not automatically establish breeding. [10] [9] Presence within a country must also be distinguished from the role of a particular site: a bird may use one lake to rest, another to feed, or stop for a few days before continuing its journey. Country lists cannot replace dated site records, and a single observation cannot establish peak timing or a long-term population trend. How can it be distinguished from similar ducks? A male in bright plumage has a chestnut head, a pale forehead stripe, a pinkish breast, a grey body and a dark rear. A large white wing patch may be visible. The bill is short, blue-grey and black-tipped, and the head is rounded: useful structural clues when colours are unclear. [2] Females are brown or grey-brown, young birds resemble them, and males in eclipse plumage become less striking. A white belly may show in flight, but is not a sufficient standalone feature. American Wigeon, especially females, and hybrids can cause confusion. If the combination of features is unclear, leaving identification unresolved is more accurate than forcing a name onto a distant photograph. [3] [6] A duck that grazes and feeds near the surface The diet is predominantly plant-based, including leaves, stems, seeds and other plant parts. Wigeon graze on land and take food at or just below the water surface, sometimes benefiting from plants brought up by other waterbirds. Invertebrates also contribute, particularly during growth and breeding. Feeding can occur by day or night, and groups resting or moving together may include other duck species. [4] [6] Life cycle: northern breeding and mobile winter quarters The breeding range lies in northern Eurasia near freshwater, including boreal woodland and tundra-edge habitats. The female selects a ground site concealed by vegetation, builds a down-lined nest, incubates and cares for the ducklings. This nesting description should not be transferred to an Arab wintering site as though the birds seen there normally breed at that location. [4] A typical clutch contains 8–9 eggs, with natural variation, and incubation takes about 24–25 days. Ducklings leave early and feed themselves under the female’s care, flying at roughly 40–45 days. Breeding is followed by moult and renewed plumage; replacement of the wing feathers brings a temporary flightless period before seasonal movements resume. [5] Value, conservation and careful observation Comparing Wigeon with Shoveler and Pintail shows that ducks sharing a wetland do not all feed in the same way. Maintaining a variety of water depths, vegetation and quiet margins therefore retains feeding and resting options. A site’s value is not only the number of birds present, but also whether they can use it without repeated disturbance. The global category is Least Concern, but local monitoring and protection against habitat loss and degradation remain necessary. Watch from a distance; do not chase birds to expose a wing patch or obtain a closer photograph. Record what you actually observed, including limits to identification confidence. Hunting permission is a separate matter governed by applicable local rules, not a species name or one day’s abundance. articles.title: European Goldfinch
articles.body: European Goldfinch Carduelis carduelis Identity and identification European Goldfinch Carduelis carduelis belongs to Fringillidae. Adults combine a red mask, black-and-white head and broad yellow wing bar; juveniles lack the red mask. The pointed conical bill extracts small seeds. A yellow wing bar alone does not distinguish it from European Greenfinch. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Orchards, farmland, woodland edges and gardens provide habitat, especially where seed-bearing plants remain. It clings to thistle heads to extract seeds and also takes insects, particularly when feeding young. Outside breeding, mobile flocks announce themselves with bright, liquid calls. Breeding and parental care The female builds a neat cup among tree branches. BTO gives a typical clutch of five eggs, incubated by the female for 12–14 days. Young leave at about 14–17 days after hatching and remain dependent on feeding afterwards. Two broods are possible; local climate and geography determine laying dates. Range and Arab occurrence Its natural range spans Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It is familiar in the Maghreb and Levant. Lebanon’s updated checklist describes a common breeding resident supplemented by passage and winter immigration. That status does not imply native residence throughout the Gulf. Seasonality and observation It can be watched throughout the year in resident areas, with flocks particularly apparent in autumn and winter. Lebanese breeding principally extends from spring into summer. November observations fit resident presence and winter additions, rather than demonstrating late nesting. Ecological role and conservation It consumes seeds and insects and benefits from varied wild vegetation. Illegal capture and trade, together with loss of edge habitats, are pressures. Leaving thistles and other seed plants to mature and reducing pesticides maintain food supplies; wild observation supports a different relationship from cage keeping. articles.title: European Serin
articles.body: European Serin A yellow orchard songbird: recognition, breeding and winter occurrence of the European Serin Identity and recognition The European Serin Serinus serinus is a very small finch, with a compact body, short comparatively stout bill and forked tail. Males show lemon-yellow on the face, breast and rump, with streaking on the back and flanks. Females are browner and less yellow; juveniles resemble them and lack the conspicuous yellow underparts. The yellow rump is visible in flight, while the rapid, continuous song adds a useful behavioural cue. Arabic references use al-Na’ar al-Urubbi, with minor spelling variants referring to the same species. Distinguishing similar birds It must be distinguished from the Syrian Serin Serinus syriacus, a separate Levantine species, and Eurasian Siskin Spinus spinus. Conspicuous streaking and the very short bill help identify European Serin. Siskin has a relatively longer, finer bill, yellow tail sides and, in males, a black cap. The two serins resemble one another, so combined views of head, wings and rump, together with voice, are preferable to judging yellow colour alone. A small yellow bird in Lebanon’s mountains is not automatically Syrian Serin. Habitat, food and behaviour Gardens, orchards, parks and woodland edges provide habitat, particularly where song and nest trees occur beside seed-bearing ground vegetation. Food includes seeds, buds, small plant parts and invertebrates. Birds may feed among short herbs before returning to trees. Populations range from resident through partially migratory to migratory, with migration more pronounced farther north. EURING connects some European winter movements with northwest Africa and records conspicuous autumn migration across Europe in October. Breeding and annual cycle The female constructs a small compact nest in a tree or shrub, using outer branches or a sheltered position near the trunk. Three or four eggs are usual. BTO summarises incubation at about 11–13 days and the nestling period at 13–18 days. More than one brood is possible. Breeding schedules vary with climate and altitude. Arab-region distribution and seasonality A study published in 2016 confirmed breeding at Anjar, Lebanon, during spring 2015 through nest and young-bird evidence. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes common winter occurrence in coastal orchards, low hills and the Beqaa, with autumn passage in October and November. Syria’s 2025 review records resident breeding in the west and winter occurrence in Al-Jazira and the Euphrates region. Jordan confirms winter-visitor status while leaving possible residency uncertain. Morocco’s 2017 checklist lists resident breeders and winter arrivals. Ecology and conservation The current global category is Least Concern and must remain distinct from the conservation-sensitive status of Syrian Serin. Its ecological role involves seed and invertebrate consumption within networks of gardens and orchards. Excessive weed removal and herbicide use reduce food-producing plants; retaining diverse ground vegetation alongside suitable nesting trees is helpful. Observing nests from a safe distance and documenting food delivery to young provide stronger breeding evidence than the presence of a singing male or a lone bird in spring. articles.title: Glossy Ibis
articles.body: Glossy Ibis Plegadis falcinellus — an iridescent wetland wanderer Name and identity The Glossy Ibis, Plegadis falcinellus, belongs to Threskiornithidae, the ibis and spoonbill family, within Pelecaniformes. This placement follows AviList 2026. Arabic references also use the name al-anuq al-lamiʿ. Its distribution spans parts of Eurasia, Africa, Australasia and the Americas. These widely separated populations do not all share one migration route, and a bird appearing at a new wetland does not establish that the species is resident or breeding there. The Lebanese guide also uses the Arabic name Abu Minjal al-lammaʿ. Recognition and similar birds From a distance it looks dark, but good light reveals chestnut body feathers and green-bronze iridescence on the wings. The long, downcurved bill, extended neck and long legs form a distinctive outline. It flies with its neck stretched forward, unlike a heron. Sexes have similar plumage and should not be assigned from an ordinary photograph. Young birds are browner and less glossy, often with pale neck streaking; non-breeding adults also lose some richness. Its feathered head distinguishes it from the Northern Bald Ibis. Apparent blackness alone is not a useful identification. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses marshes, shallow pools, flooded ground and wet farmland, including fresh and brackish habitats. Probing soft mud and picking prey from the surface, it takes insects and larvae, worms, molluscs and crustaceans, with other small aquatic prey. Feeding and roosting can be communal, sometimes alongside other waterbirds. Its occurrence near farmland does not quantify an agricultural benefit: what can be established is its place in wetland food webs and its dependence on accessible shallow water and workable mud. Breeding and movements It nests colonially, sometimes in mixed heronries. The pair builds a platform of twigs and vegetation in a tree, shrub or reedbed, and both parents contribute to brood care. Breeding timing depends on local conditions, so one regional calendar should not be applied throughout the Arab world. Post-breeding dispersal accompanies seasonal migration in some populations. Ringing studies have connected northern Algerian colonies with other western Mediterranean locations, illustrating why a network of wetlands matters rather than an isolated protected patch. Arab distribution and November context Lebanon’s updated photographic guide, published in June 2026, reports localised, irregular summer breeding at Al Mansoura and uncommon passage through coastal and inland wetlands, not regular winter visitation. Kuwait lists uncommon passage and rare winter occurrence, whereas Oman’s database describes abundant passage and winter visitation. Morocco and Algeria have documented breeding sites as well as seasonal movements; breeding at Morocco’s Sebkha Bou Areg was documented in 2024. November therefore provides a winter-wetland context in Oman, not evidence of Lebanese abundance or proof that every North African ibis is a visiting migrant. Conservation and responsible observation Globally it is Least Concern, not a guarantee that every local population is secure. Wetland drainage, pollution, pesticides, colony disturbance and killing remain concerns. Protecting reedbeds, water quality, shorelines and roosts supports its habitat needs. Observe without changing the birds’ behaviour; entering a colony for a photograph is inappropriate. Global conservation status does not determine whether hunting is legal in a particular country. articles.title: Tempted delivers Godolphin’s first Everest victory as attention turns to her next start
articles.body: Tempted leads a group of horses during The Everest at Randwick. The Australian filly reverses the 2025 result against Ka Ying Rising, with Flemington and Randwick among the options being considered. Tempted gave Godolphin its first Everest victory when she won the 1,200-metre sprint at Australia’s Randwick racecourse on Saturday, 17 October 2026. The four-year-old filly beat Ka Ying Rising, reversing the result of their meeting in the 2025 edition. Ridden by Chad Schofield and trained by Ciaron Maher, she defeated a rival who arrived with 21 consecutive victories. The result added one of Australia’s leading sprint titles to Godolphin’s record. Six wins in 2026 Bred by Godolphin in Australia, Tempted now has ten wins from 15 starts. The daughter of Street Boss and Calliope has won all six of her starts in 2026, including the Group One Surround Stakes and Everest. Two options for the next start Her next race has not been decided. In an interview published by Racing.com on 18 October, Godolphin Australia Racing and Bloodstock Manager Jason Walsh said the team was considering the 1,200-metre Champions Sprint at Flemington on 7 November. The 1,300-metre Russell Balding Stakes at Randwick on 31 October remains another option. The decision will depend on Tempted’s recovery and her trainer’s assessment. Experience on Flemington’s straight course could help inform plans for future campaigns, but any next destination remains a possibility until a decision is announced. articles.title: Goldcrest
articles.body: Goldcrest Regulus regulus Identity and identification The Goldcrest is a tiny Regulidae species with olive upperparts, pale underparts and two pale wing bars. The black-bordered crest is yellow with an orange centre in adult males and entirely yellow in females; juveniles lack the coloured crest. The absence of a bold white eyebrow and dark eye stripe helps distinguish it from Firecrest. Habitat and food It moves actively through branches, especially in conifers, picking off tiny insects. Scan the outer foliage and listen for fine calls without pursuing the bird. Breeding and development BTO reports a typical clutch of 6–8 eggs and female incubation lasting about 16–19 days. Young require care in the nest and normally fledge after 16.5–18 days. British breeding dates should not automatically be transferred to Lebanese woodland. Arab occurrence and seasonality The 2026 Lebanon guide records a scarce, localized resident breeding population alongside very rare, irregular winter visits. November observations may therefore involve local birds or visitors; all Lebanese birds should not be described as winter migrants. Observation and conservation The species is globally listed as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List; local habitat protection remains important. The Lebanon guide also identifies disturbance and illegal hunting as pressures. Protecting mixed woodland and conifers from degradation and insecticides preserves its habitat. Photograph birds from paths without approaching or revealing nest sites. articles.title: Great Egret
articles.body: Great Egret Ardea alba — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Great Egret, Ardea alba, is a large white heron in the family Ardeidae, order Pelecaniformes. Its slender silhouette combines a very long neck, long legs and a dagger-shaped bill. European birds measure approximately 85–102 cm in length, with a wingspan of 140–170 cm; measurements vary geographically. Plumage is white in both sexes and at all ages. Males average larger, but size alone rarely allows reliable sexing in the field. Juveniles resemble nonbreeding adults and lack the long ornamental back plumes. The bill is generally yellow outside breeding; breeding birds of the Eurasian population can develop a largely black bill, greenish facial skin and brighter upper legs. Bill colour must therefore be interpreted with season and population, not used as an absolute rule. Compared with Little Egret, it is substantially larger, longer-necked and lacks that species’ conspicuous yellow feet and paired nape plumes. Cattle egrets are stockier and shorter-necked. Intermediate-sized white egrets demand closer examination: in Great Egret the gape extends behind the eye. In flight the neck is folded and the legs trail behind, unlike the extended neck of a flying stork or spoonbill. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses freshwater marshes, lake margins, rivers, flooded fields and fishponds, but also lagoons, estuaries and coastal wetlands. Accessible shallow water matters more than whether a site is entirely natural. Dense reeds, trees and shrubs provide nesting or resting cover. A bird often waits motionless or walks slowly before striking at prey. Fish are important, supplemented by amphibians, aquatic invertebrates and occasionally small terrestrial vertebrates. It may feed alone or among other waterbirds, while defending a profitable feeding patch. Communal roosting does not mean that individuals cooperate while hunting. Flight is steady and deliberate; harsh calls are especially noticeable around colonies. Breeding and life cycle Breeding timing follows local conditions: spring and summer in temperate areas, with rainfall and water availability more influential farther south. Nests of sticks or reeds occur in trees, bushes or reedbeds, singly or in colonies. Courtship includes displaying the fine back plumes. A typical clutch contains 3–5 pale blue-green eggs; both parents incubate for about 25–26 days and feed the young. Young birds can climb outside the nest before they fly, usually at around six weeks. Nest departure and independence are not the same event. Distribution and regional seasonality The broadly defined species occupies extensive parts of the Americas, Africa, Eurasia and Australasia. Northern populations migrate; others disperse or remain near suitable wetlands. Arabia chiefly receives passage and winter visitors. In the Mashriq, Lebanon has passage and wintering birds, with occasional nonbreeding summer records. Egypt is principally a passage and wintering area. In the Maghreb, Moroccan and Tunisian wetlands support winter visitors and migrants; summer presence alone does not establish breeding. Ecology and conservation As a predator it links aquatic prey to wetland food webs. Global status is Least Concern, not a guarantee of local security. Drainage, altered water regimes, contaminated runoff and disturbance can degrade feeding or nesting sites. Protection needs both safe colonies and surrounding feeding habitat. Historical plume hunting illustrates how demand for ornamental feathers can damage populations. Observe from a distance and never approach a colony to obtain a closer photograph. References AviList. articles.title: Greater Flamingo
articles.body: Greater Flamingo Phoenicopterus roseus Identity and identification Greater Flamingo Phoenicopterus roseus belongs to Phoenicopteridae. Long legs and neck accompany a pink bill with a black tip. Adults are whitish pink; young birds are grey. Compared with Lesser Flamingo, it is larger with a paler bill. Pinkness alone is not a reliable identification character. It is placed in the order Phoenicopteriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Coastal lagoons, saltpans and shallow lakes provide feeding grounds. It filters small crustaceans, larvae and other aquatic organisms with its inverted bill. Dietary pigments produce its pink colour. Water depth, salinity and prey availability determine where flocks can feed. Breeding and parental care Colonies nest on mud mounds topped by a shallow hollow. Usually one egg is incubated by both parents for about 27–31 days. Both feed the chick with a nutritive secretion. Young later gather in crèches before attaining flight at roughly 65–90 days. Local water conditions influence nesting dates. Range and Arab occurrence It occurs widely around the Mediterranean, North Africa and Middle East. Abu Dhabi’s Environment Agency documents breeding at Al Wathba, whereas Lebanon’s checklist describes scarce, irregular passage and winter visits. Winter flocks therefore do not by themselves demonstrate a local breeding colony. Seasonality and observation Some Gulf sites support year-round birds alongside seasonal concentrations. In November, winter lagoons and saltpans attract mobile flocks. A colony may fail or relocate if water levels or disturbance become unsuitable. Protected viewpoints allow observation without entering crèche areas. Ecological role and conservation Conservation depends on functioning wetlands and their water regime. Pollution, altered water levels, power infrastructure collisions and disturbance are pressures. Flocks fly with necks and legs extended; repeatedly forcing them into flight costs feeding and resting time. articles.title: Green Sandpiper
articles.body: Green Sandpiper Tringa ochropus — White rump and dark wings: an Arab wetland visitor nesting in northern trees Identity and recognition The Green Sandpiper, Tringa ochropus, is a shorebird in the family Scolopacidae, not a predominantly green bird despite its English name. Dark brown, almost black upperparts contrast with a white belly and a conspicuous white rump in flight. The head and breast carry fine markings, while the tail tip shows broad dark bars. Its straight bill is dark and its legs grey-green. At roughly 21–24 cm long, it is a compact wader. Age, sex and similar species The sexes look alike. Juveniles have buff-spotted feather margins; non-breeding adults show less upperpart spotting. Green Sandpipers generally look darker than Wood Sandpipers, and the underwings appear dark in flight. Common Sandpipers show an obvious white wing stripe and lack the same broad white rump. Common Greenshanks are a different, larger species with a longer bill; their similar English names should not obscure these distinctions. A combination of rump, wing, bill and call helps resolve a brief encounter. Habitats, diet and behaviour It favours freshwater margins around pools, streams, marshes, ditches and treatment ponds, often appearing alone or in small numbers. Insects and other invertebrates are picked from the surface and shallow water; worms, crustaceans and molluscs are also eaten. It bobs its body, head or tail and gives a clear whistle when alarmed. Flight may begin low and zigzagging before the bird climbs away. This wariness helps explain why encounters can be fleeting glimpses of a white rump rather than prolonged views on an exposed shore. Breeding and life cycle Breeding occurs near water in wet wooded parts of northern Eurasia. Unusually among waders, it uses old nests of other birds in trees instead of invariably making a ground scrape. A typical clutch contains four eggs. Incubation lasts about 20–23 days, and young reach flight at approximately 27–29 days; chicks hatch down-covered and mobile. The association with water and trees on the breeding grounds contrasts with a bird using the edge of an Arab pond during migration. Both habitats support different stages of the same annual cycle. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes fairly common spring and autumn passage and scarce November–February winter occurrence. Qatar lists a common passage migrant and winter visitor, with records in every month; Oman describes abundant passage and winter occurrence. Regional references also document its presence in Egypt, Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania. The end of October passage in the Levant thus connects with winter residence elsewhere. Small pools can matter alongside larger wetlands for this dispersed species. Ecology and conservation Its global conservation category is Least Concern. An invertebrate consumer and prey for predators, it belongs to shallow-water food webs; its ecological importance is not measured by flock size alone. Draining pools, removing natural margins and polluting water can reduce feeding and resting opportunities. Because it uses ditches and small waterbodies, even a localized alteration of a stream edge can affect its habitat. Clean water, varied shallow margins and nearby cover, together with observation from a respectful distance, help birds use successive stopovers without repeated disturbance. articles.title: Griffon Vulture
articles.body: Griffon Vulture Gyps fulvus Identity and identification Griffon Vulture Gyps fulvus belongs to Accipitridae. Large, with broad wings, dark flight feathers and a pale-brown body, it has a long pale-down-covered neck with a ruff at the base. The tail is relatively short. Juveniles differ; large size alone cannot separate vultures and eagles. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It searches widely for carrion above mountains and plains, using rising air. Feeding is often social and requires available, safe carcasses. A vulture near livestock is not evidence of attacks on healthy animals: carrion is its principal resource. Breeding and parental care Colonies occupy cliff ledges and pairs usually lay one egg. Both parents incubate and feed the chick regurgitated food; rearing takes months. A slow reproductive cycle makes adult loss and nest failure consequential. One successful season cannot readily replace a lost breeding pair. Range and Arab occurrence Its Mediterranean and western Asian range includes Arab mountain regions, with local declines or losses. Lebanon’s checklist documents historical breeding but uncertain current resident and breeding status, alongside scarce passage. Historical records must not be presented as proof of a colony active today. Seasonality and observation Residents may be seen year-round near occupied areas, with movements beyond them. November mountain viewpoints help locate soaring birds. Never use an unverified carcass to attract vultures: an ordinary appearance does not establish freedom from poison. Ecological role and conservation Carrion removal is a major role, but poisoning, electrical hazards and disturbance threaten it. One contaminated carcass can kill several birds. Nest protection, poison prevention and organised livestock-carcass management belong together; supplementary feeding needs specialist management. articles.title: Hen Harrier
articles.body: Hen Harrier Circus cyaneus Identity and identification The Hen Harrier is an Accipitridae raptor with long wings and tail. Adult males have a grey head and breast, pale belly and extensive black wingtips. Females and juveniles are brown with a white rump, but that feature alone does not identify every harrier. Habitat and food It quarters fields, open ground and wetlands in low flight for small mammals and birds. Wing shape, plumage and flight style together help separate it from Pallid and Montagu’s Harriers. Breeding and development BTO reports a typical clutch of 4–5 eggs and female incubation of about 34 days. Young depend on parental care and normally fledge after 36.5–41.5 days. These general stages do not demonstrate breeding in a passage or wintering country. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor. Oman’s official list, version 8.0 dated 1 January 2026, gives the same broad status. November belongs to the passage and wintering context; a sighting does not establish local breeding. Observation and conservation The Hen Harrier is globally classified as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List. Deliberate persecution and loss of feeding and breeding habitat threaten it. Watch raptors from a distance without pursuing them or approaching communal roosts. Reducing poisoning and electrocution and retaining open habitat supports their conservation. articles.title: Hunting Tourism in Egypt, Iraq and Jordan
articles.body: A traditional boat in the Iraqi marshes; transport and guiding are among the services associated with visits to natural environments. Local services, the cost of organising a trip and falconry in Burqu: three different ways of examining how hunting tourism can contribute to development. When a hunter travels to another country, they are not buying only an opportunity to hunt. They need somewhere to sleep, a guide who knows the terrain, transport, food and services throughout the trip. This is where economic value can begin to reach villages and areas far from major tourism centres. But that benefit is not automatic: a trip may be expensive while local people receive very little of its value. After our visits to the Gulf countries and the Maghreb, we conclude this series in Egypt, Iraq and Jordan. Three different cases raise one question: how can regulated hunting, where it is permitted, become an activity that serves the local economy without depleting the wildlife on which it depends? Lake Qarun in Fayoum: natural diversity that can enrich the visitor experience. Egypt: the value of a trip lies in what surrounds the hunt Egypt offers enough variety to combine several experiences in one trip. In Fayoum, for example, the Egyptian Tourism Authority presents a mix of countryside, lakes, desert, traditional crafts and local food. These services can extend a visitor’s stay and spending, rather than limiting the visit to one activity and a few hours. For the organiser of a licensed hunting trip, this means opportunities to buy services from rural accommodation providers, hire local drivers and guides, and add a craft visit or a meal featuring the area’s cuisine. But the presence of a lake or an abundance of birds does not make a place available for hunting. The tourism product must be built around the permits, species, sites and dates that are allowed, not an attractive advertising photograph. In 2026, the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency announced the implementation of Decision No. 559 regulating hunting, alongside campaigns against violations in Burullus. These measures show that regulating the season and protecting places where birds congregate are two aspects of managing the same resource. A responsible trip cannot be marketed outside the rules that protect it. Burullus also offers a practical example of broadening bird-related sources of income. Nature Conservation Egypt reports that a programme began in 2023 to train bird hunters and a local tourism agency in birdwatching, and that Camp Burullus worked with a hunter who uses his boat for these trips. The man retained the value of his knowledge of the area and the usefulness of his boat while offering visitors a different service. This does not make birdwatching another name for hunting. It demonstrates how local work can be diversified, particularly where hunting is prohibited at a site or its season has ended. A guide who understands birds’ movements can also help people watch and photograph them, while boats, accommodation and food retain their value after the season ends. Qasr Burqu and the lake in Jordan’s Badia — archive photo A broader trip, a wider benefit Accommodation, guiding, transport, food and local crafts widen the circle of people who benefit from a hunter’s visit, without requiring more game to be taken. Iraq: regulating entry is not enough to create development Iraq’s rules for the 2025–2026 season clearly illustrate that receiving foreign hunting groups requires arrangements extending beyond booking accommodation. The document published through the UAE Embassy in Baghdad set a season from 1 December 2025 to 1 February 2026, with groups of five to fifteen hunters, entry procedures, security escorts and a temporary hunting permit from the Ministry of Agriculture. The cost table listed US$125,000 for a group of five hunters, including US$25,000 for food and transport for the accompanying security detachments. These figures concern the arrangements for that particular season. They are not a current price for a tourism package, nor evidence of how much reached local communities. This is the economic question: what share goes towards procedures and security services, and what share becomes wages for local guides, purchases from producers, accommodation, meals and transport within the area? Regulatory fees and costs alone do not answer that question, however high they may be. If this activity is to serve development, local services should be an explicit part of its design: contracts with transport and accommodation providers, training for guides who know the permitted species and limits, and purchases whose benefits to local people can be tracked. Protecting habitats and water remains a prerequisite for the continuity of any economy that depends on wildlife. Discussing Iraq’s wetlands here does not automatically make the marshes hunting grounds. Their tourism and ecological value is broader than that, and any activity must comply with the site’s legal status and applicable restrictions. Nor do the rules for a past season establish that a new season has opened on the same terms. Where does a visitor’s spending go? Measuring local wages and purchases reveals a trip’s contribution to development more accurately than looking only at the amount of its fees. Jordan: falconry becomes a tourism experience in Burqu In the northeastern Badia, the Burqu area provides a direct example of the connection between hunting with falcons and travel and accommodation services. The Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature presents an experience in training falcons using captive-bred houbara bustards, within an area covering no more than 20% of the reserve. In November 2025, the society included Burqu’s sustainable-hunting experience among successful case studies implemented in its reserves. The tourism dimension of this experience is apparent in the programme offered to visitors to Jordan by Falconry Experiences. According to its published services, the trip begins with the reception of falconers at Queen Alia International Airport or the Al-Omari border crossing. It includes accommodation, meals, four-wheel-drive transport and guides, as well as facilities for caring for falcons. The visitor is buying not an isolated activity but a trip combining hospitality, transport, guiding and specialist services. This is not an invitation to hunt wild birds without restrictions. Under the programme rules published by the company, captive-bred houbara are specified for falcon training, and the use of guns is excluded from this experience. The distinction matters: organised falconry tourism does not mean opening the entire reserve to hunting or treating wild houbara populations as a resource freely available to visitors. Through these advertised services, Burqu shows how a trip’s economic value extends to what surrounds the hunt: accommodation, food, transport, field knowledge and bird care. These are the services that can connect visitors with the area’s economy, rather than reducing a visit to the number of birds taken. How much of that value reaches residents, however, requires data on employment and local procurement. The existence of a programme cannot be turned into an assumed number of jobs or an unverified revenue figure. A complete trip, not unrestricted hunting Falcon training with captive-bred houbara, accommodation, transport and guiding are specific elements of the Burqu experience, not general permission to hunt wild birds. What remains for local people? This tour brings together three lessons: diversify the services within a trip, distinguish its cost from the share that reaches residents, and connect the activity with specific travel and accommodation services. Successful hunting tourism does not require open-ended promises of abundant game. It needs a protected natural resource, enforceable rules and a service that makes visitors want to return. At the end of this series, the yardstick remains simple: when a hunter leaves, do they leave behind income, skills and opportunities for the local community, while wildlife remains capable of renewing itself? Only then does the idea of hunting as a resource for development become more than an appealing headline. articles.title: International shooting: Ratner handed three-year ineligibility sanction and €30,000 fine
articles.body: Archive aerial view of the Olympic shooting facility near Munich. Illustrative image, unrelated to the case. The ISSF announces sanctions against Alexander Ratner over the European Shooting Confederation’s 2025 presidential election. The International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) announced on 8 November 2026 that Alexander Ratner, a member of its Council and Executive Committee, had been sanctioned with a three-year period of ineligibility and a €30,000 fine in connection with the European Shooting Confederation’s presidential election held in Yerevan in October 2025. According to the statement, the Integrity Unit’s independent Adjudicatory Panel found violations involving improper influence over the electoral process, gender-based discriminatory statements and the concealment of election recordings during the investigation. The decision was issued on 6 November and is immediately enforceable. It may be appealed before the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but an appeal does not suspend enforcement of the sanctions unless the court orders otherwise. As for the sanction’s implications for Ratner’s candidacy for the ISSF presidency, the statement said the Electoral and Nominations Commission would decide the matter early the following week. Ratner’s name appeared on the candidate list published on 14 October, ahead of the elections scheduled for 13–14 December in Rome. When publishing the list, the federation noted that eligibility could be reassessed if new information emerged or circumstances changed. articles.title: Lesser Crested Tern
articles.body: Lesser Crested Tern Thalasseus bengalensis A black crest and a warm-coloured bill The Lesser Crested Tern, Thalasseus bengalensis, is a graceful seabird in the gull and tern family, Laridae. Arabic names also describe it as the small crowned tern or Bengal tern. Its populations connect Arab breeding islands with distant feeding and resting shores, from Libya, the Red Sea and the Gulf to the Indian Ocean. It measures about 35–43 cm long, with a wingspan of approximately 88–105 cm. It is larger than the smallest, delicate terns, but less bulky than Greater Crested Tern, which may stand beside it in the same flock. The adult has a long orange to yellow-orange bill, a black cap ending in a crest, and black feet. Its upperparts are grey and underparts white, with grey extending over the rump and centre of the tail. Outside the breeding season, the forehead becomes white, while black remains more evident behind the eye and on the nape. This change does not mean that the bird belongs to another species or is ill: it is part of the annual plumage cycle. Males and females look similar, and cap colour alone cannot distinguish them. Separating similar terns Direct comparison with Greater Crested Tern is helpful. The latter is bulkier and has a heavier bill that is usually more yellow, whereas Lesser Crested is slimmer and its bill tends towards orange. Adult Sandwich Tern normally has a black bill with a yellow tip. The rump and tail colour, bill shape and body proportions provide further useful evidence. Bill colour by itself does not establish identity in a photograph with strong lighting or an unnatural colour balance. A juvenile carries markings on its wing and back feathers rather than the adult’s cleaner surfaces, and its bill may look paler or duller. In autumn, young birds that can already fly may continue following their parents and asking them for food. It is therefore important to distinguish downy chicks near an active colony from a fully feathered juvenile that has reached a distant shore. The latter’s presence does not establish that it hatched at the place where it was seen. Fishing from the air and resting ashore This tern searches for small fish and crustaceans in coastal waters, in and beyond the surf zone. It flies over the surface scanning the water and may hover briefly before plunging head first towards its prey, then returning to the air. It can also take food close to the surface. This behaviour sustains its marine life and allows parents to carry fish to chicks. Their success nevertheless depends on prey of a suitable size being available within waters they can reach. It uses beaches, sandy islands and exposed resting sites, often mixing with other tern species. A breeding colony, a roost and a feeding flock do not necessarily occupy the same place. An island suitable for laying eggs also needs accessible marine food resources, while a winter beach holding hundreds of birds may never be used for nesting. Conserving the species therefore means protecting breeding islands, the waters that supply their food, and safe places used during movements between them. Life inside the colony The pair nests in a shallow ground scrape within colonies that can be extremely dense. The Saudi reference describes a usual clutch of one egg and incubation lasting 22–25 days, with both parents sharing incubation and care. Mediterranean sources give slightly different ranges and occasionally two eggs. The contents of a single nest should therefore not be treated as an absolute rule for every population. Exposed nests are concentrated on low ground, where the shade provided by a parent’s body becomes important in hot weather. Chicks leave their individual nest sites after a few days and gather in crèches protected and fed by adult birds. Flight usually begins at about a month, with a range of 32–35 days in the Saudi reference. Flying does not end parental care: the Gulf ringing study published in 2017 describes young remaining dependent for additional months. This explains why a juvenile may beg for fish away from its natal island and why quiet surroundings and feeding areas remain important after egg laying has ended. Arab countries on two marine routes Libya is the main Mediterranean breeding centre for the regional population. Research programmes have studied its island colonies and coastal nesting around Benghazi, and ringing has linked them with the West African route. This does not imply breeding in every country the birds pass through. A regional Mediterranean assessment reports small numbers in winter counts along the coasts of Libya, Algeria and Morocco, while many birds travel farther. Such winter occurrence is different from the presence of a substantial breeding colony. Farther east, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden reports document breeding in Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia. In the Gulf, established colonies occur in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, confirmed by joint ringing research rather than simply by lists of passing birds. Qatar’s current checklist describes the species as a resident breeder, with winter visitors, passage migrants and records in every month. The Saudi reference describes a common breeding migrant from April to October, with smaller numbers in other months. These accounts need not be made identical: each refers to a country and its local pattern. Autumn movements and modern taxonomy Libyan and Gulf birds do not necessarily follow the same winter route. Ringing studies show movement from the Libyan population through northwestern Africa towards wintering areas farther down the continent’s western side. Gulf research instead records birds ringed in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia reaching the Indian subcontinent. These are records of identifiable ringed individuals. They do not mean that every bird from a colony travels to one destination, or that every individual seen in November belongs to a particular breeding site. AviList 2026 distinguishes the subspecies emigratus, breeding in Libya, from bengalensis, which breeds in the Red Sea and Gulf and connects with the Indian Ocean. Some older papers used different subspecies arrangements. Their field records of ringed birds remain informative even when the taxonomic names change. For an observer, practical identification should first establish the species. November offers opportunities to study non-breeding coastal groups, recording ages and rings that can be read from a distance without pursuing their wearers. Protection from sand to sea AviList 2026 lists Lesser Crested Tern as globally Least Concern. Nevertheless, concentrating many nests on a limited number of islands creates considerable local vulnerability. Coastal construction, damage to islands, egg collection, introduced predators, pollution and disruption of food supplies can affect an entire colony. Low-lying nesting places also need attention to inundation and shoreline change. Abundance across the world is not a justification for losing one of the species’ Arab breeding or resting sites. Visits should follow permitted routes and remain far enough away to avoid flushing adults or causing chick groups to rush away. Observers should not land on a breeding island merely because it seems uninhabited by people, nor separate a juvenile from its group to finish a photograph. A clearly visible ring can be documented with binoculars or a long lens and reported to the relevant ringing organisation. Protecting this tern requires continuity between countries: the Arab breeding island, migration stopover and winter shore are interconnected parts of the same bird’s life. articles.title: Little Ringed Plover
articles.body: Little Ringed Plover Thinornis dubius Identity and identification Little Ringed Plover belongs to Charadriidae in the order Charadriiformes. Its Arabic name is الزقزاق المطوق الصغير and its French name Petit Gravelot. The accepted scientific combination is Thinornis dubius; many references use the older Charadrius dubius for the same species. At about 14–17 cm, it is a delicately built plover with a slender dark bill, grey-brown upperparts and white underparts. Its yellow eye-ring is particularly conspicuous in breeding plumage. Breeding adults show a dark breast band and a black-and-white head pattern. The female’s markings are usually less black; juveniles and non-breeding birds are duller and their breast band may weaken or become incomplete. An incomplete band alone therefore does not establish Kentish Plover. Compared with Common Ringed Plover, look for the dark bill, finer build, eye-ring and absence of a conspicuous white wingbar. Use several characters rather than leg colour alone. Habitat, food and behaviour Open freshwater margins are important: river shingle, small islands, and the edges of pools and reservoirs. Flooded gravel workings and other artificial sites can provide habitat where suitable bare ground remains. Coastal and muddy habitats are also used during movements; a freshwater preference does not mean exclusive dependence on fresh water. It hunts small invertebrates with short runs, pauses and picking movements, sometimes trembling a foot to disturb hidden prey. Small, loose groups may gather. Watching feeding behaviour explains why a shallow, exposed edge matters, rather than simply the area of open water. Water can remain while the usable margin disappears. Breeding and development The nest is a simple ground scrape, with eggs that blend remarkably well with stones. BTO gives a usual clutch of four eggs, with recorded extremes of three to five. Both parents incubate, typically for 24–25 days; young normally reach flight age about 25–27 days after hatching. Downy chicks become mobile early. Leaving the egg site therefore does not mean independence or an ability to fly. These are general developmental intervals, not a universal breeding calendar. A summer adult alone is not proof of nesting: evidence should be reliable and collected without endangering birds. Range and Arab occurrence The range extends from Europe and North Africa across Asia. Northern populations migrate to Africa, southern Asia and Southeast Asia, while parts of southern Asia hold resident populations. In the Arab region, the 2026 Lebanon guide describes a rare summer breeder and common passage migrant on wetlands, islands and shores. Oman’s official list records an uncommon breeder, passage migrant and winter visitor. These categories describe genuine national differences; the Omani breeding category does not establish that every individual is resident. Kuwait’s rarities committee list describes an uncommon passage migrant, scarce winter and summer visitor, with breeding recorded previously. What November means In November, passage and wintering should be distinguished. A bird at suitable Omani habitat fits the recorded winter status, whereas Lebanon’s seasonal description does not justify expecting a regular winter population. Record numbers, dates, shoreline conditions and water levels: a single visit cannot distinguish a brief stop from a longer stay. Duller November plumage still retains useful identification characters. Conservation and responsible observation Globally the species is Least Concern (LC), but individual sites remain vulnerable. The Lebanon guide identifies habitat loss, pollution and illegal hunting among pressures. Walking across gravel or reshaping banks can affect the places it needs. Observe with binoculars from an established route, avoiding exposed islands and searches for eggs. If a bird repeatedly retreats or alarms, move away rather than press closer for a photograph. A quiet shoreline is a significant conservation resource. articles.title: Little Stint
articles.body: Little Stint Calidris minuta — A tiny shorebird linking Arctic tundra with Arab passage and winter shores Identity and recognition The Little Stint, Calidris minuta, is a tiny shorebird in the family Scolopacidae, with a fine straight black bill, black legs and white underparts. Approximately 12–14 cm long, it is markedly smaller than the Dunlins that may accompany it. Plumage changes seasonally: breeding birds show rufous tones on the head and upperparts with dark markings, while winter birds become predominantly grey above. Bill, body and leg proportions remain useful when the warm colours have faded. Age, sex and similar species The sexes look similar in the field. Juveniles have pale feather edges and light lines on the back that can form a V-shaped pattern, appearing more patterned than winter adults. Temminck’s Stints have paler olive or yellowish legs; Dunlins have longer, more curved bills. Sanderlings are larger and much paler in winter. Red-necked Stints can be particularly similar outside breeding plumage. Unusual records therefore benefit from clear photographs showing several views rather than identification based only on breast colour. Habitats, diet and behaviour Exposed mud, lake margins, lagoons, saltpans and intertidal flats provide feeding habitat in fresh and saline water. It runs quickly and picks small prey from the surface or extremely shallow water. Foods include insects and their larvae, crustaceans, small molluscs and worms. It may join mixed flocks, then gather at resting sites when rising water covers the feeding flats. A bare shore is consequently not empty ground for this bird: it is a feeding surface supported by small animals and the timing of mud exposure. Breeding and life cycle Breeding takes place on northern Eurasian tundra, far from Arab passage and wintering sites. A typical clutch contains four eggs; incubation lasts roughly 20–25 days and young fly at approximately 15–21 days. Chicks hatch down-covered and mobile. Arctic studies describe a system in which one parent can care for a clutch alone; a female may leave one clutch with a male and tend another. Summer invertebrate availability provides resources for rapid chick growth. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records common spring and autumn passage, the latter from early August to late October. In Qatar it is a common passage migrant and winter visitor recorded in every month; Oman lists abundant passage and winter occurrence. The UAE national assessment distinguishes birds staying for winter from those continuing south, with some immatures remaining through summer. Western wintering sites extend to Mauritania, where waterbird counts document its presence. Late October may thus mark the end of passage in one country and the beginning of a longer stay in another. Ecology and conservation Its global category is Least Concern, but dependence on successive safe sites makes shore and roost protection important throughout the journey. The UAE assessment identifies potential pressures from changing coastal land use and oil pollution. As an invertebrate consumer and prey for raptors, it participates in wetland food webs. Unreclaimed mudflats, clean shallow water and quiet resting sites help maintain habitat functions. A crowded flock at one location does not by itself establish the trend across an entire migratory flyway. articles.title: Long-legged Buzzard
articles.body: Long-legged Buzzard Buteo rufinus Identity and identification Long-legged Buzzard Buteo rufinus belongs to Accipitridae. Broad wings, often a pale head and a frequently rufous, sparsely barred adult tail are useful clues. Colour forms overlap with Common Buzzard. Combine carpal patches, wing and tail patterns and proportions rather than relying on rufous colour. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Steppe, semidesert, slopes and open farmland provide hunting grounds. Rodents, reptiles, small birds and invertebrates contribute to its diet. It watches from a perch or soars before attacking. The importance of each prey group varies with habitat and availability. Breeding and parental care A twig nest stands on rocks or in a tree and may be reused. A small southwestern Iranian study documented three-egg clutches, incubation around 31 days and parental cooperation. This is a local sample, not a universal value; young require weeks of care before independence. Range and Arab occurrence Its range spans North Africa and parts of the Middle East and Asia. Lebanon’s checklist describes a breeding resident supplemented by passage and winter birds. Geographical populations vary; appearance or a single sighting cannot determine an individual’s origin or migration strategy. Seasonality and observation Lebanese residents can be seen in November alongside possible immigrants. Suitable thermal conditions permit distant observation of soaring birds. Clear wing and tail views are important, especially when several buzzard species migrate together. Ecological role and conservation Rodent predation connects it with open-country food webs. Poisons, pesticides, electrocution, persecution and habitat loss are pressures. Raptor protection requires careful rodent and poison management because contaminated prey can transfer toxins to predators. articles.title: Marbled Duck
articles.body: Marbled Duck Marmaronetta angustirostris Identification beyond the marbled pattern Marbled Duck Marmaronetta angustirostris, also called Marbled Teal, is a small duck about 39–42 cm long. Its sandy grey-brown plumage carries pale spots across the back and flanks, contrasting with a darker eye mask. A slim dark bill and slightly elongated feathers behind the head complete its appearance. Unlike many familiar ducks, the sexes have broadly similar plumage rather than a brightly coloured male and a plainly patterned female. Males tend to be a little larger, with more developed rear head feathers, but these differences are subtle in the field. Juveniles are generally greyer and show less distinct spotting. Female teal and other small brown ducks can cause confusion at a distance: assess the mask, bill, overall pale appearance and pattern together. In flight, pale underwings and relatively pale secondaries contrast with darker wing tips; a fleeting view alone is not always sufficient. A specialist of shallow, vegetated water The species uses shallow wetlands with emergent and submerged vegetation, often brackish, seasonal or semi-permanent. Open feeding spaces among plants are valuable, as are sheltered margins. It can use managed or artificial wetlands, but their suitability depends on water quality, depth and vegetation. A reservoir's mere existence does not guarantee appropriate habitat for a duck adapted to shallow feeding areas. Its movements reflect changing water conditions. Seasonal wetlands may become highly productive after filling, yet dry too early for breeding to succeed. Conservation therefore requires a connected choice of sites that retain useful habitat at different times. Deepening an entire wetland or clearing all its vegetation can remove the shallow margins on which the species depends, even if water storage increases. Food and daily behaviour Marbled Ducks take seeds, other plant material and aquatic invertebrates. Feeding commonly occurs near the surface or in very shallow water rather than through the sustained deep diving associated with pochards. Their fine bills are suited to collecting small food items among vegetation. A bird's use of a particular pool may consequently change as water retreats and accessible feeding areas shift. Diet studies show differences between ages and places: small aquatic seeds are especially important to adults, while ducklings take proportionally more invertebrates. At Sidi Moussa in Morocco, autumn samples contained many Ruppia seeds together with charophytes and midge larvae. Food composition changed in spring. Larger young have occasionally been seen diving for food, although surface feeding remains much more characteristic of the species. Nesting and the demands of brood rearing Nests are concealed near water, beneath dense vegetation or shrubs; breeding accounts also describe nests among emergent aquatic plants. The species can lay a relatively large clutch. SEO/BirdLife reports an average of about twelve eggs in its account, with unusually large clutches potentially involving more than one female. The female incubates for approximately 25–27 days. These values describe the species' biology and should not be interpreted as proof of a particular local breeding event. The young leave the nest and feed for themselves, usually accompanied by the female; some males also remain with broods. Green’s CSIC synthesis reports flight at 50–54 days in captivity, a reference that should not be read as a measured fledging age for every wild population. Birds can breed at one year old. Late nesting makes persistent shallow water and cover particularly important during the ducklings’ development. Range, movements and North African populations The global distribution is fragmented across the Mediterranean region, south-west Asia and parts of Africa. Movements include migration and dispersal in response to wetland conditions. SEO/BirdLife describes movements between Morocco and Andalusia across the Strait of Gibraltar, which may occur outside a simple spring-and-autumn timetable. This flexibility helps birds find water but does not make wholesale habitat loss harmless. Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia form part of its established western breeding range, as documented by international waterfowl reviews. They also hold birds outside the nesting season, with local occupation depending on hydrology. Libya requires a more specific statement: Etayeb and colleagues established breeding at Mallaha, Tripoli, from two ducklings found in June 2012 and identified genetically. Their 2014 paper is firm evidence for that event, not a measure of the present size or regularity of Libya's breeding population. Iraq and other Arab countries Iraq is important for both local breeding and wintering. Salim and colleagues' national review describes resident breeding in central wetlands and a wider distribution in the southern marshes. The KBA account for Dalmaj independently identifies it as a major breeding area. Counts and conditions at individual marshes can change greatly, so older assessments of international importance should not be mistaken for current population totals. AEWA lists Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Oman as vagrant countries. Oman's official bird list likewise treats it as a vagrant. These classifications differ fundamentally from Iraqi or North African breeding status. AEWA records native occurrence in Syria, Jordan and Egypt, but that broad category alone does not establish a regular season or breeding population in each country. National and site-specific evidence is needed before making stronger claims. Conservation and field records The 2022 IUCN Red List assessment classifies Marbled Duck globally as Near Threatened (NT). Drainage, unsuitable water management, pollution and loss of vegetation affect the food and shelter needed by adults and ducklings. Protecting a single wetland is not enough if it repeatedly dries or becomes isolated from alternative sites. Successful management needs to follow both the annual water cycle and the longer alternation of wet and dry years. Watch from a distance and avoid driving broods into open water. Record the habitat and behaviour as well as numbers, and document ducklings without approaching their refuge. A dated record from an unexpected country is valuable, but it should be assessed as an individual occurrence before being used to revise maps of breeding or regular migration. articles.title: Al-Melwah closes with 60 winners and a wider field
articles.body: A falconer holds a falcon during the exhibition’s 2026 Al-Melwah activities, photographed before the final day. Al-Melwah racing concluded on 9 October 2026 at the International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition in Malham, north of Riyadh, with 60 winners recognised over six days. According to the Saudi Press Agency report carried by UrduPoint, SAR 723,000 in prizes covered the top five places in each of the twelve heats. Two winners lead the final day The closing day featured two heats for local owners and amateurs. In the Gyr-Shaheen heat, Ali Khalifa Al-Mansouri won with “8”, followed by Baddah Al-Dosari with “Hakem” and Rashed Al-Duaij with “018”. In Gyr-Taba, Majed Al-Qahtani took first place with “Ateem”. Fahad Hajras Al-Dosari with “Jabr” and Fahad Mohammed Al-Dosari with “378” finished second and third. Twice as many heats The programme expanded from six heats last year to twelve: six for owners and amateurs and six for professionals and elite competitors. The expansion creates two competitive pathways, with five prize-winning places in each heat. Across 200 metres from the starting point, known as the sanah, to the lure, or melwah, the race tests a falcon's speed and responsiveness. It also puts the falconer's training to a practical test, bringing a living heritage into a setting where performance and results can be followed. From breeding farms to competition Entry was restricted to young falcons purchased at the International Falcon Breeders Auction. This connection gives farm-bred falcons a direct place in competition: acquisition begins at the auction, training prepares the bird, and racing tests its abilities. Alongside its awards, the expanded Al-Melwah programme offers a window into the practical skills of falconry. Racing ended on 9 October, while the exhibition programme runs through 10 October.

articles.title: From Sayd’s Memory: A Journey of Awareness and Responsibility… Personalities and Voices in Nature’s Sanctuary (2016–2024)
articles.body: Prepared by: Editorial Board Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar — from Sayd magazine’s archive. Since its launch, Sayd magazine was never merely a platform for hobby details and equipment. It was a dialogue space that brought together artists, poets, businesspeople, and pioneering women of the outdoors under one ethical charter: respect for nature, compliance with the law, and opposition to random hunting. Here we revisit, in a documented chronological sequence, some of the most notable conversations Sayd’s pages carried that embody this long record: March 2016 | Businessman-hunter George Khashan: “Maturity leads us to protect nature” In early 2016, businessman George Khashan offered a responsible reading of the hunter’s relationship with the wild, explaining that protecting game begins with self-discipline before fear of enforcement. He said: “I do not hunt in large quantities out of fear of the law, but so that I can keep going hunting and so the next generation can go too… There is no written law in nature itself; we are the ones who set it through our ethics and upbringing.” September 2016 | Artist Nicola Al-Asta: “Hunting is a refined sport spoiled by selfishness” In autumn 2016, the magazine met Lebanese artist Nicola Al-Asta, who spoke of his long-standing love of the mountain and offered a model of an artist who sees the gun as a means of contemplation and calm, not of boasting about bags. With his characteristic candor he said: “My mother used to consider me a ‘hapless’ hunter… but for me hunting is art, patience, and a renewal of positive energy. Hunting is a refined school of ethics, and the worst thing in it is human greed and the selfishness of turning it into a slaughter.” August 2020 | Visual artist Mukhtar Hadi Yazbek: A brush that distinguishes the hunter from the “indiscriminate shooter” In summer 2020, the magazine recorded a distinctive artistic contribution by Mukhtar Hadi Yazbek, who designed two paintings adopted by the Society for the Protection of Nature in Lebanon (SPNL) and the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting for regional awareness work. He told the magazine: “The language of color crosses borders; with my brush I wanted to document the fundamental difference between a sustainable hunter who respects balance and an indiscriminate shooter who assaults wildlife.” November 2022 | Poet and journalist Hani Nadeem: “What spoils hunting is lack of awareness” In late 2022, poet Hani Nadeem spoke in depth, treating his going to the mountain as a return to humanity’s first roots before the falsehood of modernity. He said: “I return as a real human being without the cosmetics of city life… I am a son of the land and the soil. Hunting is a sport of nobles, and what spoils it is only lack of awareness and recklessness toward the environment—which requires firmness and strict application of the law.” February 2024 | Lebanese hunter Sarah Akiki: “Hunting is communion with the land and a challenge with elegance” In early 2024 the magazine devoted distinctive space to women’s presence, interviewing agricultural engineer Sarah Akiki, who trained in hunting from childhood. She pushed back against the traditional view of the woman hunter, affirming: “Abroad, a woman does not lose her femininity if she practices hunting, and woman has been a hunter since time immemorial. What matters to me is not the number of bags but the pleasure of walking and connecting with nature, and our care as women hunters for keeping the mountain clean and not leaving trash far exceeds that of others.” February 2024 | Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar: “Learn from the woman how to be a hunter, not a show-off” Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar — from Sayd magazine’s archive. In the same month, the magazine documented the experience of Rita Habib Al-Shaar, a Lebanese mother who combines family commitments with a passion for regulated hunting, raising a firm cry against chaos and night hunting: “Hunting is joy, calm, and adventure. The value of hunting is not in boasting by posting numbers of dead birds as a crime of extermination, but in preserving balance… And my constant message to the Ministry of Environment: no leniency with night hunting and violators.” In closing, this timeline shows that Sayd was never a fleeting publication, but a living record of shifts in environmental awareness in our community, and a platform where different groups—from stars, intellectuals, and businesspeople to women hunters and field pioneers—met to root an unchanging principle: hunting is an art, a responsibility, and a true partnership to protect the land.
