articles.title: Moustached Warbler
articles.body: Moustached Warbler Acrocephalus melanopogon Identity and identification The Moustached Warbler is an Acrocephalidae species with a broad pale eyebrow contrasting with a dark crown and darker cheek. It has streaked brown upperparts and pale underparts with brownish flanks; a clear view of the head helps separate similar reedbed warblers. Habitat and food It searches aquatic vegetation and reeds for small invertebrates, including beetles and tiny snails. Dense wetland vegetation is central to its habitat, making drainage and reed burning important pressures. Breeding and development SEO/BirdLife describes a cup nest within aquatic vegetation and a clutch of 3–6 eggs. Both parents incubate for about 14–15 days and feed the chicks, which become capable of flight at around 12 days. Breeding dates vary between regions. Arab occurrence and seasonality The 2026 Lebanon guide lists it as a common summer breeder, scarce passage migrant and rare winter visitor. Its breeding abundance does not imply similar winter numbers; this account does not give precise dates for autumn passage. Observation and conservation The species is globally listed as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List; local habitat protection remains important. The Lebanon guide also lists pesticides and illegal hunting among the pressures affecting the species. Wait for it at a vegetation edge rather than forcing a route through reeds. Failure to detect this secretive bird during a short visit does not establish absence. articles.title: Namaqua Dove
articles.body: Namaqua Dove Oena capensis A small dove with an unusually long tail The Namaqua Dove, Oena capensis, belongs to the pigeon and dove family, Columbidae, but its proportions are quite unlike those of a familiar domestic pigeon. Its total length is about 28 centimetres, much of which is contributed by a long, pointed tail. The body itself is small and slender, with a little head and a delicate appearance. On the ground it walks in short steps while collecting seeds. Total length therefore gives a misleading impression of bulk when this bird is compared with a much heavier dove. The adult male has a striking black face, throat and upper breast, contrasting with grey on the head and neck and white on the belly. His bill has reddish or orange colouring and a yellow tip. Dark spots on the wing can show blue or purple iridescence when the light catches them. That sheen is not visible from every angle, so its absence in a distant photograph is not an exclusion feature. Both sexes show chestnut colouring in the wings in flight, together with the distinctive trailing tail. Females, young birds and possible confusion The female lacks the male's extensive black mask and has a darker bill and less conspicuous overall colouring. Juveniles have more spotted or pale-edged plumage and can resemble the female more closely than an adult male. A bird without a black face is therefore not necessarily another species, and absence of the mask alone does not distinguish an adult female from a juvenile. Wing and shoulder feather patterns, bill colour, good photographs and the date all help to resolve that question. Laughing and Eurasian Collared Doves are more substantial birds and do not combine this very long, narrow tail with such a small body. A rapidly passing Namaqua Dove can initially suggest a long-tailed songbird, particularly if its face is hidden. Identification should combine head size, wing shape, chestnut flight feathers and tail proportions. A damaged tail or the incompletely grown tail of a young bird can obscure the most obvious feature, making patient observation more useful than reliance on a single mark. Uneven occurrence across Arab countries The species ranges widely across sub-Saharan Africa, including the Sahel from southern Mauritania eastwards, Sudan, Somalia and other parts of eastern and southern Africa. Its Asian range includes the Arabian Peninsula and the southern margins of the Levant. Current taxonomy distinguishes the widespread African and Arabian subspecies from the Madagascan subspecies. An isolated observation beyond the familiar range should not automatically be interpreted as a new, established breeding population. In Saudi Arabia it is a common breeding resident in suitable habitat. Its former concentration in the southwest, particularly the Tihamah and the edges of the highlands, has expanded with agricultural development into central and eastern areas and north towards Tabuk. Kuwait presents a different picture: it is described as an uncommon resident, a rare breeder and a scarce disperser in spring and autumn. Neither description justifies calling it uniformly common throughout the Gulf. The range includes parts of Yemen, Oman and the wider peninsula, but numbers and persistence vary with habitat. It also reaches adjacent southern Jordan. The current taxonomic reference treats occurrence on Socotra as occasional, so a record on an island or at an isolated oasis is not in itself evidence of permanent residence. November can bring encounters with residents as well as local or winter movements. The species should not be assigned a single autumn migration schedule that supposedly explains every Arabian observation. Habitat, seeds and access to water Namaqua Doves use dry and semi-arid open country where exposed feeding surfaces occur alongside bushes or small trees offering shelter and nest sites. In southwestern Saudi Arabia they occupy acacia scrub and cultivation near villages; in central regions they are particularly associated with farmland. Bare dunes alone are not their typical habitat. Equally, the presence of a tree does not make a site suitable without accessible food and appropriate ground around it. Small grass and herb seeds form the main diet, collected largely from the ground. Birds are often seen alone or in pairs, but water and particularly rich feeding patches can attract larger gatherings. Such concentrations do not establish that the birds nest colonially or occur at the same density across the surrounding landscape. Agriculture and reliable water can allow settlement in previously unsuitable places, while natural patches remain important parts of the species' habitat. Pair formation and nest construction Breeding birds form socially monogamous, territorial pairs. The male's low, quiet vocalisations can reveal a bird perched on an exposed branch before it is noticed visually. Breeding timing varies geographically and with conditions, including food associated with rainfall or cultivation. A breeding peak documented in southern Africa cannot simply be transferred to every Arabian site. The useful question is what the birds are doing locally, rather than whether a distant calendar says they should be nesting. Both adults help construct a thin platform of twigs and rootlets, with finer material inside, usually low in a bush. The Saudi account records nests approximately 0.2–1.5 metres above the ground. The structure can appear remarkably slight compared with a deep songbird nest, but that is normal for this dove. Moving branches for a better view or trying to reinforce the platform is inappropriate: intervention can expose the eggs and alter the shelter chosen by the birds. Eggs, nestlings and continued development The Saudi account describes the usual clutch as two eggs, while African references include clutches of one or two. Both parents incubate, with incubation lasting about 13–16 days. They also share care of the young. The Saudi account gives a nestling period of roughly 12–16 days. These are approximate developmental intervals, not deadlines for handling or removing a chick. Leaving the nest also does not demonstrate complete feeding independence at that same moment. Two or three broods may be produced when conditions permit, but this does not mean every pair succeeds that often each year. Replacement nesting after failure is different from raising successive successful broods, and distinguishing the two requires careful, non-disruptive observation. Young birds begin with plumage unlike that of fully developed adults, and their appearance changes as they grow and replace feathers. A recently fledged youngster being fed is stronger evidence of local breeding than the presence of an adult pair alone. Conservation and responsible November observations The global conservation category is Least Concern, LC. Its extensive range and ability to benefit from some agricultural development do not guarantee the security of every local population. Indiscriminate shooting is identified as a local threat in Kuwait. Finding birds near a farm does not grant access to that property, and a global threat category does not determine national hunting law. Scientific status, land access and legal protection remain separate questions. For a useful November record, note the number of birds, apparent sex and age, the resource they are using and whether they remain on subsequent visits. Observe from a distance that leaves routes to water open and does not cause repeated flushing. Avoid playback and close inspection of bushes that may hold nests, and do not publicise active nest locations. These details turn an attractive photograph into a record that helps distinguish established residents from birds simply passing through. Photo: karim Attouche / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Nathalie Denolf: An eagle’s trust is earned, not imposed
articles.body: Nathalie Denolf with one of her eagles From a childhood fascination with birds of prey to almost seventeen years of work across several European countries, Nathalie Denolf speaks to SAYD about trust, the intelligence that continues to amaze her, and the line between care and exploitation. She shares experiences with her eagle Oropherion and advocates responsible falconry that puts birds’ welfare first, alongside conservation that reaches across borders. Nathalie, how did your journey with birds of prey begin? What inspired you to dedicate your life to these magnificent creatures rather than pursue another career? My fascination with birds of prey began when I was a very young child. There was always something about these magnificent creatures that captivated me, long before I ever imagined making a career out of working with them. The real turning point came when I found myself face to face with my Golden Eagle. At that moment, I knew without a shadow of a doubt that this was what I wanted to dedicate my life to. Growing up, I was actually a very shy person. But working with birds of prey gave me a confidence I had never known before. Around these animals, I felt completely at ease and didn’t need to be anyone other than myself. Almost 17 years later, having worked with raptors across several European countries, that passion has only grown stronger. Birds of prey didn’t just give me a career. They gave me a purpose. In your videos, we see an extraordinary bond between you and the eagles, particularly Oropherion. How does such trust develop between a human and such a powerful bird of prey? Do you believe these birds are capable of expressing emotions similar to love and affection? I believe the foundation of any meaningful relationship with a bird of prey is trust, patience, respect, and above all, understanding. You cannot force an eagle to trust you. You have to earn that trust through consistency, communication, and by learning to understand the world from their perspective rather than expecting them to adapt to ours. With Oropherion, that relationship has developed over years of working together. He knows what to expect from me, understands my intentions, and feels comfortable expressing his own preferences and boundaries. As for love and affection, I absolutely believe birds of prey are capable of forming strong emotional bonds. Whether they experience love in exactly the same way humans do is something we cannot scientifically establish, but that doesn’t make their relationships any less meaningful. Oropherion voluntarily seeks physical closeness, greets me by touching his beak to my nose, and often wraps me in his enormous wings. These are behaviours he chooses to express, not something I demand from him. And for me, that is what makes our relationship so extraordinary. He is an incredibly powerful, independent animal who has learned to trust me, and who chooses to share that closeness with me. “You cannot force an eagle to trust you.” Throughout your years of working with birds of prey, have you ever experienced a moment with a particular bird that completely changed your perception of their intelligence or personality? Is there a story you will never forget? After almost 17 years of working with birds of prey, their intelligence still manages to intrigue and fascinate me. One experience that stands out with Oropherion, my Martial Eagle. On several occasions, strong winds have carried him into dense woodland. With a wingspan of approximately 2.2 metres, he cannot simply fly down through the tightly packed branches to reach me. But rather than becoming distressed, he finds his own solution. He moves through the forest canopy, following me from tree to tree while I walk underneath. We essentially navigate the forest together until we reach a clearing, where he immediately flies back onto my glove. What fascinates me is his ability to assess the situation, adapt his behaviour, and work with me to overcome an obstacle. Experiences like these remind me that birds of prey are far more intelligent and resourceful than many people give them credit for. Or when given enrichment toys, they are so quick and problem-solving to figure them out. And even after all these years, I still feel there is so much more for us to discover about their remarkable minds. Nathalie receives one of her eagles on her glove Some people believe that birds of prey belong in the wild, flying freely in the sky, rather than being trained or kept under human care. How do you respond to this debate? Where do you draw the ethical line between caring for a bird and exploiting it? I absolutely agree that birds of prey belong in the wild, and ideally, that is where every species should be able to thrive. Unfortunately, the reality is that we humans have made much of their natural world increasingly unsafe. We’ve destroyed habitats, depleted prey populations, poisoned food chains, and created countless dangers through human encroachment and persecution. However, simply opening an aviary door and releasing a captive-bred bird is not necessarily giving it freedom. Without the appropriate survival skills and preparation, it could be a death sentence. Responsible human care can play an important role in conservation breeding, education, research, and providing a safe home for birds that cannot survive in the wild. I also strongly believe in the educational value of responsible, well-conducted flight displays. There is something incredibly powerful about witnessing a bird of prey in flight, seeing its natural abilities up close, and learning about the challenges its wild counterparts face. That firsthand experience can turn curiosity into admiration, admiration into understanding, and ultimately, understanding into action. If someone leaves a display inspired to speak up for birds of prey or support their conservation, then we have achieved something truly meaningful. But there is a very clear ethical responsibility attached to keeping these animals. For me, the line between care and exploitation is crossed when human ambitions, entertainment, or financial interests are placed above the bird’s physical and psychological welfare. A responsible falconer must understand the species, respect the individual bird’s needs and boundaries, provide appropriate living conditions, and allow opportunities to express natural behaviours. My birds are not props that exist purely for human entertainment. They are living, intelligent individuals whose wellbeing must always come first. The privilege of working with a bird of prey should never outweigh the responsibility we have towards it. “My birds are not props that exist purely for human entertainment.” You work closely with eagles, falcons, and owls, each with very different characteristics and behaviors. What surprises you most about their intelligence? Do you believe every bird has its own personality and a unique way of interacting with humans? Absolutely! One of the things I love most about working with birds of prey is discovering just how different they all are, even individuals of the same species. Some are incredibly confident and curious, others are cautious or shy. Some enjoy interacting closely with their falconer, while others prefer their independence. They all have their own personalities, preferences, and ways of communicating. I find them remarkably perceptive. They notice subtle changes in our behaviour, body language, and routines, often responding to things we don’t even realise we’re communicating. What surprises me most is that their intelligence is still so frequently underestimated, sometimes even by people who work with them professionally. I believe we have barely scratched the surface of understanding their cognitive abilities. The more opportunities we give these birds to think, explore, make choices, and express their individual personalities, the more they reveal to us just how extraordinary they truly are. Nathalie with two owls Based on your experience, what are the greatest threats facing birds of prey today? Do you believe current international conservation efforts are sufficient to protect them from illegal hunting, poisoning, and habitat loss? Without a doubt, the greatest threats facing birds of prey today are caused by humans. Habitat destruction, declining prey populations, illegal hunting, deliberate poisoning, electrocution on unsafe power lines, and wildlife trafficking are all taking a devastating toll on raptor populations worldwide. What I find particularly heartbreaking is that these birds are often persecuted simply for doing what nature designed them to do: hunting to survive. And no, I don’t believe our current conservation efforts are sufficient. There are extraordinary organisations and individuals working tirelessly to protect these species, often with very limited resources. But conservationists cannot keep fighting an uphill battle while habitat destruction, persecution, and illegal wildlife trade continue around them. We need stronger enforcement of existing wildlife protection laws, greater international cooperation, better education, and more investment in protecting habitats and addressing human-wildlife conflict. We also need to recognise that conservation doesn’t stop at national borders. Migratory birds can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing numerous countries, and they need protection throughout their entire journey. A bird protected in one country should not face being shot or trapped the moment it crosses into another. Ultimately, conservation cannot succeed through the efforts of a few dedicated organisations alone. It requires governments, local communities, falconers, hunters, and the wider public to take responsibility. We already know many of the threats these magnificent birds face. What we desperately need now is the collective determination to do something about them. Nathalie beside a vulture Falconry is an ancient tradition dating back thousands of years, with deep historical roots in both Europe and the Arab world. How can falconry and responsible hunting coexist with wildlife conservation? In your opinion, what distinguishes a responsible falconer from someone who exploits birds of prey? Falconry has an extraordinary history, and I believe there is something very special about a tradition that has connected humans and birds of prey for thousands of years. But tradition should never be used as an excuse to disregard animal welfare or conservation. I believe responsible falconry and sustainable hunting can coexist with wildlife conservation, provided they are practised ethically, within the law, and with genuine respect for both the birds and the wider ecosystem. For me, a responsible falconer is someone who puts the welfare of their bird above personal ambitions, understands its physical and behavioural needs, and is willing to dedicate the enormous amount of time and effort these animals require. A responsible hunter must also understand the impact their activities have on wild populations and recognise that sustainability means taking only what nature can genuinely afford to lose. What concerns me is when birds of prey become status symbols, disposable possessions, or tools for entertainment, rather than being treated as the extraordinary living creatures they are. I also believe falconers have a unique opportunity to contribute to conservation. Our knowledge, experience, and passion can be powerful tools for education, research, and protecting wild raptors. To me, the difference between a responsible falconer and someone who exploits birds of prey is simple: one asks what they can do for the bird, while the other only considers what the bird can do for them. Ultimately, preserving the tradition of falconry should go hand in hand with preserving the birds and natural habitats that make that tradition possible. One of Nathalie’s eagles lands on her glove Lebanon lies along one of the world's most important migration routes for birds of prey traveling between Europe and Africa. Unfortunately, some of these birds are illegally shot during their migration, sometimes simply for entertainment or photographs. What message would you like to send to those who shoot these magnificent birds? Let me be absolutely clear: shooting a magnificent bird of prey for amusement, a photograph, or a trophy is an act of sheer cowardice. There is no skill, no bravery, and certainly no honour in killing a defenceless animal simply because you can. Pulling a trigger against a creature that poses no threat to you does not make you powerful, brave, or more of a man. Quite the opposite. It exposes a complete lack of respect for life and everything that true courage and honour should represent. These birds have travelled thousands of kilometres, overcoming extraordinary challenges, only to have their lives needlessly ended for someone’s entertainment. A real measure of character is not how much power you have over a vulnerable creature, but whether you have the decency and compassion to let it live. If you truly want to demonstrate strength and courage, put down the gun and stand up for the wildlife that cannot defend itself against you. The Middle East Center for Sustainable Harvest and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP), through its Anti-Poaching Unit (APU), works to protect migratory birds and combat illegal hunting. How important do you believe international cooperation between falconers, wildlife experts, and field conservation organizations is in protecting these birds throughout their migration routes? International cooperation is absolutely essential. Wildlife does not recognise political borders, and neither should our conservation efforts. We cannot expect to protect migratory birds successfully if we only safeguard them in certain countries while leaving them vulnerable elsewhere along their journey. Falconers, wildlife researchers, conservation organisations, and anti-poaching teams all bring different expertise to the table. By sharing knowledge, migration data, resources, and practical experience, we can achieve far more together than any organisation could accomplish alone. I have enormous respect for the people working on the ground to combat illegal hunting. Organisations such as MECSHAP and their Anti-Poaching Unit play an important role because protecting wildlife requires more than raising awareness. It also requires people willing to take action where these crimes actually occur. As someone working in both falconry and conservation, I strongly believe we have a responsibility to bridge the gap between these communities and work towards a common goal. Conservation should never be about individual recognition or competing organisations. It should be about combining our strengths to achieve what matters most: keeping these magnificent birds alive in the wild. “Organisations such as MECSHAP and their Anti-Poaching Unit play an important role…” Finally, if you could change just one thing about the relationship between humans and birds of prey, what would it be? And what message would you like to share with the readers of SAYD Magazine, particularly hunters and nature lovers across the Arab world? If I could change just one thing, it would be the way humans perceive their place in the natural world. We need to stop seeing ourselves as masters of nature and start recognising that we are part of it, with a responsibility to protect it. Birds of prey have fascinated humanity for thousands of years. They represent strength, freedom, and extraordinary beauty, yet we continue to destroy the very habitats they depend upon and persecute them for simply following their natural instincts. To the readers of SAYD Magazine, particularly the falconers, hunters, and nature lovers across the Arab world, I would say this: you have an extraordinary cultural connection to birds of prey, and with that heritage comes an equally extraordinary opportunity to help protect them. Whether you are a falconer, a hunter, or simply someone who admires wildlife, your choices matter. Respect the animals you encounter, challenge illegal persecution, and pass on a genuine appreciation for nature to the next generation. Tradition and conservation should never be enemies. The greatest legacy we can leave is not simply preserving our traditions, but ensuring that the wildlife which inspired them will still exist for generations to come. And perhaps most importantly, remember that these magnificent birds do not belong to us. We are simply privileged to share this planet with them. Photographs supplied by Nathalie Denolf for this interview. Two-owl photograph: NECKARBOX Fotoboxvermietung.

articles.title: After the Bekaa: 24,750 square metres of illegal hunting nets removed in northern Lebanon in four hours
articles.body: The field team beside nets removed in northern Lebanon. Net removals in northern Bekaa and northern Lebanon have reached a combined 63,030 square metres. The Internal Security Forces’ Northern Investigation Detachment, working in the field and sharing information with the Anti-Poaching Unit’s joint operations team, removed 24,750 square metres of illegal hunting nets in northern Lebanon in just four hours. The operation follows the removal of 38,280 square metres of nets in northern Bekaa, bringing the combined total for northern Lebanon and the Bekaa to 63,030 square metres. Tall nets between orchard trees during the field operation. High nets among the orchards The density of the nets, their spread among orchards and their considerable height made removal a demanding field operation. The operation was coordinated with the head of the command and control room for northern Lebanon, the head of the Northern Investigation Detachment and officers from the detachment. It involved the joint operations team of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU), affiliated with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS). Field work on the nets between the trees. From the Bekaa to the north The earlier campaign in northern Bekaa was carried out with the Internal Security Forces’ Bekaa Investigation Detachment and resulted in the removal of 38,280 square metres of nets. The northern operation adds a further achievement to the cooperation between the Directorate General of the Internal Security Forces and the Anti-Poaching Unit team in protecting birds and nature in Lebanon. Nets collected after removal, with the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) emblem visible. Sources: Internal Security Forces: northern operation; Internal Security Forces: Bekaa total

articles.title: Pallid Swift
articles.body: Pallid Swift Apus pallidus Identity and identification Pallid Swift Apus pallidus belongs to Apodidae. Similar to Common Swift, it is often browner and paler, with a broader pale throat and contrast between wing coverts and flight feathers. The face may look paler. Light and age alter these subtle features; an overexposed photograph cannot identify it. It is placed in the order Apodiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It catches insects and airborne invertebrates over towns, coasts and farmland. Mixed swift feeding flocks occur, tracking weather and prey height. Sickle wings and flight distinguish swifts from swallows but do not separate all Apus species. Breeding and parental care Building and rock cavities support nests, sometimes in colonies. Both parents contribute to incubation and feeding. Food and weather affect nestling development, while breeding timing varies among coastal sites and regions. Common Swift statistics should not be presented as measurements for this species. Range and Arab occurrence Its range is associated with the Mediterranean, North Africa and parts of the Middle East. Lebanon’s updated checklist describes local migrant breeding and passage. Seasonal strategies differ across the wider range; a summer colony does not establish winter residence. Seasonality and observation Lebanese spring passage extends from February to May and autumn passage from June to September. A November record therefore requires particular attention to identity and location. Well-exposed views of throat, face and wings help, without overstating distant photographs. Ecological role and conservation It needs safe cavities and aerial insects. Sealing occupied building openings can trap birds or prevent provisioning. Repairs outside nesting periods and retained suitable entrances help colonies coexist with maintained buildings. References Ramadan-Jaradi et al. — Updated checklist of the birds of Lebanon, Sandgrouse 42 (2020), 186–238. British Trust for Ornithology — BirdFacts: Pallid Swift. articles.title: Peregrine Falcon — Falco peregrinus
articles.body: Peregrine falconPhoto: Sumeet Moghe — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Range: One of the most widespread birds in the world: found on every continent except Antarctica. In Lebanon it is recorded year-round, and it is also among the raptors that pass with migration routes over the country. Life cycle and habitat: It nests on rock cliffs, and has often taken skyscrapers and bridges as nest sites in cities. It hunts medium-sized birds in the air: watching from a height or soaring, then stooping toward the prey in a rapid dive. It usually kills with a bite to the neck after the strike or the seize. Lifestyle: A flying hunter specialized in taking birds. Ordinary flight speed, according to the Cornell Lab, is about 40–55 km/h, and in a direct chase it may reach about 112 km/h. In a dive from great height, stoop speed may approach about 320 km/h (around 200 mph)—which is why it is counted among the fastest creatures on Earth in a dive. Its Latin name, Falco peregrinus, points to the “wanderer”: many individuals migrate long distances, and some nest sites have remained in use for successive generations. Hunting status: Across Arab countries the peregrine is treated as a protected bird of prey; hunting it as quarry is generally prohibited. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else—including all birds of prey—is protected year-round and may not be hunted; the peregrine is not among the permitted quarry. Despite legal protection, it still faces illegal shooting in some seasons and along some flyways. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Its numbers collapsed in the mid-twentieth century because of pesticides such as DDT, then recovered after bans and captive-breeding and release programs; in the United States it was removed from the threatened-species list in 1999. Traits: Falconers have prized it among the finest hunting birds for more than a thousand years, and their techniques later helped breed it in captivity to rescue collapsed populations. The oldest ringed peregrine known lived more than 19 years. Today it is seen over coasts, cities, and cliffs alike.

articles.title: Pharaoh Eagle-Owl
articles.body: Pharaoh Eagle-Owl Bubo ascalaphus Identity and identification Pharaoh Eagle-Owl Bubo ascalaphus belongs to Strigidae. A large desert owl, it has sandy mottled plumage, orange-yellow eyes and head feather tufts. It differs from larger Eurasian Eagle-Owl, but dark photographs alone cannot reliably separate owls. The tufts are feathers, not external ears. It is placed in the order Strigiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Cliffs, wadis and rocky desert provide habitat. Nocturnal hunting takes rodents, birds, reptiles and other locally available prey. Specialised wings permit quiet approaches. A bird resting near a cavity by day is not necessarily ill. Breeding and parental care It nests on cliffs and in sheltered cavities, sometimes using old raven nests, according to Abu Dhabi’s Environment Agency. Young depend on adult prey deliveries and site protection. Quiet habitat and food determine success; cavities must not be illuminated to count eggs or chicks. Range and Arab occurrence It is resident in parts of North Africa and Arabia, with occurrence and monitoring documented in Abu Dhabi. Suitable desert distribution does not mean equal presence in all Arab countries. New records require face, eye and structure comparisons alongside location. Seasonality and observation Residents can be observed in November. Listening at a distance is preferable to approach or repeated call playback. Exact cavity locations should not be publicised if they would attract disturbance to a sensitive breeding site. Ecological role and conservation It consumes desert rodents and other prey and faces poisoning, hunting and cliff destruction. Rodenticides can poison predators through prey. Protecting cavities, reducing toxicants and respecting nocturnal activity help; repeated flash or deliberate luring should be avoided. References Environment Agency–Abu Dhabi — Pharaoh Eagle Owl. articles.title: Qatar's Law 4/2002: The statutory limits that apply beyond hunting seasons
articles.body: Six provisions address prohibited locations, times, nests, marine turtles, enforcement and penalties. Al Zubarah Fort, Qatar Qatar's seasonal hunting notices are implementing decisions, not the hunting law itself. The legal framework includes Law No. 4 of 2002, issued on 11 May and published on 20 May 2002, listed as in force by Qatar's official Al Meezan legal portal. Article 1 forbids hunting wild mammals, birds and reptiles in natural reserves, on islands, within cities and villages, within 500 metres of public roads and on private land without the relevant owners' consent. Article 2 permits hunting elsewhere only during specified seasons, between sunrise and sunset. Separate implementing decisions determine eligible quarry species and permitted hunting tools. Article 3 protects marine turtles and their eggs, bird eggs and nests, and wild flora. Article 4 provides for authorized enforcement officers to investigate offences. Article 5 provides, unless another law prescribes a more severe penalty, for imprisonment not exceeding one year or a fine up to QAR 10,000, or both. Equipment and weapons used in the offence are confiscated, and repeat offences attract the statutory increased punishment. These are provisions of a law enacted in 2002 and explained in 2026; they should not be confused with any new seasonal notice. Original source: Al Meezan Qatar Legal Portal, Law No. 4 of 2002, Articles 1–6. Original statute at the official source

articles.title: Qatar aims to protect 30% of its land and marine areas by 2030
articles.body: Arabian oryx as part of wildlife conservation efforts in Qatar. Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change reaffirmed its target of increasing protected terrestrial and marine areas to 30% by 2030 to safeguard natural habitats and biodiversity. It said terrestrial reserves currently cover around 25% of the country’s land area. The ministry outlined its wildlife conservation efforts in a statement marking World Animal Day on 4 October, including the provision of suitable environments for native species to breed. Khalid Jumaa Al-Muhannadi, Director of the Wildlife Development Department, said reserves provide animals with food, shelter and breeding opportunities while protecting their habitats from encroachment. Breeding and care programmes include Arabian oryx, sand gazelles and ostriches, alongside reintroductions into suitable natural environments. The ministry urged the public to avoid chasing, hunting or disturbing wild animals and to comply with laws governing hunting and the protection of nature reserves.

articles.title: Red-breasted Goose
articles.body: Red-breasted Goose Branta ruficollis Striking plumage on a small goose Red-breasted Goose Branta ruficollis is a small, short-necked goose whose chestnut breast, fore-neck and cheek patches are outlined by bold white lines against black plumage. A pale patch between the bill and eye and the contrasting flank pattern add to its distinctive appearance. Both sexes share this colour scheme; the richness of the chestnut alone does not identify a male. Young birds are duller and less cleanly patterned. AEWA's monitoring guidance describes smaller, less sharply defined cheek patches, a paler mottled breast and neck, and greyer wing feathers with less distinct white bars. Ageing becomes harder as young birds acquire adult-like body plumage. At a distance the chestnut can disappear into the dark body, allowing confusion with Brent Goose or causing a bird to be overlooked in a flock of Greater White-fronted Geese. Its short bill and compact silhouette are useful supporting features. Tundra in summer, farmland and lakes in winter The breeding range is concentrated in Arctic Russia, notably the Taymyr, Gydan and Yamal peninsulas. Nesting habitat includes tundra near rivers, sloping banks and elevated ground. Winter life is very different: grassland and agricultural fields supply food, while lakes and other waterbodies provide drinking and roosting places. The species often mixes with Greater White-fronted Geese outside breeding. In the western Black Sea region, conservation organisations describe feeding on winter wheat and barley, maize stubble, spilled grain and pasture plants. Birds commute between these fields and water rather than feeding exclusively at the shore. In Bulgaria, roosts can be on lakes, on lake ice when frozen, or occasionally on the sea. Thus the quality and safety of the surrounding farmland are part of wetland conservation for this goose. Nesting near formidable neighbours One of the species' best-known behaviours is nesting near birds of prey, especially Peregrine Falcons; associations with Snowy Owls are also reported. The territorial defence of these neighbours can reduce access by ground predators such as Arctic Foxes. The geese may form loose nesting groups, but the relationship is not a guarantee against predation and varies with the local predator community. A long-term Taymyr study by Kostin and Mooij showed that breeding success depends on several interacting factors: the condition of adults on arrival, temperature, precipitation, snow cover and predation. Lemming abundance can also influence the pressure exerted by predators on geese. This makes reproduction sensitive not only to events on the nesting grounds but also to the feeding opportunities available before the birds arrive. Eggs, young and the annual cycle The nest is on the ground and lined with vegetation and down. Reference tables in Clinical Avian Medicine give clutches of 3–7 eggs and incubation of 23–25 days. These are broad reproductive reference values, not measurements from every wild population. The female incubates, and the downy young leave the nest while still unable to fly, continuing to feed and grow under parental care. The short northern summer must accommodate nesting, growth of the young and the adults' wing moult. Weather affects the timing of arrival, incubation and hatching, as the Taymyr field study demonstrated. A delayed snowmelt and poor adult condition can consequently alter the proportion of birds that breed and their productivity. Annual variation in the number of juveniles reaching wintering flocks is therefore an important part of the species' population dynamics. Migration clarified by tracking The principal migration links Siberian breeding grounds to wintering areas around the Black Sea, with major staging regions in Kazakhstan and Russia. It is a journey made in stages, with repeated use of lakes and feeding areas, rather than a single continuous flight. The distribution of wintering birds can shift with conditions, so the entire population is not necessarily concentrated in the same country each winter. Petkov and colleagues' study published in October 2026 analysed GPS tracking from 2019–2023. It identified important staging areas in northern Kazakhstan and the Orenburg region, and winter cores around coastal Romania with adjacent Bulgaria and Ukraine, the Sivash area in Crimea, and the Veselovskoie region of southern Russia. The tracked sample provided no evidence of a major previously unknown wintering area. These findings sharpen understanding of the main flyway without making every rare record elsewhere part of a regular route. Iraq, Syria, Oman and historical Egypt OSME describes Red-breasted Goose as a rare winterer in Iraq. This is marginal winter occurrence, not an Arab breeding population. In Syria, its regional list cites a vagrant pair at Sabkhat al-Jabboul in February 2010. Oman is also a vagrant destination: the first record dates to November 2013, and the official list continues to classify the species as accidental rather than a regular winter visitor. Egypt's EORC checklist of 2019 places the species in Category B, for wild records before 1950 with none later accepted in that list. Historical Egyptian presence must therefore be kept separate from modern records in Iraq, Syria and Oman. The species is also maintained in captivity; unusual sightings need assessment of wild origin, especially where they are distant from established migration and wintering areas. Conservation and unobtrusive observation AEWA and BTO report the global category Vulnerable. Hunting pressure, disturbance, habitat loss and changes in climate and land use affect different parts of the annual cycle. Concentration at a limited set of staging and winter sites makes the loss of safe feeding grounds or roosts particularly consequential. Protecting water alone leaves the birds exposed if adjoining fields are heavily disturbed. International monitoring combines counts, assessment of the proportion of young birds and tracking of movements. Observers can contribute clear photographs and precise records without approaching feeding flocks or forcing birds to fly. Where mixed goose flocks are present, patient scanning from a distance is more useful than repeated pursuit, and allows the Red-breasted Goose's striking pattern to be appreciated without interrupting its feeding. articles.title: Red-breasted Merganser
articles.body: Red-breasted Merganser Mergus serrator Identity and similar species Red-breasted Merganser, Mergus serrator, is a long-bodied, fish-eating duck with a narrow reddish bill and a loose, spiky crest. Adults measure roughly 51–65 cm. In breeding plumage, the male has a dark green head, a contrasting white neck collar, a rusty, dark-marked breast and grey flanks. The crest can appear dishevelled or flattened according to posture. Its fine bill separates its silhouette from the broad-billed ducks commonly feeding beside it. Females have a brown head and greyish body. Juveniles resemble females, and males become much less distinctive outside their full breeding plumage. Female Common Mergansers are a particular source of confusion. Red-breasted Merganser usually has a slimmer bill and a less sharply defined transition between the brown neck and pale breast. Common Merganser has a more solid-looking bill and typically stronger contrast at the throat and lower neck. Young birds can be difficult, so the whole head-and-neck pattern matters more than the presence of a crest alone. Waters and fishing behaviour The breeding habitat includes northern lakes and rivers within boreal forest and tundra landscapes. Outside that season, the species is strongly coastal, using bays, estuaries and other marine waters, though some birds remain on large ice-free inland waters. It can forage around rocky shores, piers and sheltered coastal inlets. A marine winter habitat does not imply that nesting takes place on the same shoreline. Small fish form the main adult food. The narrow bill has serrated edges that help hold slippery prey; these are specialised bill structures, not mammalian teeth. The birds search and pursue underwater, returning to the surface between dives. They also take aquatic invertebrates, and insects are important to young ducklings. Groups sometimes appear to drive fish towards shallow water, where prey can be caught without a full dive. The availability of fish and access to clear feeding water are more informative than the simple distinction between freshwater and salt water. Courtship, nesting and young Several males may display around a female, using repeated movements of the head, neck and forebody. Display can begin away from the eventual nesting area. Unlike the familiar cavity-nesting pattern of Common Merganser, Red-breasted Merganser usually nests on the ground. The female selects a sheltered place near water, under dense vegetation or protective debris, and lines a depression with down. Islands and shore margins provide potential nest sites where suitable cover is available. BTO gives a typical clutch of 8–10 eggs and female incubation of 31–32 days. The downy ducklings enter the water soon after hatching and find food for themselves while the female tends them. Broods can combine, and female care may end before the young become airborne. Typical fledging is around 60–65 days. These figures describe development on the breeding grounds; they are not evidence that a bird observed in a Mediterranean winter flock bred locally. A northern range with coastal wintering The species has a broad northern distribution across North America and Eurasia, with breeding areas including Iceland, Scandinavia and northern Russia. Winter movements connect northern nesting waters with extensive stretches of temperate coast. In western Eurasia its winter range includes the North Sea, Baltic, Mediterranean, Black Sea and Caspian regions. Migration may be visible as lines or V-shaped groups moving over water. There is no single “Arab status” that captures this distribution. A bird can be a recognised winter visitor in one country and an exceptional arrival in another. The distinction is particularly important between the Atlantic–Mediterranean sector and much of the Arabian Peninsula. Geographic proximity to a wintering coast does not establish annual occurrence at every neighbouring wetland. Country records in the Arab world Morocco's national rare-bird committee lists Red-breasted Merganser as a winter visitor, using a category explicitly defined as regular winter presence. Egypt's Ornithological Rarities Committee includes it in category A of its 2019 national checklist, meaning accepted wild occurrence since 1950; that category alone does not quantify abundance or assign a season. Lebanon has particularly informative published records. Ramadan-Jaradi and colleagues reported seven birds on an islet off Tripoli on 7 March 1998, then five at Qleiaat on 5 November 2018, describing the latter as the country's second record at the time. Three of the five birds in 2018 were killed by hunters. These dated observations establish exceptional occurrence, not regular Lebanese wintering. OSME's regional list version 10.2 subsequently adds a third Lebanese record, at Tripoli in December 2021. OSME's regional list version 10.2 records Jordan's first observation in the Jordan Valley in December 2016. It treats Oman as a vagrant destination and cites its fifth record at Al Mouj, Muscat, in January 2021. Kuwait's third record was at Jahra Pools in January 2021, following a second in February 2015; the sixth United Arab Emirates record was at Al Barsha in March 2019. These dated records illustrate occasional eastern arrivals, contrasting with Morocco's winter-visitor status; their ordinals describe the cited records, not a live national total. Conservation and careful observation Global Least Concern status, as reported by BTO, does not mean every population is stable or every site safe. Concentrations at feeding and migration sites make local disturbance consequential. Fishing areas, sheltered roosting waters and nesting margins are connected parts of the bird's annual requirements. The documented Lebanese losses also show why identification and enforcement against illegal killing matter for scarce visitors. Watch from a fixed point and allow feeding birds to approach naturally. Avoid driving a boat between a flock and the water it is using, and never disturb nests to verify species identity. For a regional rarity, photographs showing the bill profile, throat, neck and wing pattern are especially helpful. Record the date, locality, count and behaviour without converting a single visit into a claim of regular seasonal presence. articles.title: Red-throated Pipit
articles.body: Red-throated Pipit Anthus cervinus Identity and identification Red-throated Pipit is called الجشنة الحنائية, also الجشنة حمراء الزور, in Arabic, and Pipit à gorge rousse in French. Anthus cervinus belongs to Motacillidae in the order Passeriformes. Despite visiting wetlands, it is not a wader. About 15 cm long, it has a fine bill, pale legs and strongly streaked brown upperparts. Breeding plumage includes rusty to pink colour on the throat, breast and face, generally most evident in males. Females and autumn birds are duller, and juveniles may lack red altogether. A white throat therefore does not exclude the species. Strong back stripes, a heavily streaked rump, breast and flanks, and two pale lines along the back help identification. Compare Meadow Pipit, Tree Pipit and other pipits, considering shape, streaking and calls rather than naming any streak-breasted bird from one character. Habitat, food and behaviour Northern tundra provides breeding habitat. On migration it uses fields, short meadows, damp cultivated land and watersides. Association with wetlands does not mean spending the day inside reeds: open, low vegetation allows walking and finding food. It can mix with other pipits, making individual examination important. It takes insects and small invertebrates from the ground and low vegetation, walking and probing between plants. A sharp call during natural flight can help, but a single heard call does not replace visual evidence or a useful comparison recording. Wait at the field edge for birds to appear rather than following them through vegetation and displacing them from food. Breeding and development Breeding takes place far to the north, with a ground nest in concealing cover. Audubon gives five or six eggs as usual, with a range of three to seven. The female incubates for about 11–13 days and the male feeds her during incubation. Both parents feed the nestlings, which leave the nest around 11–15 days after hatching. Nest departure is more precise than assuming every chick acquires full flight ability on one particular day. These intervals describe development, not an Arab breeding season. Red plumage likewise does not establish local breeding: a migrant can carry breeding feathers far from its nesting grounds. Range and Arab occurrence The breeding range runs from northern Norway across Russia and Siberia, with a small presence in northwestern Alaska; wintering areas extend into Africa and Southeast Asia. The 2026 Lebanon guide describes a common passage migrant and possible rare winter visitor. It occurs especially in damp and cultivated areas from sea level to about 1,800 m, with many records from the Beqaa and Aammiq. Passage from late February to mid-May is generally more conspicuous than September to mid-November, and few records fall in midwinter. Oman’s official list instead records a common passage migrant and winter visitor: uncertainty over Lebanese winter status should not be extended across Arabia. Kuwait’s committee list records a common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, adding another regional distinction. What November means The first half of November remains within the Lebanese autumn passage window described, while Omani presence also fits wintering. These seasonal patterns do not guarantee arrival on a particular day. Repeat visits to damp fields, recording dates, counts and land use, are useful. One image, or simply seeing the species again, cannot distinguish successive migrating flocks from the same group staying. Conservation and responsible observation The global category is Least Concern (LC), but local populations depend on feeding habitat. Lebanon’s guide lists agricultural intensification, habitat loss, illegal hunting and climate change among pressures. Reducing pesticide use and preserving damp field margins help maintain food and cover. Watch from permitted routes, respect crops and private property, and avoid playback or following birds into fields. Withholding precise nest locations helps protect a life cycle that does not require visitor intervention. articles.title: Hunting firearms at the Riyadh exhibition: broader participation and Beretta’s 500th anniversary editions
articles.body: Rifles on display before visitors at the Saudi International Falcons and Hunting Exhibition — archive photograph. More than 5,000 products in the firearms, ammunition and accessories area, as the number of hunting and sport shooting firearms companies rises from eight to eleven. The firearms, ammunition and accessories area at the Saudi International Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 brings together more than 5,000 products, including hunting and sport shooting firearms and airguns, alongside ammunition, maintenance and cleaning tools, secure storage equipment, protection and training supplies. Organised by the National Center for Falcons, the exhibition runs from 1 to 10 October at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Center in Malham, north of Riyadh. The firearms area hosts 11 hunting and sport shooting firearms companies, up from eight last year, an increase of 37.5%, alongside four airgun companies and nine suppliers of equipment, tools and accessories. More than 181 brands are represented across these categories. This year’s exhibition coincides with five centuries since Italian manufacturer Beretta began making firearms in 1526. Its participation, through Saudi agent Al Rumaih, includes limited editions marking the anniversary, alongside hunting firearms and accessories, as well as commemorative watches and clothing. A celebration is scheduled for the exhibition’s final day, 10 October, with representatives of the Italian company attending. Al Rumaih chief executive Ahmed Saleh Al Rumaih said the company sold a shotgun for 120,000 Saudi riyals at last year’s exhibition, its most expensive firearm sale during that edition.

articles.title: Riyadh hears the horses again… the racing season begins
articles.body: Saudi horse racing in action — archive photograph. The 2026–2027 Riyadh racing season opened at King Abdulaziz Racecourse on Friday 16 October. Running until 17 April next year, the season brings together leading stables, trainers and jockeys. According to the latest announcement from the Jockey Club of Saudi Arabia, the season offers a record SAR 236.3 million in total prize money and includes the Saudi Cup meeting. The programme brings more than higher purses. The club is introducing the Riyadh Crown series for locally bred horses and the Riyadh Sword series for imported mares. The first comprises three rounds with total prize money of SAR 6 million, while the second offers approximately SAR 1.54 million. The Saudi Derby has also been upgraded to Group 2 (G2). Several cups receive prize increases, including the open Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques Cup, a Saudi Cup qualifier, whose purse rises from SAR 1.5 million to SAR 2 million. Purebred Arabian horses also feature in the programme. The Listed race for Arabian mares has been renamed in honour of Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman, with a SAR 300,000 purse, as part of the King Abdulaziz Founder's Cups meeting scheduled for 12 March 2027. As competition begins, the racecourse once again combines racing with visitor and hospitality experiences, in a season stretching from Riyadh's autumn into its spring. Update, 5 November 2026: 24 races in week four King Abdulaziz Racecourse in Riyadh hosts the season’s 27th and 28th meetings on Friday and Saturday, 6 and 7 November. The programme features 24 races, with 12 on each evening and more than SAR 2.1 million in total prize money. Friday’s highlights include the Crown Prince Cup preparation races for locally bred horses and the open division, both over 2,000 metres. The week’s programme also includes the Jockey Club Cup, a domestic Group 3 over 1,600 metres worth SAR 165,000. Saturday features the Prince Saud bin Salman Cups for two-year-old fillies and colts, both over 1,600 metres and each offering SAR 300,000. Update, 23 October 2026: the second week The Jockey Club’s programme, announced on 22 October, lists 24 races across the 23–24 October meetings, with over SAR 1.6 million in prizes. It includes the General Intelligence Cup and Africa Cup, alongside Saturday’s preparation race for the Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup over 2,000 metres, worth SAR 120,000. articles.title: Rock Bunting
articles.body: Rock Bunting Emberiza cia Identity and names Rock Bunting, Emberiza cia, is a small passerine of the bunting family Emberizidae. Its French name is Bruant fou; Arabic references use درسة الصخور or درسة الصخر. These are names for the same species, which should not be confused with other buntings sharing rocky landscapes. The 2026 Lebanon guide gives a length of about 16 cm, wingspan around 26 cm and weight around 30 g. A short conical bill and fairly long tail contribute to its recognizable shape. Identification The adult male combines a pale grey head with strong black stripes, a streaked brown back and warm buff to chestnut underparts. The facial pattern matters as much as the body colour: look for the arrangement of dark lines above and through the eye and below the cheek. Females and juveniles are less contrasting, with a browner head and paler underparts. White on the outer tail is useful when visible. A faded head pattern should not be mistaken for proof of another species without examining the whole bird. Habitat and food Rocky slopes with scattered low vegetation provide a mixture of cover, perches and accessible ground. Open mountain scrub, stony grassland, sparse woodland margins and some terraced landscapes can be suitable. Food changes with season: insects and other small invertebrates are important during breeding, particularly for growing chicks, while grasses and other plants supply many of the seeds eaten outside that season. Birds feed on the ground or take seeds directly from plants. Retaining rough vegetation around rocks preserves feeding patches that a uniformly cleared slope would lose. Range and Arab occurrence The range extends from northwestern Africa through southern Europe and parts of western and central Asia towards the Himalayas. Resident populations occur in the Maghreb, including Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. In Lebanon, the 2026 guide describes a common breeding resident of rocky mountains, especially near cedar-grove margins, with breeding mainly at 1,000–2,400 m and downward movement in winter. Kuwait presents a sharply different picture: the local reference classifies Rock Bunting as an extremely rare vagrant and non-breeder. A mountain resident in one country is therefore not necessarily a regular winter visitor throughout the Arab world. Breeding and development The female builds a cup nest on the ground, sheltered by vegetation or rock. Specialist references describe a usual clutch of 3–5 eggs and female incubation lasting roughly 13–15 days. Both parents feed the chicks. Young may leave the nest after about 9–13 days but still need parental care; departure is not immediate independence or necessarily strong sustained flight. The Lebanese guide places local breeding from late April to late July. Nesting schedules vary elsewhere, so this country-specific season should remain distinct from the species’ wider breeding calendar. November and responsible observation In November, lower slopes may become more relevant than the high summer nesting grounds. Outside breeding, birds can gather in small feeding groups; neither a group nor a single late-autumn record proves long-distance migration. Watch from a path or a stable viewpoint and note the ground vegetation, altitude and flock size. Avoid pushing birds across exposed terrain to obtain a flight photograph. A quiet pause often allows feeding to resume and gives time to examine the head stripes, bill and tail without chasing the group. Conservation The global conservation category is Least Concern, LC. This is not permission to overlook local habitat damage or indiscriminate shooting. The Lebanese guide identifies habitat loss and degradation, illegal hunting and warming among pressures. Conserving a varied mountain landscape means retaining seed-bearing vegetation, scattered shrubs and undisturbed nesting cover alongside the rocks. Records with dates, locations and behaviour are particularly valuable where the species is rare, because they distinguish a documented exceptional visitor from an unsupported claim of regular seasonal presence. articles.title: Ruddy Shelduck
articles.body: Ruddy Shelduck Tadorna ferruginea — From Atlas lakes to Levantine winters: not a visitor everywhere Identity and identification Ruddy Shelduck, Tadorna ferruginea, is a member of Anatidae whose classification is retained in AviList 2026. Its rusty-orange body, paler head and black bill and legs are conspicuous. The relatively large body and upright stance can suggest a goose, but this is neither a grey goose nor simply an unusually coloured domestic duck. Age, sex and similar species The adult male develops a narrow black neck ring in breeding plumage; the female lacks this ring and usually has a whiter face. Juveniles resemble females, so absence of the ring does not establish sex, especially outside the breeding season. In flight a broad white wing panel contrasts with black flight feathers, with a glossy green speculum. Common Shelduck instead combines a red bill with strongly patterned white, black and brown plumage. Identification photographs should include body, head and bill, since lighting alone can alter the apparent rusty colour. Habitats, food and behaviour The species uses lakes, open wetlands, slow rivers and water bodies in semi-arid country, including the mountain lakes of the Atlas. It eats grasses, aquatic plants and seeds, together with invertebrates such as insects, molluscs and crustaceans. Feeding takes place on land, along margins and in shallow water. Birds may occur as pairs or gather outside the breeding season. Their loud calls help attract attention, but apparent tolerance of people is not a reason to approach a family or nest. Breeding and life cycle Nests occupy cavities, burrows or suitable crevices and may be some distance from the water’s edge. The female incubates, after which both parents accompany the mobile young as they leave the nest. Breeding timing changes with region, altitude and water conditions; a single calendar should not be imposed on Atlas, Levantine and Asian birds. Some populations are resident or move relatively little, whereas others migrate. Winter numbers at a lake may therefore increase even where local breeding birds are already present. Distribution and seasonality in the Arab world In Morocco the species is not merely a winter visitor: official sources document local resident breeding at lakes such as Aguelmam Sidi Ali, while other birds use Atlas sites during winter. References also document breeding in parts of Algeria and Tunisia, without implying year-round occupation of every North African wetland. Egypt lies within passage and winter occurrence, while populations using Iraq and the Levant show different movements. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist changed its classification from vagrant to an infrequently observed winter visitor; Qatar treats it as a rare winter visitor. November thus offers opportunities to observe eastern winter arrivals, whereas an Atlas bird may be local. Unusual records should consider provenance, because captive or escaped individuals do not establish natural migration. Ecological role and conservation The global category is Least Concern, LC. By taking plants and invertebrates, the species links terrestrial grazing with aquatic habitats, but this category does not protect a small local population from habitat loss. Wetland drainage, pollution, disturbance and hunting are pressures, and breeding families need secure, quiet space. Maintaining water, varied shorelines and suitable nesting cavities is preferable to feeding birds to draw them into photographs. Calling a population resident neither grants hunting permission nor demonstrates stable numbers from year to year. References AviList 2026 — Tadorna ferruginea. articles.title: Sand Martin
articles.body: Sand Martin Riparia riparia Identity and identification Sand Martin Riparia riparia belongs to Hirundinidae. Small and brown above, it has white underparts crossed by a distinct brown breast band. This band, head shape and flight separate it from white-rumped House Martin. Closely related sand martins may require more detailed comparison. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It catches flying insects above water, fields and wet plains. Migrants gather at feeding and roosting sites, sometimes using reeds for sleep. Concentrations reflect food and resting opportunities rather than proving a nesting colony. Breeding and parental care A horizontal burrow is excavated into a sandy or earthen face, often in colonies. BTO gives four or five eggs, shared incubation around 14–15 days and young leaving at about 19–21 days. Two broods are possible. A stable bank and unobstructed entrance are essential. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds widely in temperate regions and winters farther south. Lebanon has common passage; possible nesting near the Assi remained unconfirmed in the 2020 checklist. Large migrant numbers must not be equated with residence or breeding. Seasonality and observation Lebanese passage extends through February–May and August–November. November falls within the end of autumn passage. Multiple views confirm the breast band; counts must avoid repeatedly counting circling birds. Ecological role and conservation Bank destruction while occupied, polluted water and insect declines are pressures. Stable nesting faces away from hazardous work help. Observe burrows from a distance: standing at entrances prevents parents from provisioning young.
