articles.title: Sayd Arab Radar: 23 Enforcement Operations and More Than 2,700 Birds Freed
articles.body: October 2026 roundup: 57 people apprehended or detained, 399 reported game animals seized, and thousands of metres of illegal hunting nets removed. In news published during October 2026, Sayd recorded 23 enforcement operations involving people in connection with wildlife hunting across six Arab countries, involving 57 people according to the reported figures. In Egypt, Iraq, Algeria and Lebanon, the number of birds freed from captivity or released exceeded 2,707, alongside approximately 200 additional birds in Akkar, Lebanon. Saudi Arabia recorded the largest reported number of seized game animals, with 391 hunted wild animals, while Algeria reported the detention of 22 hunters in four operations in Sidi Bel Abbès, alongside a separate operation in Mila. In Lebanon, the area of bird-catching nets removed in the Bekaa and Akkar totalled 42,390 square metres, after subtracting the area already counted in September. Enforcement operations in 6 Arab countries 23 enforcement operations involving people in connection with wildlife hunting: 11 in Saudi Arabia, 5 in Algeria, 3 in Lebanon, 2 in Morocco, 1 in Oman and 1 in Kuwait involving entry into a reserve with the intent to hunt. 57 people apprehended or detained, according to published figures: 23 in Saudi Arabia, 22 in Algeria, 4 in Lebanon, 3 each in Morocco and Oman, and 2 in Kuwait. The total excludes people whose number was not disclosed in the incident in Mila, Algeria. Seized game animals and weapons 399 game animals with reported counts: 391 in Saudi Arabia, 5 in Morocco and 3 in Oman. Additional game animals were seized in Algeria without a published count. At least 19 weapons: 17 in Saudi Arabia, 1 in Lebanon and 1 in Morocco, alongside unspecified numbers of weapons in Algeria and Akkar. Reported ammunition totalled 2,199 rounds in Saudi Arabia, with unspecified quantities in Algeria. Birds freed from captivity or released More than 2,707 birds in four countries: more than 2,500 in Egypt, 100 in Iraq, 6 in Algeria and 101 in Lebanon, including 100 in the Bekaa and 1 kestrel released after treatment. In addition, approximately 200 birds were freed in Akkar, Lebanon, and an unspecified number were freed in Syria. Nets removed, measured in two different units More than 9,500 metres of nets in Egypt and Syria: 7,000 metres in Egypt’s northern reserves and more than 2,500 metres in Al-Nabk, Syria. These figures relate to campaigns announced during the month, without a common starting date specified for the reporting period. 42,390 square metres in Lebanon, excluding the area already counted in September. Net area and net length are not added together because they use different units of measurement. These totals reflect the published incidents and figures covered by this review, rather than a comprehensive count of all violations across Arab countries. Violation reports remain separate from the number of enforcement operations, including approximately 9 reports filed at the opening of Morocco’s hunting season. Algeria Hunting violations and seizures. An announcement published on 11 October reported the detention of 22 hunters in four operations in Sidi Bel Abbès, with guns, ammunition, partridges and hares seized in undisclosed numbers. The figures were republished on 17 October. On 16 October, a report described a fifth, separate operation at Jebel Hadid in Rouached, Mila Province, involving the detention of a group of people, confiscation of weapons and ammunition, and recovery of game animals, without specifying numbers. Rescue and release. A report published on 15 October described the release of 6 goldfinches previously seized as part of efforts to combat trafficking in protected species in Oran. Video footage bearing the TSA logo also documented the release of 4 Barbary sheep in Moutas Reserve, Tlemcen. Hunting regulation. A report published on 10 October stated that Tlemcen had issued 1,160 hunting licences, with 1,227 trained and qualified hunters and participation by 35 associations. In Mila, a report published on 14 October described the designation of 9 hunting areas and the suspension of hunting in 3 fire-affected areas covering a combined 1,359 hectares. A post attributed to Saïda Province, dated 17 October, reported the opening of the season in Oum El Hadha, in the municipality of Hassasna, and the distribution of hunting documents, without a licence count. Saudi Arabia The combined figures from 11 enforcement operations published between 4 and 29 October were 23 people, 391 hunted wild animals, 17 guns and 2,199 rounds of ammunition. These include the Prince Mohammed bin Salman Reserve incident published on 15 October, involving two people, a European turtle dove, a gun and 74 rounds, and the Medina incident published on 25 October, involving three people and 115 hunted animals. The seizure of 60 animals in King Abdulaziz Reserve was counted only once despite repeated coverage. In breeding news, a report published on 25 October recorded 19 births during the third quarter in Imam Abdulaziz bin Mohammed and King Khalid reserves: 16 sand gazelles, 2 Arabian oryx and 1 Arabian gazelle. Lebanon Violations and seized birds. On 1 October, the Internal Security Forces announced the arrest of one person and seizure of a gun in Hosh Sneid, in an incident dating to 18 September, with 4 captive birds documented in a cage. A report published on 6 October described an Akkar operation in which two people were taken to the police station, one carrying a sparrowhawk in a bag, while two others were tracked to their homes. The operation report referred to two honey buzzards hunted by the latter pair. In the Bekaa campaign announced on 8 October, CABS reported that a man had been arrested for resisting security personnel. Nets and birds freed. The newly counted area totalled 42,390 square metres, comprising 17,640 additional square metres in the Bekaa and 24,750 in Akkar. CABS reported the removal of 290 nets, including 125 in the Bekaa in early October and 165 in northern Lebanon. The Bekaa campaign freed 100 birds, while approximately 200 birds were freed in Akkar. 11 landowners were reported to the authorities, and 4 hunting devices, 3 loudspeakers and a battery were seized. Campaign details were published between 8 and 25 October. Care and release. On 16 October, CABS announced the release of one kestrel after treatment for injuries caused by its eyes being sewn shut so it could be used as bait in a trap. Bird admissions and rehabilitation. The Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds reported receiving 143 birds from 1 September through the date of its post, a reporting period spanning September and October. The latest arrival was a Short-toed Snake Eagle. Birds received by the association are usually injured or require rehabilitation before release. This is a tally of admissions for care, not of birds released, and is not added to the release totals. Mammal rescue. A report published on 30 October described the rescue of one hyena from a trap in Mishmish, Akkar, followed by treatment and its return to its habitat. Egypt Birds freed and nets removed. In a statement published on 25 October, the director-general of the northern region’s reserves reported that more than 2,500 birds had been freed, 7,000 metres of nets removed and 7 sound devices seized. In an interview published on 23 October, the minister of local development and environment announced that more than 2,300 birds had been returned to the wild, as part of a broader account of reserve activities. The two bird totals are not added together because their scope and reporting periods may overlap. Freeing birds from captivity also does not necessarily mean that all are released immediately; veterinary care may precede release. Rescue and care. A report published on 7 October described the rescue of 9 migratory birds in Red Sea reserves, including 6 white storks. A report published on 22 October described veterinary care for one snake eagle in the New Valley. Birds receiving care remain outside the release total. Animal seizures. Animals seized in two possession or transport incidents totalled 38. Reports published on 19 and 28 October respectively described the seizure of 8 monkeys in 10th of Ramadan City and 30 young crocodiles on a train in Assiut. A subsequent press report stated that 3 crocodiles from the same seizure had died. Syria A report published on 9 October described the dismantling and destruction of more than 2,500 metres of nets in Al-Arqoub, Al-Nabk. On 27 October, a report on an enforcement campaign in Al-Nabk and Yabroud described the destruction of more than 500 metres, alongside the freeing of an unspecified number of birds. Both figures are presented because they appeared in different reports, but only the higher published figure is included in the total until it is clear whether the two operations were separate. Qatar A report published on 29 October described the seizure of 112 prohibited bird-attraction devices at various sites in Al Reem Reserve. The figures were republished on 30 October. On 24 October, a report gave a total of 275 animals rescued from January 2025 to the end of August 2026, of which 57 were released and 218 were sheltered. All three figures relate to that same extended reporting period. Morocco A report published on 6 October recorded approximately 9 violation reports at the opening of the hunting season, and an average of 1.91 partridges per hunter. Reports published on 24 and 26 October described two separate operations in Nador Province involving 3 people, with 5 partridges and 1 weapon seized, according to the available counts. Iraq A report published on 25 October described the release of 100 Iraqi white-cheeked bulbuls in Al-Zawraa Park, Baghdad, after their seizure at Al-Ghazl Market. The birds were counted once in the release total. Oman A report published on 4 October described the apprehension of 3 people in an incident involving the hunting of 3 Arabian gazelles in Dhofar Governorate. Kuwait A report published on 16 October described the apprehension of two people who entered Sabah Al-Ahmad Reserve in a vehicle without number plates with the intent to hunt. The measures taken included confiscation of hunting equipment and the vehicle. Palestine A report published on 27 October, and repeated on 30 October, described the completion of a national list comprising 186 bird species, in preparation for completing procedures to protect them from hunting and trade. United Arab Emirates A report published on 30 October described the colour-ringing of 604 birds in Abu Dhabi from January 2025 to mid-October 2026. The total comprised 256 shorebirds, 266 terns and gulls, and 82 ospreys. Somalia An update published on 2 October described care for 4 cheetah cubs previously seized as part of efforts to combat wildlife trafficking in Somaliland. The update covers care provided in July 2026. Tunisia An announcement published on 14 October described a meeting to combat the illegal hunting, capture and trafficking of wild birds, scheduled to bring together 10 partners from 8 Mediterranean countries. The meeting took place from 16 to 18 October; the two figures describe the participation announced beforehand. Coverage and Counting Method This edition covers news published from 1 to 31 October 2026. A publication date does not necessarily mean that the event took place during the same month. Extended reporting periods are therefore stated explicitly, including Qatar’s rescue totals, bird ringing in the UAE, third-quarter births in Saudi reserves and care for cheetah cubs in July. Each incident was counted once when coverage was repeated. Where two totals could overlap, the higher published figure for each measure was used rather than adding them together. Enforcement operations were kept separate from violation reports, and birds receiving care alone were kept separate from birds freed from captivity or released. Incidents already counted in September are excluded from the October total, including the case involving 1,500 goldfinches in Algeria and the previously counted area of nets removed in Lebanon’s Bekaa. Photos: SPA, Sayd, Tout sur l’agriculture en Algérie, TSA, Cairo24, Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency, Oman Environment Authority, Kuwait Ministry of Interior.

articles.title: Sooty Gull
articles.body: Sooty Gull Ichthyaetus hemprichii A dark gull of the region’s seas The Sooty Gull, Ichthyaetus hemprichii, is one of the birds that give the Red Sea and Arabian Sea coasts their distinctive character. Arabic names include al-asḥam, al-askham and al-fāḥim; older references place it in the genus Larus as Larus hemprichii. These names refer to the same species, not to different birds. A member of the gull family, Laridae, it measures about 43–48 cm long, with a wingspan of approximately 105–118 cm. It is a medium-sized coastal gull, rather than one of the large white gulls that arrive conspicuously in winter. The adult has a dark brown head, neck and upper breast, separated from the back by a narrow white collar most evident at the sides of the neck. Its back and wings are dark, while the belly and tail are white. The long, strong bill has a pale base and a red area towards the tip, with dark markings; the feet appear olive. The sexes have similar plumage, so colour alone does not establish whether a bird is male or female. The hood becomes less dark outside the breeding season without turning the bird into a white-headed gull. Recognising different ages White-eyed Gull is the main confusion species in the Red Sea. Identification should therefore combine several features. Sooty Gull is relatively robust, with a clearer contrast between the pale bill base and its coloured tip. Adult White-eyed Gull has a darker bill and more conspicuous white markings around the eye. Sunlight and shade alter the apparent brown of a Sooty Gull’s head, while backlighting can make it look almost black and conceal useful distinctions. A side-by-side comparison, or a photograph showing the head, bill and wing, is more reliable than the overall impression. Juveniles are paler, browner and more patterned. Pale edges to the back and wing feathers create a scaled appearance. The tail carries a dark band, while the adult’s white collar and red bill tip are less evident. This appearance changes gradually through feather replacement, and immature birds may combine features from different stages. Adults and juveniles can occur together in November. Their differences do not necessarily indicate a second species, and a distant photograph is not enough to assign every bird an exact age. Coastal habitat, food and behaviour The Sooty Gull’s life connects breeding islands with shores that provide food. It uses sandy and rocky coasts, reef margins and harbours, resting alongside other gulls in safe places. A bird may forage alone before joining a group where food becomes plentiful. Its presence beside a fishing boat or fish market does not make it wholly dependent on people. Such a place is one part of a wider network of shores, islands and nearby waters. It eats small fish, shrimps, fish remains and carrion, and may steal food from other seabirds or take their eggs and chicks, as well as turtle hatchlings. This is natural dietary diversity, not a reason to treat the gull as a pest to be eliminated. Human disturbance can increase the damage at other birds’ nests: when parents leave eggs exposed, a gull gains an opportunity that did not exist before people approached. Protecting the colony from disturbance addresses that problem more effectively than blaming only the predator that took advantage of it. From nesting to independence The pair nests on the ground on a quiet island, in a shallow scrape sometimes surrounded by a few sticks or fragments of vegetation. The site may be sheltered by a bush or rock, or lie in the open. Birds breed as spaced pairs or in small, loose groups, rather than necessarily forming the dense crowds associated with some terns. The Saudi bird reference gives a usual clutch of two or three eggs and an incubation period of about 25 days, shared by both parents, which also care for the chicks. Chicks leave the nest site shortly after hatching but still need parental food and protection. Walking does not mean independence. The regional references used here do not provide a reliable fixed age at first flight that can be applied throughout the species. Breeding dates also vary. The PERSGA regional report records egg laying in April and May in the northern Saudi Red Sea, later in June and July farther south, and Egyptian nests between July and September. These are recorded patterns, not a timetable binding every island in every year. Arab-world distribution: resident here, passing elsewhere The Red Sea and Gulf of Aden lie at the heart of the species’ range; its presence there is not simply a winter arrival from Europe. References document breeding in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Sudan, Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia. The 2003 PERSGA report brings together evidence from these countries, while Saudi surveys published in 2014 and 2024 confirm the continuing importance of islands for the species. Estimates in older reports must be treated as information from their own period, not converted into a count of populations alive today. In Saudi Arabia it is a breeding resident on Red Sea islands, with birds also appearing in the southern waters of the Arabian Gulf. The United Arab Emirates has direct nesting evidence, including a 2019 study of nest materials on Sir Bu Nair Island. Qatar’s local checklist instead describes it as a scarce passage migrant, not a breeding resident. Oman’s coast also falls within its known range. These differences matter: neighbouring countries cannot automatically be assigned the same breeding status or abundance. What does a November sighting mean? The range covers the northwestern Indian Ocean, extending east towards southern Pakistan and south along East Africa. Some birds stay near their usual areas, while others disperse after breeding; non-breeding movements reach the Tanzanian coast. Its annual life therefore cannot be reduced to a single north-to-south migration. A November sighting on a suitable Arab coast may involve a local or a dispersing bird. Month and colour alone cannot establish the individual’s origin. Autumn offers opportunities to compare ages, feeding behaviour, and the use of harbours and resting places. Observations become more valuable when counts are repeated from the same point and accompanied by notes on sea conditions, tides and observation effort. Absence on one visit does not prove disappearance from that coast. A larger gathering around fishery waste does not demonstrate growth of the breeding population either. Keeping these interpretations separate turns an enjoyable sighting into information that can be compared over time. Conservation and responsible observation AviList 2026 lists Sooty Gull as globally Least Concern, but a favourable global status does not guarantee the safety of an individual colony. Threats include coastal oil pollution, changes to islands and shoreline habitats, egg collection and disturbance. The Sir Bu Nair study documented human-made debris in nest materials. Plastic in a nest shows contact between the island and human activity; by itself, it does not measure pollution throughout the surrounding sea. The best observation is from shore or a boat at a distance that does not cause birds to leave their positions. Visitors should not approach nests, chase juveniles for photographs or offer food to attract a gathering. Precise locations of active nests are better shared with responsible authorities than publicised in ways that increase pressure. The Sooty Gull belongs to a coastal system involving predation, scavenging and the movement of food. Its protection begins with safeguarding that system, rather than merely keeping an attractive photograph. Photo: Tero Linjama / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Spotted Redshank
articles.body: Spotted Redshank Tringa erythropus — from summer black to winter grey Identity and names The Spotted Redshank, Tringa erythropus, is distinct from the Common Redshank, Tringa totanus. Both belong to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. AviList 2026 retains this scientific name. Arabic references use variant forms of “spotted red-legged sandpiper”; attaching the scientific name avoids confusion between local names. Neither spotting nor red legs alone identifies it, because its plumage changes markedly with the season and several other waders have reddish legs. Summer, winter and juvenile plumage Breeding adults become strikingly black, with white spotting above. In winter they turn grey-backed and white below, with a conspicuous white eyebrow. Juveniles have brown, pale-spotted upperparts and more strongly barred underparts; some juvenile markings disappear progressively during autumn. Sexes look alike outside the breeding season, so an ordinary winter photograph should not be sexed. The bill is long and fine, dark with reddish colour at the base of the lower mandible. Legs may appear reddish or very dark depending on plumage and lighting. The bill is not wholly red. Separating it from Common Redshank Compared with Common Redshank it appears more slender, longer-billed and longer-legged, and greyer and paler in winter. A particularly useful flight character is the absence of Common Redshank’s broad white trailing edge to the wing; it still has a white wedge extending through the back and rump. It can mingle with redshanks and greenshanks, so a familiar flock need not contain only one species. A grey November bird should not be rejected merely because it differs from photographs of black spring adults. Food, breeding and migration It uses pools, shallow lakes, mudflats and fresh or brackish water, not only marine shores. Food includes insects and larvae, worms, crustaceans and small fish; birds may swim or tip forward into the water to reach prey. Breeding takes place in northern Eurasian tundra and wetlands near trees, with a ground nest. The male carries most incubation responsibility, and chicks are mobile after hatching: equal parental care should not be assumed for every bird species. Winter distribution extends from parts of Europe and Africa into southern and eastern Asia, requiring safe feeding and resting sites along the journey. Arab distribution and seasonal context Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes scarce passage and rare winter and summer visitation on coasts, islands and wetlands. Its 2020 checklist placed passage mainly in March–April and late July–September; the newer guide takes precedence for current status without implying winter abundance. Kuwait records scarce passage and winter presence; Oman lists it as common in both seasons. Documented winter range includes Egypt, southern Iraq and Yemen, and historical counts confirm winter presence in Morocco and Libya. A November profile therefore suits Arab winter wetlands, while abundance must remain locally qualified. Country presence does not imply occurrence everywhere, and old surveys cannot establish unchanged present-day numbers. Conservation and observation Its global status is Least Concern. Wetland integrity, water quality and prey availability remain essential, threatened by drainage, reclamation, pollution and disturbance. Observe far enough away for feeding to continue, and record date, location and plumage without publicising sensitive sites where this would increase pressure. Global status does not decide hunting legality, and a single sighting cannot establish a change in migration routes without comparable observations over time. articles.title: 80,000 Visitors and 158 Exhibitors from 15 Countries… Suhail 2026 Closes a Decade of Passion for Hunting and Falconry
articles.body: Doha — Sayd See the Suhail 2026 photo album: falcons, visitors, and faces of the fair → The Katara International Hunting and Falcons Exhibition “Suhail 2026” concluded its tenth edition in Doha after five days that saw attendance exceeding 80,000 visitors and broad participation by specialized companies and entities, completing the exhibition’s first decade as it has become one of the region’s foremost appointments for hunting, falconry, maqnas (desert hunting trips), and overland travel enthusiasts. This year’s edition ran from 8 to 12 September under the slogan “A Decade of Passion and Heritage.” At its opening, the exhibitor list comprised 158 entities and companies from 15 countries, spanning fields from falcons and their equipment and hunting gear to camping, vehicle outfitting, modern technologies, and logistics services. Suhail’s identity is no longer limited to being a fair for selling hunting supplies. The tenth edition showcased more than 20 innovations and inventions related to hunting, shooting, and travel—an indicator of a specialized market in which modern technologies intersect with heritage practices. Falcons at the heart of the event The Suhail falcons auction remained one of the fair’s biggest draws for the public and falconers, with a selection of distinctive and rare falcons on offer and competition to acquire them. Mohammed bin Abdulatif Al-Misnad, vice-chair of the organizing supreme committee, described the auction as one of Suhail’s most prominent activities, and noted that this year’s edition coincided with the start of a new season for falconry and maqnas. Falcons topped the interest of visitors to Suhail 2026 and its specialized auction. Source: QNA The exhibition halls presented a broad picture of contemporary hunting: falcons and training and care equipment; gear for trips and outdoor camps (kashtat); vehicle fittings; products for hunters and falconers; and traditional crafts and arts inspired by the desert and hunting. At the same time, the environmental dimension appeared in a number of participations and experiences, including sustainable hunting, alongside entities such as the Department of Antiquities at Qatar Museums, which used the presence of desert-goers to raise awareness about protecting archaeological sites while practicing outdoor hobbies. From hobby to a specialized market Suhail’s figures point to the expansion of the economy surrounding hunting and falconry in the region. Exhibition director Abdulaziz Al-Bu Hashem Al-Sayed spoke of strong purchasing activity in the halls, considering that the goal is no longer merely to hold a commercial fair, but to consolidate a specialized gathering that brings together hobbyists, companies, and interested parties from different countries. A scene from falcon activities at Suhail 2026. Source: QNA This expansion is also visible in the nature of the participants themselves. Alongside specialized companies, institutions offering shipping and storage services took part—including Qatar Post—while the fair included vehicle-outfitting and camping sectors and services linked to falcons and hunting. The edition also enjoyed support from the “Daem” fund for the ninth consecutive year. At the close of the exhibition, DTS won the Best Stand award, while the Best Garage award went to “Al-Muharrik Al-Sahrawi” (The Desert Engine), alongside specialized competitions in making falcon hoods (baraqi‘) and other elements tied to falconry culture. Media as a partner in Suhail At the close of the edition, Malaka Mohammed Al-Shreem, member and secretary of the organizing supreme committee, stressed the importance of local, Arab, and international media in conveying the image of the exhibition, and considered the media a strategic partner in strengthening Suhail’s presence and introducing Qatari heritage worldwide. After ten editions, the road appears open to a new stage for the fair. The supreme committee has already begun thinking about the next edition, with a drive to keep developing the event and consolidating its place as an international gathering for falconers, hunting and maqnas enthusiasts, and specialized companies. Thus Suhail 2026 closes its first decade—but the figures and the breadth seen this year suggest that the first ten years may be only the beginning. Source: Qatar News Agency (QNA).

articles.title: Syria’s Helice shooting champions crowned in Saydnaya

articles.title: Temminck’s Lark
articles.body: Temminck’s Lark Eremophila bilopha Feather horns above the desert floor Temminck’s Lark, Eremophila bilopha, is a small member of the lark family, measuring about 13–15 centimetres in length. Its black-and-white face and two raised feather tufts on the head nevertheless make a strong impression. These tufts are neither true horns nor external ears. The striking markings contrast with sandy upperparts that blend into the ground, making the bird easier to identify when it raises its head than when it bends down to search for food. Its Arabic names include the desert horned lark and horned lark. The scientific name distinguishes this species from other horned larks, especially mountain birds that may show similar facial patterns. Membership of the genus Eremophila does not mean that all its species occupy the same habitat. This lark is associated particularly with dry plains in North Africa, the Levant and the northern Arabian Peninsula, rather than the high snowy peaks associated with some of its relatives. Plumage, age and possible confusion The adult has a black mask and a broad black patch on the upper breast, separated by white areas on the face and throat. The male usually looks more strongly contrasting, with more conspicuous feather tufts, while the female has more subdued head markings. However, the position of the feathers and the light both affect appearance. A lark can lower its tufts until they are difficult to see in a photograph, so their absence in a single image is not enough to rule out the species. The juvenile initially lacks the adult’s complete facial pattern, and its upperparts look spotted or edged with pale fringes. Someone looking only for the “horns” may therefore confuse it with other small desert larks. Body shape, bill, tail pattern, face and habitat should be considered together. Sandy coloration alone cannot establish a subspecies or an exact age: lighting, dust and feather wear make colour shades less consistent than an ideal field-guide photograph might suggest. What kind of desert does it need? Its typical habitat is open, level ground with a firm or gravelly surface, scattered stones, grasses and widely spaced low shrubs. Bare sand dunes or steep rocky slopes are not equivalent substitutes for this habitat. In North Africa it is also associated with dry steppe and plateaux supporting drought-tolerant plants. In Saudi Arabia, the national reference describes stony and sandy plains with scattered rocks and sparse vegetation, particularly in the north. It moves over the ground by walking and making short runs, and can seem to disappear simply by standing still among stones. Failure to see it during a quick visit does not establish that it is absent. Scanning quiet areas with binoculars is more useful than driving aimlessly across them. Describing its habitat is not intended to reveal a nest site, but to explain that deserts contain different environments. Protecting an area of dunes does not automatically compensate for the loss of a gravel plain where this lark feeds and breeds. Food and movement outside the breeding season It picks up seeds from the ground and low plants, supplementing them with insects and occasionally fruit. Food availability is connected to small plants that may seem unimportant to a visitor: they produce seeds, support invertebrates and protect parts of the ground surface. Feeding locations may change after rain or as vegetation dries out. Nevertheless, seeing a bird near a green plant does not by itself prove that it is eating that particular plant. Groups may be seen outside the nesting season, whereas pairs and territories become more apparent during breeding. The species is primarily resident but capable of wandering; residency does not mean remaining within a few metres throughout the year. The Saudi reference mentions possible southward movement in winter. In November, observing these movements and gatherings can be useful, without assuming that every new arrival has made a long migration from another continent or that a large count on one day represents the national population. Courtship and the ground nest The male performs a short aerial display accompanied by song, alongside behaviour on the ground. Pairs establish territories during the breeding season. The starting date varies between regions: references generally place the season between late winter and spring, with variation linked to rainfall and local conditions. The arrival of a particular month is not enough to conclude that all birds in Morocco, Jordan and Saudi Arabia are breeding simultaneously, and song alone does not demonstrate the presence of eggs. The nest is a small depression in the ground, lined with grasses, roots and soft material, often sheltered by a low stone or a plant. A row of pebbles or soil may lie along its exposed side. The Saudi reference describes the female as doing most of the construction and probably most of the incubation, with both parents caring for the young. “Probably” should not be replaced with excessive certainty: distinguishing the sexes’ roles requires repeated observations rather than a single visit near a nest. Eggs and chicks: more than the day of first flight The Saudi reference gives a clutch of two to three eggs, while general references describe a broader range extending to four. Incubation lasts about 13–14 days. The same Saudi source describes chicks leaving the nest at around ten to eleven days, remaining hidden nearby, and then becoming capable of flight at about 15–16 days. These are approximate reference values, not fixed timetables for every nest in the Arab region. Newly hatched chicks need warmth, food and care, and do not become independent simply by leaving the depression. The site therefore remains sensitive after the nest appears empty. Opening vehicle tracks or searching for chicks to photograph may separate them or expose them to heat and predation. Responsible behaviour means moving away when an adult carrying food delays approaching its young, and not touching or relocating a chick simply because it is on the ground. That position is a normal part of its development. Distribution across Arab countries The African range extends from Mauritania through suitable desert and semi-desert environments in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya to Egypt. Its occurrence within each country varies with the terrain, rainfall and vegetation; this broad range does not mean that it occupies the entire Sahara. These countries form a core part of the range of a species with year-round Arab connections, rather than necessarily hosting a European visitor that passes through for a few days and disappears. In the Levant and adjoining areas, the regional review describes resident occurrence in Jordan, southern Syria and western and southern parts of Iraq. In Saudi Arabia it is a resident breeding lark of the northern plains, and may extend southward in some years. Kuwaiti references establish breeding together with uncommon wandering occurrence in autumn, winter and spring. Regional residency is therefore compatible with changing numbers of sightings at a particular Kuwaiti site from one season to another. The Saudi pattern should not be extended to every Gulf country. The regional reference records vagrant occurrence in the United Arab Emirates; a vagrant is neither a breeding resident nor a winter visitor guaranteed to arrive. Observations should preserve this distinction between inclusion on a national list and the nature of the species’ occurrence. Similarly, a desert photograph from one Arab country does not automatically document another, however similar the sand and stones may look. Conservation and a quiet visit AviList 2026 lists the species globally as Least Concern, or LC. This does not mean that its habitats are unaffected: land levelling, road expansion, off-road driving and deteriorating vegetation may alter the plains on which the birds depend. Older population estimates remain dated estimates, not a live census that can establish the condition of every local population or its rate of change. Good observation starts with choosing an existing route and stopping far enough away for the bird to continue its behaviour. Visitors should not approach repeatedly until it flies, provide food to lure it into a photograph, or publish the coordinates of an active nest. Record the number, time and habitat, and identify uncertain birds as such rather than turning every sandy lark into this species. Protecting the desert includes small details, from a seed-producing plant to a motionless chick between two pebbles. Photo: Justin Philbois / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: The awsaj thornbush: reading the land, and the wild’s old pharmacy under the spines
articles.body: Dense green Arabian boxthorn (Lycium shawii) in the Negev.Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. A knowing hunter does not walk the open country blind, waiting for a bird to pass by chance. He reads the scrub, feels the soil, and often senses where game may drop before he sees it. In our Arabian deserts and wadis, few shrubs tell the place as clearly as awsaj (Lycium shawii). You find it in the belly of a shuʿayb — tangled, sharp with thorns — a small fortress against summer drought, waiting for the first hint of rain. A migrant’s inn and fuel stop A green, living awsaj in bare ground is a meaningful drop point. A tired migrant — a small warbler-type dukhaykhla, a shrike, or a dove that has flown hundreds of kilometres — finds here what many other bushes lack: Cover: The woven spines shelter small birds from many raptors, including peregrines, and make it harder for ground predators such as foxes to push into the heart of the shrub. Inside, small birds rest and roost. Energy fruit (“wolf grapes”): Small round red berries, known locally as ʿinab al-dhiʾb or awsaj berries, offer moisture and natural sugars a spent bird can use before the next leg. That is why many hunters sweep awsaj first at dawn for a flicker of feathers deep inside. Red berry of Arabian boxthorn (Lycium shawii) on a leafy branch, Aqaba.Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. From the folk field pharmacy Elders did not pass awsaj lightly; it belongs to long-standing Arabian folk medicine. What follows is heritage as told in the field, not modern medical advice, and it does not replace clean water, proper dressings, or care when needed: Cuts and scratches: Folk telling has it that if someone took a nick from sharp stone or thorn and feared contamination, they would take a handful of tender awsaj leaves, rub and crush them between two clean stones, and set the juice as a dressing straight on the wound. The astringents in the leaves, the story goes, stop light bleeding and act as a natural disinfectant against infection. Sand in the eyes: It is told that in sudden sandstorms the Bedouin used to boil awsaj leaves in a little clean water, leave it to cool fully, then use it as a wash for irritated eyes — to cool them and clear sand grains. Camp stomach upset: Folk accounts also say that for a sudden camp cramp, or after drinking water that sat badly, boiling a few awsaj leaves and sipping the bitter water slowly works as a natural soother and anti-spasmodic. Nature is not an enemy to defy, but an open book; those who learn the language of its shrubs lose their way less often.

articles.title: Water Rail
articles.body: Water Rail Rallus aquaticus Identity and identification Water Rail Rallus aquaticus belongs to Rallidae. Adult plumage combines a long reddish bill, grey face and breast, and black-and-white barred flanks. Its narrow body passes through reeds; the long bill helps separate it from many shorter-billed crakes. Habitat and food It picks invertebrates from mud and water margins and also eats plant material. Dense wetland vegetation usually conceals it, so calls may reveal a bird that remains unseen. Breeding and development The vegetation nest is hidden close to water. BTO gives a typical clutch of 6–11 eggs and incubation of 19–22 days. Downy chicks become mobile early: leaving the nest site is distinct from being able to fly or becoming independent. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes common passage and winter presence from early September to early May, with scarce summer breeding. Qatar’s current list describes a rare winter visitor and passage migrant. November therefore suits observation in both countries, with different abundance and status; these descriptions do not establish the same status throughout the Arab world. Observation and conservation Retaining reeds, suitable water levels and clean margins protects habitat. Watch from a distance without entering cover or using playback near potentially breeding birds. articles.title: Western House Martin
articles.body: Western House Martin Delichon urbicum Identity and identification Western House Martin Delichon urbicum, also called Common House Martin, belongs to Hirundinidae. Glossy dark upperparts contrast with a white belly and diagnostic white rump above the tail. Its forked tail is shorter than Barn Swallow’s. Martins are not swifts: the latter belong to another family and have more strongly sickle-shaped wings. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It catches flying insects over farmland, water and settlements, using open feeding areas near nest sites. Mixed flocks with other swallows occur. Water and mud are necessary for construction, while airborne food varies with weather. Breeding and parental care A nearly enclosed mud nest with a small entrance is built beneath an eave or overhang. BTO gives four or five eggs, shared incubation for 13–19 days and young leaving after about 19–25 days. Two broods are possible. Weather and food affect these reference durations; they are not a fixed local calendar. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds in parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia and migrates to Africa. In Lebanon it is a migrant breeder and passage migrant around suitable buildings and cliffs. Old winter mud nests do not show that their occupants remain present. Seasonality and observation Lebanon’s checklist places breeding from March to mid-July and passage in February–May and September–early November. Early November can catch late passage. White rump and nest structure aid documentation without disturbing colonies. Ecological role and conservation It consumes aerial insects and is affected by insect declines and nest removal during building work. Scheduling repairs outside nest occupation and maintaining access help. Nest boxes cannot replace lost feeding habitats or counter extensive pesticide use. articles.title: Western Yellow Wagtail
articles.body: Western Yellow Wagtail Motacilla flava — Identification, habitats, breeding and seasonal occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Western Yellow Wagtail, Motacilla flava, is a slender member of the family Motacillidae, with dark legs and a habit of walking or running on the ground while moving its tail. Many adults combine yellow underparts with greenish upperparts, but head colour varies among subspecies: not every male has a blue head. Modern taxonomy separates the Eastern Yellow Wagtail, Motacilla tschutschensis. Scientific names also help resolve regional names shared by different wagtails. Age and similar species Females and young birds are generally duller than males, but subspecific variation makes identification more complex. Qatar’s field account notes that some first-autumn beema may have almost no yellow below and look grey above. Absence of yellow alone therefore does not exclude a Yellow Wagtail. Immatures can be confused with Eastern Yellow or Citrine Wagtails; head, wing and tail patterns, calls when available, locality and date should be considered together. Reliable assignment of subspecies or sex requires clear views of several features. Habitat, food and behaviour Wet grassland, farmland, marsh edges, river margins and irrigation channels provide feeding habitat. The birds search for insects and other small invertebrates on the ground and among low vegetation. They may accompany livestock or take prey disturbed by animals. Irrigated fields can provide important migratory feeding stops, but a bird on a farm is not necessarily nesting there. Habitat use differs between breeding, passage and winter: a site offering a day’s food and rest may not provide the cover and water required throughout nesting. Breeding and life cycle The small cup nest is on the ground, concealed in vegetation. The female undertakes most building and incubation, while both parents feed the young. British records typically indicate five or six eggs, one or two broods, approximately fourteen days of incubation and departure of young at around 13–15 days. These are British reference values; timing varies by region. Ground nests require suitable cover; a change in field management during nesting may remove it even while the field still looks green to an observer. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Yellow Wagtail occurrence in the Arab region includes residence, breeding, passage and wintering. Egypt supports resident pygmaea associated with the Nile Valley and Delta; breeding iberiae also occur in North Africa. Jordan’s list combines limited breeding with common passage. Lebanese references document autumn passage, particularly September and October, and limited summer breeding nationally. Arabian records include passage and wintering in some areas, varying by locality and subspecies. Wet fields receive passage birds during autumn migration, while the Nile population remains resident year-round. Ecology and conservation The wagtail links invertebrate abundance to birds in farmland and wetland food webs and is itself prey for predators. The 2019 IUCN assessment lists Least Concern. Its British Red List status reflects a separate national situation, not automatic global threatened status. Loss of wet grassland, agricultural intensification and reduced prey can create pressures. Retaining wet margins, vegetation cover and insect food supports residents and passage birds while recognizing their different seasonal needs. articles.title: White-crowned Wheatear
articles.body: White-crowned Wheatear Oenanthe leucopyga A rock-dwelling bird without an invariably white crown White-crowned Wheatear, Oenanthe leucopyga, is among the most striking birds of rocky deserts. Many adults combine a dark body with a white crown, while the pale rump and tail flash as the bird moves. Arabic names include “white-crowned” and “white-capped”, with local names such as Umm Ghunayman in Saudi Arabia. It belongs to the flycatcher family Muscicapidae and measures about 17–19 cm. Despite a superficial resemblance, it is not Black Wheatear, Oenanthe leucura. The name alone can mislead an observer. Young birds and birds in their first year have black heads, and some older individuals retain a dark crown. Absence of white therefore does not exclude this species, and a black head alone cannot establish an exact age. The sexes are broadly similar, and an ordinary photograph does not always permit reliable sexing. These distinctions matter in November, when birds of different ages may be encountered in the same habitat. The tail is more useful than the crown in difficult cases Black extends down the underparts towards the area between the legs, while the lower belly and undertail remain white. The tail is largely white, with substantial black on the central feathers, but normally lacks the continuous black terminal band characteristic of Black Wheatear. Young birds can have limited dark tips on outer feathers: “an entirely white tail” is therefore an unsafe shortcut. Watching the tail spread as a bird settles is particularly useful. Male Hooded Wheatear, Oenanthe monacha, shares the contrasting colours and a similar tail pattern, but its white belly reaches much farther up the underparts; White-crowned retains a broader black lower body. Lighting can also make glossy plumage look dull in photographs. Reliable identification combines the extent of black, structure, tail pattern and possible age, rather than relying on head colour alone. A broad but discontinuous Arab desert range Its range crosses rocky parts of North Africa towards Sinai, the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula. Morocco, Mauritania, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt form part of this extensive desert setting, with an African extension towards Sudan. Suitable areas are nevertheless fragmented. Mountains, wadis and buildings may offer conditions absent from open sand seas. Density varies between regions, so a coloured area on a distribution map does not mean that every part of that desert is occupied. Saudi regional references describe a widespread breeding resident in western areas and parts of the central plains, the Tuwaiq escarpment and the edge of the Summan. Jordan BirdWatch also lists it as resident in Jordan. It is resident in parts of Palestine and Sinai as well. A record in a neighbouring country is a different matter: these established populations should not be extended by assumption to every Gulf state, nor should an unusual sighting near the range boundary be converted into a permanent breeding population. Residency and autumn movement The species is primarily resident, with some local or short-distance movements, including in winter. It can therefore be seen in November in its usual rocky habitat without the sighting indicating the arrival of a European migrant. Not every individual follows an identical calendar. Residency means that the species remains in a region, not that each bird stays on the same rock throughout its life. Demonstrating individual movements requires ringing or sustained tracking, rather than simply comparing counts on two visits. A paper published in Sandgrouse in 2019 describes some records outside the main range, including rare occurrences in Iran and elsewhere in the region. These help explain the possibility of dispersal, but do not establish a permanent range expansion. When a bird appears in an unusual place, clear photographs, the date and a description of habitat matter more than an immediate declaration of residency. Breeding needs independent evidence, such as food carried to young or chicks actually observed. Harsh habitat and varied food White-crowned Wheatear favours stony slopes, cliffs, dry wadis, lava fields and arid areas with crevices. It may use old walls or the edges of villages and oases where buildings imitate rock cavities and provide hunting perches. It is not a sand-dune specialist, and a place labelled “desert” is not automatically suitable. The fine structure of the habitat, from a raised stone to a shaded crack and an open patch, shapes opportunities to feed and shelter. It watches the ground from a perch before dropping onto prey, also searching by walking and hopping, and sometimes taking an insect in flight. Food includes beetles, ants, flies, spiders and other invertebrates, alongside fruit, seeds and occasionally small reptiles, depending on availability. Such flexibility does not make human food necessary. Keeping the surroundings natural is more helpful than leaving scraps beside a road or campsite, where birds may be drawn towards vehicles or become more accessible to cats. Nests and eggs: using available crevices Pairs nest in rock cavities, beneath large stones or within old walls. The cup is built from plant material and lined with hair, wool and feathers. Small stones may be placed around the entrance or along the approach. This is a recognised wheatear behaviour, but does not justify opening a cavity or moving its stones to check for eggs. The arrangement belongs to the bird's nesting activity and may be in use even when the site seems quiet. References describe breeding concentrated mainly between late winter and spring, with timing varying by region and conditions. The Saudi account gives clutches of 3–4 eggs and incubation of about 14–15 days, while accounts covering the broader range allow for 3–5 eggs. The female builds and incubates, and both parents care for the young. These differences show why neither one number nor a particular month should become a rigid rule for every Arab desert. From hatching to independence After hatching, chicks require food and protection inside the cavity. The Saudi account gives a nestling period of about 14–16 days, with the possibility of two broods in a season. Leaving the nest does not mean instant independence, since parental care continues afterwards. Black-headed birds in their first year can also breed. This provides another reason not to equate a dark crown with a recently fledged youngster that has not reached breeding age. Success depends on food resources being available when chicks need them. A wadi that has received rain may offer different conditions from a dry neighbouring site, although rain alone cannot establish that a nest is present. Young birds may disperse after the breeding season, while rocky habitats and shelters remain valuable throughout the year. Protecting crevices and walls therefore concerns more than the days when eggs are present: it also preserves resting places and future nesting opportunities. Habitat protection and undisturbed watching AviList v2026 records the species as globally Least Concern, LC, but that assessment does not measure the condition of each desert wadi or village. Removing rocks, filling cracks, demolishing an occupied wall and driving indiscriminately off established tracks can alter a small but important local resource. Building restoration or tourism development should take account of wildlife use, rather than assume an arid setting is empty of life. Watch from a distance and allow the bird to continue feeding. Stop approaching if it repeatedly alarms or moves away each time. Playback and bait are unnecessary for a photograph. Document unusual sightings through the tail pattern, the extent of black and behaviour, rather than a crown photograph alone. Residency in a country does not imply permission to hunt: local regulations and the protection of breeding sites are separate matters from scientific classification. articles.title: White-headed Duck
articles.body: White-headed Duck Oxyura leucocephala A diving duck with a distinctive profile White-headed Duck Oxyura leucocephala is a small, heavy-headed member of the stiff-tailed ducks. About 43–48 cm long, it sits low in the water, often with its narrow tail raised. The adult breeding male combines a white face and head with a dark crown, brown body and striking blue bill. The swollen base of that bill gives the profile particular character; identification should consider its shape as well as colour. Females are grey-brown with pale cheeks crossed by a dark stripe and a grey bill. Young birds resemble females, so a brown-headed individual is not necessarily an adult female. Introduced Ruddy Duck is an important comparison because it can hybridise with this species. Suspected hybrids need expert assessment: an unusual head pattern or intermediate bill is a reason to obtain photographs, not to force an identification from one feature. Wetland structure and feeding This is a bird of lakes and marshes rather than open coastal seas. It uses natural and artificial waterbodies, including somewhat saline waters, but breeding sites need substantial emergent vegetation. Reeds and bulrushes provide concealment, while open water allows feeding and escape. A wetland can therefore lose breeding value when its vegetation is stripped even if its surface area appears unchanged. Food is obtained by diving and includes aquatic invertebrates, notably insect larvae, together with seeds and other plant material. Water depth, underwater vegetation and food availability all influence which parts of a lake are used. Protecting the species involves the functioning aquatic habitat, not simply preserving a patch of water on a map. Excessive nutrient loading and introduced fish can alter that habitat and its food resources. Courtship, nesting and young Breeding males display and compete for access to females. The nest is concealed in waterside or emergent vegetation and formed from plant material. The female incubates and tends the brood. Published breeding ranges differ between accounts and populations; SEO/BirdLife describes clutches of 5–10 eggs, incubation of 25–26 days and young capable of flight at 60–70 days. Ducklings can swim and dive soon after hatching and obtain their own food while accompanied by the female. Maintaining water through this growing period is crucial. A lake that fills in spring but dries while broods remain flightless may attract nesting birds without allowing successful recruitment. A fragmented range and different movements The distribution extends discontinuously from Spain and North Africa through the eastern Mediterranean into central Asia. The international action plan distinguishes western Mediterranean, North African, eastern and south Asian populations. Western groups include resident birds, whereas substantial eastern populations migrate between breeding, moulting and wintering sites. Local dispersal can also follow changing rainfall and wetland conditions. Large moulting concentrations are known at sites including the Sudochie wetlands in Uzbekistan and Lake Tengiz in Kazakhstan. The 2018 plan describes departures from eastern breeding localities beginning in late August and continuing into autumn, with substantial passage through the Amu Darya delta. Western birds need not undertake these long journeys, but can disperse between wetlands as conditions change. The degree of exchange between the western Mediterranean and North African populations remains uncertain. Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia Morocco supports breeding, wintering and passage occurrence. Maire and colleagues documented breeding at Dar Bouazza, west of Casablanca, in 2025: young were photographed in June after spring courtship. The report places the site within a wider recovery of Moroccan occurrence following its return in the early 2000s. Algeria also supports breeding and wintering populations. A study published in 2026 describes a pair with five ducklings at the Mekrenaz reservoir in Tiaret on 18 May 2020, presenting it as the first confirmed breeding record in western Algeria. Tunisia is likewise listed for breeding, staging and wintering in the 2018 international plan. The eastern Arab range Syria is included for breeding, staging and wintering in the 2018 action plan, whose breeding estimates refer to 2011–2012. That dated evidence establishes its importance, but is not a current census of Syrian wetlands. For Iraq, Salim and colleagues’ 2012 national checklist describes a rare or uncommon winter visitor to the central and southern marshes. The 2018 action plan nevertheless identifies Iraq as a survey priority because information remains insufficient to assess its wider importance for the species. Egypt's 2019 EORC checklist includes White-headed Duck in Category A, meaning accepted wild occurrence after 1950. That classification alone supplies neither a regular wintering season nor evidence of breeding. Distinguishing a verified occurrence from a population's seasonal role is especially important near the edges of this fragmented range. Conservation and considerate observation Drainage, water abstraction, drought, pollution and disturbance can undermine breeding and wintering habitat. Hybridisation with introduced Ruddy Duck is an additional, distinctive concern; habitat restoration alone does not resolve it. International conservation work consequently combines wetland management, monitoring and control of the invasive species by competent authorities. Observe from established viewpoints with a telescope, avoiding repeated approaches that drive birds from cover. Do not enter reedbeds to search for nests or separate a female from her brood. Useful records include the date, site, number, sex or age where reliable, and evidence distinguishing feeding, courtship and breeding. Photographs of suspected Ruddy Ducks or hybrids should be sent to the appropriate ornithological or conservation body for assessment. articles.title: White-spectacled Bulbul
articles.body: White-spectacled Bulbul Pycnonotus xanthopygos Identity and identification White-spectacled Bulbul Pycnonotus xanthopygos belongs to Pycnonotidae. A black head and conspicuous white eye-ring accompany a grey-brown body and yellow undertail. The eye-ring differs from White-eared Bulbul’s large white cheek patch: these are distinct species. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Gardens, orchards, scrub and open woodland near people provide habitat. It eats fruit and insects, visiting fruiting trees in pairs or small groups. Calls are strong and varied. Native plants fruiting at different times sustain food through the season. Breeding and parental care A cup nest of fibres and plant material is placed in a shrub or tree. Both parents feed young; clutch and developmental measurements vary among study sites. Vegetation cover and nest position matter. Garden trees should not be penetrated to watch chicks at close range. Range and Arab occurrence It is associated with the eastern Mediterranean and parts of Arabia. Lebanon’s updated checklist describes a widespread breeding resident from the coast to moderate elevations. A shared bulbul name does not give the three species identical ranges or field marks. Seasonality and observation Residents can be followed in November around fruit and tree cover. Document the eye-ring, yellow undertail and location; frontal photographs may conceal the yellow area. Ecological role and conservation Fruit feeding contributes to dispersal of some seeds, while insects are also consumed. Scrub removal, simplified gardens and pesticides reduce food and nests. Diverse native planting and dense cover provide more suitable resources than indiscriminate human scraps.
